Advanced Kotlin/JVM for Senior Androidexpand / collapse

Senior mental model#

Senior-level reasoning keeps three contracts visible at once: Kotlin source type system → JVM ABI/bytecode → Android DEX/ART execution. A construct can be safe in Kotlin source yet erased, boxed, or awkward for Java; compiler, R8, and ART optimisations may change representation without changing the observable contract.

Causal map: API ownership and variance → generated JVM signature and metadata → boxing/captures/dispatch → D8/R8 and ART → compatibility for already compiled consumers. Design the contract first, then inspect the artifact and measure the hot path.

Stage 2 already covers nullability/platform boundaries and state modelling. This stage does not repeat them; it focuses on lowering, interoperability, and library evolution.

Internals: from the type system to ART#

Generics, variance, and projections#

Generic declarations are invariant by default. out T permits producer positions and covariance; in T permits consumer positions and contravariance. A use-site projection restricts one view: MutableList<out Animal> can safely be read as Animal but cannot accept an arbitrary Animal; MutableList<in Dog> accepts a Dog, but reads as Any?. * is a safely unknown argument interpreted according to declaration variance, not an alias for Any?.

interface Codec<in Wire, out Domain> {
    fun decode(value: Wire): Domain
}
fun copyDogs(from: List<out Dog>, to: MutableList<in Dog>) =
    from.forEach(to::add)

fun inspectUnknown(values: MutableList<*>) {
    val first: Any? = values.firstOrNull()
    // values.add(Dog()) // forbidden: the actual element type is unknown
}

On the JVM, type arguments are mostly erased: runtime normally sees a raw class, bridge methods or casts, and Kotlin metadata, not a fully checkable List<Dog>. @JvmSuppressWildcards/@JvmWildcard tune Java signatures, but they are API/ABI choices rather than a way to disable type safety.

inline, noinline, crossinline, and reified: exact boundaries#

  • inline asks the compiler to copy the body and inlinable lambdas into the call site. This can remove a function-object allocation and virtual call at that site, but increases bytecode and does not guarantee that the complete toolchain creates no allocations.
  • noinline keeps a selected lambda parameter as an object: it can be stored, returned, or passed to a non-inline context; a non-local return from it is forbidden.
  • A regular inlined lambda can perform a non-local return from its enclosing function when the invocation structure permits it. crossinline forbids that return when the implementation may invoke the lambda indirectly, for example inside a Runnable. It is not a thread-safety or asynchronous-execution guarantee.
  • reified T is allowed only for a type parameter of an inline function or property accessor. It enables operations such as is T, as T, and T::class for a runtime-available type at the call site. It does not restore erased nested arguments: value is List<String> cannot prove every element is a string.
inline fun <reified T : Parcelable> Bundle.requireParcelableCompat(key: String): T {
    val value = BundleCompat.getParcelable(this, key, T::class.java) // typed API on 34+, deprecated below
    return value ?: error("$key is missing or not ${T::class.java.name}")
}

inline fun dispatch(
    crossinline onUi: () -> Unit,
    noinline onFailure: (Throwable) -> Unit,
) {
    executor.execute { runCatching(onUi).onFailure(onFailure) }
}

A public or protected inline API effectively embeds implementation into its consumer. It cannot freely access non-public declarations; @PublishedApi internal makes a helper available to generated ABI and therefore adds a compatibility obligation. Consumers must be recompiled to receive a changed inline body at an old call site.

Delegation and delegated properties#

Class delegation such as class LoggingStore(private val base: Store) : Store by base generates forwarding for interface members and provides composition without inheritance boilerplate. An override in the wrapper intercepts external dispatch, but a call that the delegate makes to one of its own members is not magically redirected to the wrapper override.

Delegated-property lowering uses getValue(thisRef, KProperty) and, for a var, setValue. The compiler normally stores the delegate in a synthetic field such as prop$delegate, although documented optimised cases can omit it. Built-ins such as lazy, observable/vetoable, map-backed properties, and property-to-property delegation have different lifetime, synchronisation, and failure contracts.

class FragmentBinding<T : ViewBinding>(
    private val bind: (View) -> T,
) : ReadOnlyProperty<Fragment, T> {
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Fragment, property: KProperty<*>): T =
        bind(thisRef.requireView())
}
// Convenient, but this implementation recreates a binding on every access.
// A caching delegate must clear the cached view at onDestroyView().

A delegate does not prove lifecycle correctness. Review its owner, cleanup moment, exception semantics, synchronisation mode, and whether property access hides expensive work.

JVM erasure, boxing, and value-class ABI#

Because of erasure, overloads that differ only by a generic argument can have the same JVM descriptor; an unchecked cast can compile and fail later at element access. Kotlin primitives map to JVM primitives where possible, but nullable, generic, interface, or Any contexts often require wrappers and boxing. Inspect generated signatures with javap or a bytecode viewer, and inspect allocations with a profiler or benchmark rather than intuition.

An @JvmInline value class has one underlying value and may compile to an unboxed representation, but generic, nullable, and interface uses require boxing. Functions with value-class parameters are name-mangled by default to avoid clashes, so the Java/reflection surface is not identical to the Kotlin surface. For an SDK, create an intentional Java-friendly bridge using the underlying JVM type and a stable @JvmName instead of promising transparent interoperability.

@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: String)
fun find(id: UserId): User = TODO()          // mangled JVM name
@JvmName("findByUserId")
fun findForJava(raw: String): User = find(UserId(raw))

fun <T> identity(value: T): T = value
val boxed = identity(UserId("42"))           // generic representation can box

SAM, default methods, annotations, platform types, and lambdas#

Kotlin performs SAM conversion for Java functional interfaces and Kotlin fun interfaces. A function type (T) -> R and a concrete SAM are not the same ABI; a named fun interface is often a better Java-facing callback API. JVM mode, target, and consumer toolchain matter for default interface methods; do not change the -jvm-default strategy of a published library without ABI analysis.

@JvmName, @JvmStatic, @JvmField, @JvmOverloads, wildcard annotations, and use-site targets such as @get:, @field:, and @param: control the generated Java surface. @JvmOverloads creates overloads by removing trailing default parameters in order; Kotlin default and named arguments do not automatically become Java semantics.

Java nullability annotations improve Kotlin's type view, while unannotated or insufficiently annotated APIs produce platform types. As explained in Stage 2, a boundary should immediately choose an explicit nullable/non-null contract and validate untrusted input; an annotation is not runtime validation.

A capturing lambda must retain captured state somewhere; a non-capturing lambda may be reused, while inlining may eliminate the lambda object at a particular call site. The backend may use generated classes or invokedynamic, D8/R8 may transform code, and ART may AOT/JIT-compile it. Therefore, “every lambda allocates” and “inline is always zero allocation” are both false. Capturing a large owner can also extend its lifetime.

JVM bytecode, DEX, and ART: implications without myths#

The Kotlin/JVM compiler emits class files and Kotlin metadata; the Android toolchain performs desugaring/shrinking and D8/R8 conversion to DEX. ART executes DEX and may combine interpretation, AOT, and JIT depending on Android version, runtime, and profiles. JVM bytecode shape is useful for diagnosing signatures, bridges, synthetic accessors, and potential allocations, but it is not final machine code.

The practical rule is to inspect the release variant, minification and keep rules, and representative devices. Do not guarantee that a runtime compiler inlines a specific function, that an object is never allocated, or that a micro-optimisation is faster without a benchmark or profile. Language semantics are stronger guarantees than optimiser assumptions.

Binary and source compatibility for an Android library or SDK#

Binary compatibility means an already compiled consumer works with the new artifact without relinking or recompilation errors. Source compatibility means consumer source recompiles without changes. Behavioural compatibility means observable semantics remain acceptable. These sets do not coincide.

  • Changing a JVM descriptor, removing or renaming a public member, or changing class/interface shape, superclass, visibility, or default-method scheme can break binary ABI.
  • Adding a parameter, even one with a default value, is source-compatible for Kotlin callers but changes the JVM descriptor and breaks every compiled consumer (NoSuchMethodError); keep the old signature as a @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN) overload that delegates to the new one (or use @JvmOverloads deliberately). Changing a default value stays binary-compatible, but it changes behaviour for every consumer, old binaries included, because defaults are computed in the library's $default method. Only const val values and public inline bodies (including their defaults) are embedded in consumers.
  • A new overload can preserve binary compatibility but break source through overload-resolution ambiguity. A new abstract interface member breaks implementers; even a default member must be checked against Java/Kotlin targets and desugaring.
  • Changes to variance, nullability annotations, generic bounds, value-class representation/mangling, or annotations can alter Kotlin source/metadata or the Java surface without an obvious source diff.

For a published Android library, enable explicit API, generate and review an API/ABI dump, run binary compatibility validation, Java and Kotlin consumer compile tests, and an Android release smoke test. Use a deprecation cycle and bridge, a SemVer/version policy, and a changelog. A compatibility tool does not verify behaviour, resources, manifest merging, serialization, or reflection contracts.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

Safe claimDo not promise
Variance or projection restricts legal source operations.A generic argument remains fully available at runtime after erasure.
crossinline forbids non-local return; noinline permits storing a lambda.crossinline makes a callback synchronous/thread-safe, or inline removes all allocations.
A value class creates a distinct Kotlin type.It is always unboxed or automatically has a convenient Java constructor/API.
Nullability annotations influence the compiler's view.An external Java/runtime value can never violate the annotation.
An ABI checker catches modelled signature changes.It proves source, behavioural, reflection, resource, and Android runtime compatibility.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Excessive variance and projections make inference difficult; an unsafe cast only hides incorrect ownership.
  • A large public inline body inflates consumers, complicates patch rollout, and binds ABI to internal helpers.
  • A property delegate can hide lifecycle leaks, I/O, synchronisation, or exceptions behind an innocent getter.
  • A value class in a generic-heavy API boxes, while Java, framework, or reflection tooling may not see the expected signature.
  • A capturing callback stored longer than its owner causes a leak; allocation optimisation does not fix lifetime.
  • “Source still compiles” after an SDK update does not prove old APK/AAR consumers remain binary-compatible or behaviour is unchanged.

Production scenario: evolving an analytics SDK#

Hypothetically: a private Android SDK has Kotlin and Java consumers. The team wants to replace a String userId with UserId, a function callback with an inline/reified helper, and a Java listener with a lambda. Direct replacement changes JVM signatures or name mangling and breaks already compiled clients.

A safe migration keeps the old Java-friendly entry point, deprecates it, and delegates to a typed Kotlin core; adds a separately named @JvmName bridge; and exposes the listener as a stable fun interface. Nullable or platform input is normalised at the Stage 2 boundary. An API dump records overloads, wildcards, and annotations. Java and Kotlin fixture apps compile against the new SDK, while a fixture compiled against the previous artifact runs with the new one. A release benchmark checks the hot path without turning one result into a universal allocation guarantee.

Code-review/debugging trap: “typed and zero-cost”#

// Trap: unchecked nested cast + capture + value-class boxing in a generic path.
@JvmInline value class EventId(val raw: String)
private val pending = mutableListOf<() -> Unit>()

inline fun <reified T> decode(raw: Any): T = raw as T
fun enqueue(owner: Activity, id: EventId, raw: Any) {
    val tags = decode<List<String>>(raw) // does not validate each element
    pending += { owner.title = "$id:${tags.first()}" } // retains Activity
}

A review should find three independent risks: reified checks only a runtime-available outer type, the stored lambda retains the Activity, and EventId may box in a generic or string-interpolation path. Fix with schema or element validation, lifecycle-scoped callbacks or ID-based ownership, and measurement before optimisation. Inspect the Java signature separately for ABI.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Why is MutableList<Dog> not a MutableList<Animal>? Invariance prevents a caller from inserting a Cat into a dog list. A projection provides a restricted safe view; it does not change the real element type.
  2. out, in, or *? Use out for a producer, in for a consumer, and * when the argument is unknown and only safe operations are required. Start from the actual read/write contract.
  3. What exactly do noinline and crossinline do? noinline keeps a lambda as a storable/passable value. crossinline keeps it inlinable but forbids a non-local return because invocation may be indirect.
  4. What can reified not do? It cannot recover nested erased arguments or validate a schema. List<String> still needs element validation or a serializer/type-token contract.
  5. Is delegation free? It removes source boilerplate, but generated forwarding, delegate storage, and dispatch remain; a property delegate may perform work on every access.
  6. When does a value class box? Commonly in nullable, generic, and interface contexts. Exact code generation depends on use site and toolchain, so inspect and profile the artifact.
  7. How do you make a Kotlin API Java-friendly? Inspect generated surface; use named SAMs, explicit overloads or bridges, and targeted @Jvm* annotations. Avoid accidental exposure of function types, mangled value-class methods, and platform ambiguity.
  8. Does every lambda allocate? No. A non-capturing instance may be reused, an inline call may remove the object, and the backend/R8/ART can transform representation. A capturing or stored lambda often needs state; measure a release build.
  9. Is JVM bytecode what Android executes? Not directly. Class files become DEX, which ART interprets or AOT/JIT-compiles. Bytecode inspection explains ABI and lowering, not final machine code or guaranteed performance.
  10. Binary versus source compatibility? Binary concerns an old compiled client; source concerns recompilation. A new overload can be binary-safe but source-ambiguous, while inline bodies and const vals may differ between old and recompiled callers; a changed default value reaches even old binaries.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Why does a bug in a public inline function remain after updating the AAR? The old consumer already contains the inlined body. It needs recompilation; keep large or volatile logic in a non-inline function when patchability matters.
  2. You added a SAM overload and a Kotlin call became ambiguous. Is that an ABI break? The old binary may run, but source recompilation can fail through overload resolution. It is a source-compatibility regression; use a distinct name or migration path.
  3. A value-class method is visible to Kotlin but Java cannot call it. Why? Unboxed representation and name mangling do not create a normal Java constructor/signature. Add an explicit bridge and lock it in the API dump.
  4. A profiler shows a lambda allocation despite inline. What do you inspect? Check whether the parameter is noinline, stored, converted to a SAM, or whether capture/materialisation occurs elsewhere; inspect release DEX and the allocation trace. Do not infer from the source keyword alone.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Which public generic APIs in your SDK are true producers or consumers, and which are accidentally invariant?
  2. Which public inline or constant declarations are embedded in consumers, which default values would change behaviour for old binaries, and how will you migrate them?
  3. Where do your value classes box or require Java/reflection bridges?
  4. Which stored lambdas capture an Activity, Fragment, View, or large graph longer than necessary?
  5. How does each test separately prove binary, source, behavioural, and Android runtime compatibility?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do Kotlin abstractions map to the JVM and Android runtime, and how does that affect a public SDK?

~30-second answer#

I separate the Kotlin source contract from the JVM ABI and the Android runtime. Variance controls legal source operations, while generic arguments are mostly erased. Inline and value classes can remove overhead in some call sites, but neither guarantees zero allocation. For a public SDK I inspect generated Java signatures, provide explicit bridges, and validate binary and source compatibility with API dumps plus compiled Java and Kotlin consumers.

~2-minute answer#

I reason across three layers. At the Kotlin layer, declaration-site variance and projections express producer and consumer ownership. At the JVM layer, most generic arguments are erased, nullable or generic values may box, and Kotlin features create concrete signatures, bridges, metadata, and sometimes mangled names.

For higher-order APIs, inline can copy code and inlinable lambdas into the call site. A noinline lambda remains a value that can be stored, while crossinline only forbids non-local returns; it does not promise threading behaviour. Reified makes a runtime-available top-level type usable at an inline call site, but it cannot prove nested generic arguments. Capturing lambdas may retain state, and their allocation shape depends on the compiler and Android toolchain.

On Android, class files are transformed into DEX and ART can interpret or AOT/JIT-compile them, so I do not infer final performance from a keyword or JVM bytecode alone. I inspect release artifacts and benchmark representative devices.

For a published library, I treat generated JVM signatures as the real ABI. I use deliberate Java-facing SAMs and bridges, explicit nullability, API dumps and binary compatibility checks. I also compile Java and Kotlin fixtures and run an old compiled consumer against the new artifact, because binary, source, and behavioural compatibility are different contracts.

Official sources#

  • Kotlin: Generics, variance, projections, and erasure
  • Kotlin: Inline functions, noinline, crossinline, and reified
  • Kotlin: Delegation and Delegated properties
  • Kotlin: Inline value classes
  • Kotlin: Calling Java from Kotlin and Calling Kotlin from Java
  • Android: Kotlin–Java interop guide
  • Kotlin: Backward compatibility guidelines for library authors
  • Kotlin Gradle plugin: Binary compatibility validation
  • Android platform architecture: DEX and ART and D8
Android tasks, back stack, deep links, intents, and PendingIntentexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to predict which task and which Activity instance receives an intent, design a secure external and deep-link boundary, align the system task stack with the Navigation/Compose back stack, create a PendingIntent with intentional identity, and test cold, warm, and process-death scenarios with adb.

Senior mental model#

Two stacks, three boundaries: a system task contains Activity instances; each host Activity can own a Navigation back stack; the process only executes components and can die without defining task identity. The trust boundaries are the incoming Intent or URI, the internal route, and the delegated capability in a PendingIntent.

  • Task ≠ process: a task is a user-facing LIFO history of Activity instances in Recents; a process is a runtime container. One process can serve multiple tasks, and a task can remain as a system record after process death and later be reconstructed.
  • Activity class ≠ Activity instance: one class can have multiple instances in one or several tasks. launchMode, flags, affinity, and the existing stack determine reuse or creation.
  • System stack ≠ NavController stack: Back may first pop an in-Activity destination; only at the root does it finish or move the Activity/task. Design them together without conflating them.

Internals: task selection, delivery, and back dispatch#

Tasks, affinity, and launch modes#

A normal standard launch creates an instance in the caller's task even when the Activity has a different affinity. taskAffinity is a hint for reparenting and task lookup under special launch policies; it is not a process name, package, or unconditional routing rule.

MechanismExact effect and edge case
standardCreates a new instance on top of the current task; the same class can appear repeatedly.
singleTop / FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOPReuses only a matching instance already at the top and delivers via onNewIntent(). A matching instance lower in the stack does not prevent creation.
singleTask / FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK with a matching tasksingleTask: an existing instance is brought to the front, receives onNewIntent(), and activities above it are cleared. FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK alone: if a task already runs for the activity, it is brought to the front in the state it was last in — no new instance, no onNewIntent(), nothing cleared; combine with CLEAR_TOP/SINGLE_TOP (or CLEAR_TASK) to get delivery or clearing. NEW_TASK is also required when launching from a non-Activity context.
singleInstancePerTaskThe Activity can only be the task root, but separate instances can exist in separate tasks when launched with NEW_DOCUMENT/MULTIPLE_TASK.
singleInstanceThe Activity is the only member of its task; subsequent Activities launch elsewhere. This isolation often breaks expected Back and Recents UX.
CLEAR_TOPIf the target is in the task, entries above it finish. A standard target is normally removed too and recreated; adding SINGLE_TOP preserves it and delivers onNewIntent().
CLEAR_TASK | NEW_TASKClears the matching task before starting the target. It suits logout/reset flows but destroys user history.
REORDER_TO_FRONTMoves an existing instance to the top without clearing intermediate instances; it is ignored when CLEAR_TOP is also supplied.

allowTaskReparenting="true" lets an Activity temporarily launched into another task move to the task matching its affinity when that task comes forward. This makes history context-dependent and requires an explicit UX decision plus Recents tests.

Document-centric tasks, Recents, and multi-window#

FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_DOCUMENT (manifest: documentLaunchMode) models an independent document as a separate task in Recents; the Intent URI normally distinguishes documents. intoExisting matches a task by base-intent Component plus data URI, clears it, and delivers to its root; always creates a new document task; never/none prohibit or retain default reuse. MULTIPLE_TASK with NEW_TASK/NEW_DOCUMENT disables normal existing-task lookup and almost always needs a strong justification.

In multi-window, two tasks can be visible and RESUMED at once; “the app is foreground” does not imply one active Activity. Do not store selected document or an auth redirect in a process singleton. Keep the identifier in the route/intent and durable state; use SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable only for small reconstructible UI state.

Predictive Back and dispatcher boundaries#

  • OnBackInvokedDispatcher is the platform API introduced in Android 13 (API 33) for back invocation; progress callbacks for custom predictive animation belong to newer platform/AndroidX APIs. Do not register a callback permanently: it can suppress system animation and root-task behavior.
  • OnBackPressedDispatcher is the AndroidX compatibility and lifecycle boundary for Activities, Fragments, and Compose. OnBackPressedCallback.isEnabled should reflect whether the UI can currently consume Back; the most recently added enabled callback takes priority.
  • In Compose, BackHandler wraps the AndroidX dispatcher. It should be composition-aware and enabled only for active transient UI or flow. Do not recursively call legacy onBackPressed().
  • Predictive Back requires the destination to be known early. A callback that decides navigation only after gesture completion cannot guarantee a correct preview. Framework/Navigation versions and target SDK determine available behavior.

Navigation/Compose back stack and restoration#

NavController stores a NavBackStackEntry for each destination/graph with lifecycle, arguments, ViewModelStore, and saved state. popUpTo edits history; inclusive decides whether to remove the target; launchSingleTop avoids a second copy only at the top; saveState + restoreState can preserve and restore popped destination state for multiple back stacks. They do not turn repository data into durable storage.

navController.navigate(Product(productId)) {
    launchSingleTop = true
    restoreState = true
    popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) {
        saveState = true
    }
}

Pass stable IDs rather than large objects. After process death, graph/back-stack restoration can reconstruct the route and small saved state, but network data must be loaded again. A route serializer/schema is a compatibility contract; changes to argument names or types need defaults or migration.

Explicit/implicit intents, resolution, and the exported boundary#

An explicit Intent names a component and is the default for in-app navigation. An implicit Intent describes action, data, and category; Package Manager compares filters by action, data (scheme/host/port/path/MIME), and category. Activity implicit starts require a filter with CATEGORY_DEFAULT; no match throws ActivityNotFoundException, while multiple matches can show a chooser or default handler.

android:exported controls whether other apps can directly start a component; components with an intent filter must set it explicitly on modern targets. Exported means reachable, not authorised. Sensitive operations still require permissions, caller/session checks, and validation of every extra/URI. An intent filter is not a schema validator.

fun parseProduct(uri: Uri): ProductId? {
    if (uri.scheme != "https" || uri.host != "shop.example.com") return null
    if (uri.pathSegments.size != 2 || uri.pathSegments[0] != "p") return null
    val raw = uri.pathSegments[1]
    if (!raw.matches(Regex("[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}"))) return null
    return ProductId(raw)
}

Normalise and allowlist scheme, canonical host, path shape, length, encoding, and business authorisation. Never trust a query parameter as a return URL, file path, SQL key, or WebView URL. Reject malformed, duplicate, or conflicting parameters fail-closed.

Verified App Links and one deep-link router#

An Android App Link is an HTTPS deep link with android:autoVerify="true" and a successful app-to-website association through https://host/.well-known/assetlinks.json containing package and signing-certificate fingerprints. Verification provides preferred routing for a verified domain; it does not validate payload, authorise the user, or guarantee opening against user settings. State can depend on install/update, network, redirects, and domain settings.

Use one ingress/router: parse the untrusted URI → canonical typed command → authentication/entitlement gate → idempotent navigation. On a cold start, the intent enters through creation and routing waits for graph/session readiness; on a warm start, a reused Activity gets a new Intent in onNewIntent(), which must be forwarded explicitly. Do not handle one delivery in both the Activity and a composable effect: an event ID or saved handled token plus launchSingleTop/popUpTo prevents duplicate destinations.

PendingIntent: identity, mutability, replay, and security#

A PendingIntent is a transferable capability: another process or the system can later execute an operation with the creator's identity and permissions, even after the creator process dies. The system-service token, not your Intent object, persists.

  • Identity: operation type (getActivity/getBroadcast/getService), creator package/user, requestCode, and Intent fields compared by Intent.filterEquals() (action, data, type, identifier, component, categories). Extras do not determine identity.
  • FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT retains the token and replaces extras in its current Intent; the creator can update even an immutable PendingIntent. An identity collision can therefore change older notifications.
  • FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT cancels the old token and creates a new one; FLAG_NO_CREATE only looks up an existing token; FLAG_ONE_SHOT permits one successful send. Explicit cancel() makes all old copies unusable.
  • FLAG_IMMUTABLE is the default security choice: a sender cannot fill in and mutate the wrapped Intent. Use FLAG_MUTABLE only for a specific platform feature such as inline reply or bubbles; then constrain explicit component/package, action, and data and leave no unfilled fields.
  • A PendingIntent can be replayed until cancelled, one-shot, or invalidated. Even an immutable token is not single-use or fresh authorisation: recheck authentication, resource ownership, expiry, and idempotency while handling.
val intent = Intent(context, MainActivity::class.java).apply {
    action = "com.example.OPEN_ORDER"
    data = "myapp://orders/$orderId".toUri() // stable identity per order
}
val contentIntent = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context,
    orderId.stableRequestCode(),
    intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE,
)

Notification/deep-link patterns#

For a regular destination, a notification should open the expected hierarchy using manifest parent metadata plus TaskStackBuilder, or a Navigation deep-link PendingIntent. For a special transient Activity, deliberately create a separate task (NEW_TASK | CLEAR_TASK, optionally excluded from Recents). Do not mix these patterns accidentally. Every action needs distinct PendingIntent identity; narrowly target a mutable inline-reply PendingIntent to a receiver or service.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

Safe claimDo not promise
singleTop reuses a matching top instance.The task always has only one instance of that Activity.
A verified App Link establishes the configured website↔app association for a domain.The URI is safe, the user is authorised, or settings can never route elsewhere.
An immutable PendingIntent blocks sender fill-in mutation.The token is single-use, cannot be replayed, or remains authorised.
Saved state can restore a small navigation/UI descriptor.The process, an in-memory singleton, socket, or repository cache survives death.
The dispatcher prioritises enabled back callbacks.A custom callback automatically gives predictive animation on every API/library version.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Android 12 / target API 31+: every PendingIntent must explicitly specify mutability; newer platforms further restrict unsafe mutable implicit PendingIntents.
  • Android 12 changed default verified web-link handling: generic web intents directly open an app only for approved/verified domains. Inspect domain state.
  • Android 13 (API 33) introduced OnBackInvokedDispatcher; predictive Back rollout, manifest opt-in/out, target-SDK defaults, and AndroidX support changed across Android 13–15+. Check current platform and library documentation.
  • Implicit-intent matching and security restrictions depend on target SDK. From Android 13, a receiving exported component generally needs a matching filter for an intent sent by another app, subject to documented exceptions.
  • Navigation state and deep-link behavior depend on Navigation version; component APIs support multiple back stacks from 2.4+, while type-safe Compose routes are newer. Pin versions and regression-test them.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Manifest launch modes impose global behavior; intent flags are call-site policy. Aggressive singleTask/CLEAR_TOP reduces duplicates but can silently erase user history.
  • A separate task per document improves Recents and multi-window but multiplies simultaneous owners and restoration cases.
  • One external router centralises validation and deduplication. Multiple Activity filters can seem locally simpler but drift in auth and stack semantics.
  • FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT is convenient, but an identity collision updates the wrong notification's extras. A random requestCode hides rather than models identity.
  • Navigating to a privileged screen before auth finishes causes flashes/leaks or redirect loops. Preserve a canonical pending command, finish auth, authorise again, and navigate once.

Production scenario: notification → verified order link#

Hypothetically: a notification and an HTTPS link open order detail. MainActivity is singleTop; both sources submit a typed OpenOrder(id, deliveryId) to one router. The router allowlists host/path, waits for graph restoration, checks session and entitlement, then calls navigate(Order(id)) { launchSingleTop = true }. A consumed deliveryId is stored in SavedStateHandle so recreation does not duplicate the route.

The notification PendingIntent targets an explicit Activity, is immutable, and uses action/data/requestCode derived from the order for identity. Cold start, warm onNewIntent(), second tap, Back, logout, process kill, and two multi-window tasks are tested separately. Durable order data reloads from the repository; saved state contains only ID and navigation intent.

Code-review/debugging trap#

// Trap: all orders share identity; mutable implicit capability; double routing.
val pi = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context, 0,
    Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE,
)
// Activity routes in onCreate/onNewIntent, while a composable LaunchedEffect
// observes the same intent and navigates again.

Review whether the Intent is explicit/verified and the URI validated; whether extras are mistaken for identity; why mutability is required; whether every notification action has a distinct key; where one owner marks a delivery consumed; and what happens on warm start and process death. Fix with an explicit component, immutable token, stable action/data/requestCode, one lifecycle-aware router, and an idempotent command.

Testing matrix with adb#

# Cold deep link; -W reports launch, -S force-stops first.
adb shell am start -W -S -a android.intent.action.VIEW \
  -c android.intent.category.BROWSABLE \
  -d 'https://shop.example.com/p/ORDER_42' com.example.app

# Warm delivery: run once, navigate elsewhere, then repeat without -S.
adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW \
  -d 'https://shop.example.com/p/ORDER_42' com.example.app

# Inspect tasks/activities and App Links verification state.
adb shell dumpsys activity activities
adb shell pm get-app-links com.example.app
adb shell pm verify-app-links --re-verify com.example.app

# Process-death approximation while the task remains, then relaunch.
adb shell am kill com.example.app

# Explicit flag scenarios (replace the component with the test Activity).
adb shell am start -W -n com.example.app/.MainActivity \
  -f 0x24000000

Assert destination sequence, task ID/component order, onCreate versus onNewIntent, exactly one navigation event, Back destination, unauthorised/error route, malformed URI rejection, and restored state. Add instrumentation with TestNavHostController/Compose UI plus device tests; adb alone does not prove in-app state.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Are task, process, and Activity instance the same? No. A task is UI history, a process is an execution container, and an instance is one object/lifecycle. Their lifetimes and cardinality differ.
  2. Why does singleTop not remove duplicates? It reuses only the top instance; a matching instance lower in the stack does not block creation.
  3. Does CLEAR_TOP always call onNewIntent()? No. A standard target can be removed and recreated; SINGLE_TOP or a compatible launch mode causes reuse.
  4. When does taskAffinity matter? Mostly with NEW_TASK, reparenting, and task/document policies; a normal start enters the caller's task.
  5. How does the Navigation stack relate to the system stack? NavController owns destinations inside a host Activity; a system task owns Activity instances. A root Nav pop delegates Back to Activity/task behavior.
  6. What does a verified App Link add? Domain association enables direct HTTPS routing. It is not payload validation or authorisation.
  7. How do you avoid duplicate deep-link navigation? Use one ingress/router, delivery identity and consumption, the same cold/warm pipeline, and an idempotent launchSingleTop/popUpTo policy.
  8. What determines PendingIntent identity? Operation/creator, requestCode, and filter-equal Intent fields; extras are excluded, so collisions can update the wrong token.
  9. Does immutable mean one-shot? No. Immutable blocks sender mutation; one-shot/cancel and idempotent authorised handling control replay.
  10. What do you test after process death? Task/Nav route and small descriptor restoration, data reload, no singleton dependency, renewed auth/authorisation, and one delivery.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Two notifications use requestCode 0 and different extras but both open the latest order. Why? Extras are not PendingIntent identity; UPDATE_CURRENT updated one token. Use stable distinct data/action/requestCode.
  2. A warm App Link is sometimes ignored. The creation path probably handles intent, while onNewIntent() does not forward the new Intent to the router and singleTop preserves the Activity.
  3. Predictive preview shows Home but the callback opens a dialog. The handler is enabled incorrectly or decides too late; the back destination must be known during the gesture. Model the dialog in Navigation or use a progress-aware API.
  4. One order is open in two windows and a singleton “currentOrder” becomes confused. Process state is not task-local. Each task's route/ViewModel owner keeps its own ID; the repository caches by ID rather than a global selection.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Draw the system task stack and NavController stack for a cold link, a second tap, and three Back operations.
  2. Which exact Intent fields make every notification action unique?
  3. Where does a URI become a validated typed command, and where is authorisation checked again?
  4. Which state is restored after process death, and which data must be reloaded?
  5. Which back callbacks are enabled in every UI state, and are they compatible with predictive Back?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you design Android task, deep-link, Back, and PendingIntent behavior safely?

~30-second answer#

I separate the system task stack from the in-activity Navigation stack and from the app process. I use default launch behavior unless the product requires a specific task model, route every external intent through one validated and authorised typed command, and handle cold and warm delivery idempotently. PendingIntents are explicit and immutable by default, with stable distinct identity because extras do not participate in identity. I verify Back, App Links, notification taps, multi-window, and process death on device.

~2-minute answer#

I start with three separate lifetimes: a task is a user-facing stack of Activity instances, a process is an execution container that can die, and a NavController owns destinations inside a host Activity. Launch modes and flags are stack transformations, not singleton guarantees. For example, singleTop only reuses the top instance, while CLEAR_TOP can remove everything above a target and may recreate a standard target.

External intents are an untrusted boundary. I prefer explicit intents internally. For web entry I use verified HTTPS App Links, but still allowlist and parse the URI into a typed command, then check authentication and resource authorisation. One router handles both onCreate and onNewIntent so cold and warm starts have the same semantics and a delivery is consumed only once.

Back is owned by the narrowest currently enabled handler. AndroidX OnBackPressedDispatcher integrates lifecycle owners and Compose, while platform predictive Back requires the destination to be known early enough for preview. I avoid permanently intercepting root Back.

A PendingIntent is a replayable capability executed with its creator's identity. I make it explicit and immutable unless a documented feature requires mutation. Its identity uses operation type, request code, and filter-equal Intent fields—not extras—so each notification action gets a stable distinct key. At handling time I recheck auth, ownership, expiry, and idempotency. Finally, I test task dumps, verified-link state, cold/warm delivery, duplicate taps, multi-window, and process death, and I restore identifiers rather than assuming memory survived.

Android background execution: Services, BroadcastReceiver, WorkManager, foreground services, and alarmsexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to choose an API by latency, durability, user visibility, and clock precision, explain its real guarantees, design repeatable and interruptible work across process death or reboot, and inspect scheduler state rather than merely proving that an API was called. This section deepens execution reliability instead of repeating the base component catalogue.

Senior mental model#

A component is an entry point, not a resource guarantee. Process lifetime, component lifetime, thread lifetime, and durable-job lifetime are distinct. The system may defer a start, stop a component or job, kill the process, or lose alarms at reboot. Correctness comes from a durable source of truth, idempotent effects, checkpoints, and reconciliation—not from hoping that a callback completes.

  • Process ≠ component: the system raises process importance while a component handles a callback or active binding, but the process is not immortal. After the callback, do not rely on a thread, singleton, or process-scoped coroutine.
  • Scheduling ≠ execution time: enqueueing work or setting an alarm records intent. Constraints, Doze, App Standby, quota, battery restriction, thermal state, and OEM policy influence the actual start.
  • Persistence ≠ exactly once: WorkManager stores the request and attempts eligible execution, but a crash between an external side effect and a local commit can cause replay. Design at-least-once-like handling without claiming a formal delivery guarantee: stable operation IDs, idempotency keys, transactional outbox/inbox, upsert, and resumable checkpoints.

Internals: ownership, scheduling, and interruption#

Started and bound Services#

By default, a Service runs callbacks on the main thread of its hosting process; it does not create a background thread or a separate process. Blocking I/O or CPU work in a callback can cause an ANR, so use explicitly managed coroutines or executors with cancellation.

  • Started: startService()/startForegroundService() leads to onStartCommand(intent, flags, startId). The service continues independently of the caller until stopSelf(startId)/stopService() or the system stops it. Repeated starts produce start IDs but share one Service instance. START_NOT_STICKY, START_STICKY, and START_REDELIVER_INTENT are restart policies after a kill, not completion or exactly-once guarantees.
  • Bound: bindService() exposes an IBinder, and lifetime usually follows clients. Local Binder calls can run on the caller thread; remote calls use Binder threads, so thread safety and a non-blocking contract must be explicit. onServiceDisconnected() reports a lost connection after crash/kill, not a normal unbind.
  • A Service may be both started and bound: unbinding does not end the started lifetime, while stopSelf() does not destroy it while bindings remain. A separate android:process adds IPC, a failure boundary, and memory cost, but not durability.

Background-service limits introduced in Android 8 (API 26) constrain background apps: after a grace window, ordinary background services must stop. Prefer WorkManager/JobScheduler for deferrable durable work and a lawful FGS for ongoing user-visible work.

BroadcastReceiver: registration, trust, and time budget#

  • A manifest receiver can start the process for an allowed broadcast. For apps targeting API 26+, most implicit broadcasts cannot be declared in the manifest except documented exceptions. A context receiver exists only while its registering context is valid; register and unregister symmetrically to avoid leaking an Activity.
  • For runtime registration, explicitly choose ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED for app-only broadcasts or RECEIVER_EXPORTED when other apps or all privileged system senders are required. Exported controls reachability, not authorisation: sensitive actions still require permissions, explicit package/component where applicable, and payload validation.
  • onReceive() uses the main thread unless a scheduler is supplied and must finish quickly. goAsync() only extends the broadcast lifetime through a PendingResult; call finish() in finally. Official guidance still expects very quick completion, roughly under 10 seconds. It is not a long-work mechanism. For durable continuation, enqueue WorkManager/JobScheduler and return.

WorkManager: durable intent, policy, and data flow#

WorkManager is the recommended Jetpack scheduler for deferrable, guaranteed-to-be-scheduled persistent work. It stores requests in its internal database so they survive process death and reboot. It is not an exact timer and does not preserve a continuous process. Platform backends vary by API, including JobScheduler on modern Android, and constraints plus system optimisation determine eligible starts.

MechanismSenior-level consequence
ConstraintsNetwork, charging, battery, storage, and idle are conditions for starting and continuing, not a snapshot. If a constraint disappears, the Worker may stop and run later.
Unique workKEEP ignores a new request while an unfinished chain exists; REPLACE cancels existing work; APPEND inherits prerequisite failure/cancellation; APPEND_OR_REPLACE starts a new sequence after a failed/cancelled chain. A unique name deduplicates scheduling, not the external side effect.
Retry/backoffResult.retry() applies linear or exponential inexact backoff. The minimum initial delay is 10 seconds; the default is exponential with 30 seconds. Permanent input/domain errors should not retry forever.
ExpeditedFor short, user-important, latency-sensitive work and subject to system quota. OutOfQuotaPolicy explicitly downgrades to regular work or drops the request. “Expedited” never means immediate under every condition.
Foreground workersetForeground() runs a WorkManager-managed FGS with a notification for long work. FGS rules still apply; from Android 16, long-running workers can consume job quota.
Cancellation/stopCancellation changes state and sends a stop signal. A CoroutineWorker must not swallow cancellation; blocking loops check isStopped. A Result produced after stop is ignored. Close files, DB, and network resources and keep operations resumable.
Data/chainsData is a lightweight primitives/arrays container with serialized MAX_DATA_BYTES = 10,240 for input/output, not a datastore. Pass IDs or URIs; keep payload in a DB/file. Success unblocks dependents; failure/cancellation propagates downstream; an InputMerger needs explicit conflict semantics.

For side effects, persist an operation row before enqueueing, use a logical unique name, and let the Worker claim and read current durable state transactionally. A server idempotency key closes the crash window between HTTP success and local commit; local unique work alone cannot.

Foreground services: visible ongoing work, not an escape hatch#

  • An FGS is for work the user can notice. startForegroundService() creates the service, but the service must promptly call ServiceCompat.startForeground() (the platform deadline is a few seconds, traditionally described as 5 seconds) with an ongoing notification or the system stops the app/service.
  • Apps targeting Android 12 / API 31+ generally cannot start an FGS from the background except documented exemptions; violation throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException. While-in-use camera, microphone, location, and body-sensor prerequisites add further restrictions.
  • Declare android:foregroundServiceType, the base FOREGROUND_SERVICE permission, and type-specific permissions/prerequisites. Target API 34+ enforces types and permissions more strictly. The type must match real work; notification-channel or notification-permission UX does not remove the notification obligation.
  • Android 14 (API 34) introduced user-initiated data transfer jobs for long uploads/downloads explicitly started by the user. This is a JobScheduler API, requires an ongoing notification, and needs a fallback on older APIs. Use expedited WorkManager for short transfers and consider DownloadManager where its purpose-built model fits.

AlarmManager, Doze, and civil time#

  • Prefer an inexact alarm: set(), setWindow(), and setInexactRepeating() permit batching and save battery. An alarm opens only a short execution window; its receiver should enqueue durable work instead of running a network loop.
  • Use setExact*/setAlarmClock() only for genuinely user-facing precise time. Android 12 / target 31+ requires exact-alarm special access for SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM. Android 13+ offers the restricted USE_EXACT_ALARM alternative only for qualifying core use cases. Check canScheduleExactAlarms(); revocation cancels future exact alarms.
  • Doze defers ordinary alarms, jobs, and network. setAndAllowWhileIdle()/setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() are throttled and do not grant long network execution; setAlarmClock() is the most disruptive user-alarm option. App Standby, battery restriction, and OEM policy can constrain work further.
  • ELAPSED_REALTIME resists wall-clock/time-zone changes but resets at reboot; RTC follows wall-clock time. All alarms disappear on shutdown: rebuild from a durable domain schedule after BOOT_COMPLETED. For “09:00 local,” store the time zone and civil-time rule, handle time/time-zone changes, and compute the next occurrence rather than adding 24-hour milliseconds.

Guarantee / non-guarantee matrix#

Safe claimDo not promise
Service callbacks normally arrive on the hosting process main thread.A Service automatically creates a thread/process or survives a kill.
goAsync() keeps a broadcast pending until finish() within a short budget.A receiver can reliably finish a long upload after returning.
WorkManager persists the scheduled request and reschedules eligible work.Exact time, exactly-once side effects, unlimited runtime, or execution after force-stop.
An FGS exposes ongoing work and raises process importance.Immortality, bypassing quota/start rules, or unlimited duration.
An exact alarm with access narrows timing tolerance.Arbitrary long work at an exact millisecond under all system/OEM conditions.
Reconciliation and idempotency make replay safe.Every scheduler formally provides at-least-once or exactly-once delivery.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • API 26 / Android 8: background-service limits and manifest implicit-broadcast restrictions; legacy IntentService is not a modern replacement.
  • API 31 / Android 12 target+: background FGS starts are denied by default and exact alarms require special access. Inspect runtime state, not only the manifest.
  • API 33 / Android 13 target+: notification runtime permission affects app-notification visibility, but an FGS must still supply a notification; USE_EXACT_ALARM is restricted to qualifying categories.
  • API 34 / Android 14 target+: required FGS types, type-specific permissions, and runtime prerequisites; UIDT jobs start at API 34. Cached apps can receive some less important broadcasts later.
  • API 35 / Android 15 target+: dataSync and mediaProcessing FGS types each have their own six-hours-in-a-rolling-24-hours limit (tracked separately per type, shared by all of the app's FGS of that type) and receive onTimeout(); several FGS types cannot start from BOOT_COMPLETED.
  • Android 16: long-running WorkManager workers using an FGS can consume JobScheduler quota; cross-process broadcast priority is no longer guaranteed. Check target-SDK behavior and current documentation, not only SDK_INT.

Decision framework#

RequirementDefaultWhy / caveat
Only while a screen is visibleLifecycle scope; bound service only for shared IPC/resourceDo not turn UI work into a durable job.
Deferrable and survives process/rebootWorkManagerConstraints, unique policy, retry, idempotent Worker; timing is inexact.
Short important user-triggered workExpedited WorkManagerQuota and explicit out-of-quota policy.
Ongoing visible session (media/location/device)Typed FGS or purpose-built APIVisible notification, start eligibility, permission, and stop action.
Long user-initiated upload/downloadUIDT job on API 34+, versioned fallbackUser-visible transfer; JobScheduler rather than a Jetpack wrapper.
Precise user-facing clock eventExact AlarmManager only if necessarySpecial access and reboot/time-zone reconstruction.
Event may be batchedInexact alarm or WorkManagerChoose clock trigger versus durable constrained work.
Short reaction to a system/app eventReceiver → validate → enqueuegoAsync() only for brief completion.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Lower latency costs quota, battery, or user interruption; stronger durability adds database state, retries, deduplication, and migrations.
  • Constraints reduce waste but can starve work. Expose pending/last-synced state, allow manual retry, and reconcile when the app opens.
  • REPLACE can lose progress, KEEP can retain stale inputs, and APPEND can create a long poisoned chain. Make the Worker read current durable state and choose policy from domain semantics.
  • Force-stop, user battery restriction, permission revocation, low storage, reboot, and an OEM task killer are distinct test states. No app API can promise execution when platform or user deliberately blocks the app.
  • Retry without failure taxonomy turns a 401 or validation error into a battery-draining loop; cancellation without cooperative cleanup leaves partial files or locks; an FGS without a stop path is a UX and policy defect.

Production scenario: offline outbox plus user-visible attachment#

Hypothetically: a chat app stores a message and stable operationId in a Room outbox transaction, then enqueues unique WorkManager sync. Under a network constraint, the Worker claims pending rows, sends a server idempotency key, atomically records the acknowledgement, and retries only transient failure. Process death anywhere leads to reconciliation rather than a duplicate message.

A small message uses an expedited request with downgrade policy. A large attachment explicitly started by the user uses a UIDT job on API 34+, with progress notification and a documented versioned fallback. User cancel marks the domain operation cancelled, cancels the scheduler handle, and cooperative abort deletes the partial temporary file. After reboot the outbox remains the source of truth; UI reports pending or failed rather than inventing delivery.

Code-review/debugging trap#

override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
    GlobalScope.launch { api.upload(intent.getStringExtra("path")!!) }
}

class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        api.upload(inputData.getString("path")!!) // no idempotency/checkpoint
        return Result.success()
    }
}

The receiver process can die immediately after return; a raw path is untrusted or stale, GlobalScope is not durable, the Worker can replay after remote success, and cancellation may be swallowed. Ask where the durable operation row lives, how sender/URI is validated, which unique policy applies, how transient and permanent errors differ, where the server idempotency key and checkpoint live, what cleanup and user visibility exist, and how stop/reboot/quota is reproduced. Fix with a short receiver → transaction/outbox → ID-based WorkManager pipeline, cooperative cancellation, and reconciliation.

Testing and debugging#

adb shell dumpsys activity services com.example.app
adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler
adb shell dumpsys alarm
adb shell am force-stop com.example.app
adb shell am kill com.example.app
adb shell cmd jobscheduler run -f com.example.app JOB_ID
adb shell cmd jobscheduler get-job-state com.example.app JOB_ID
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle
adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example.app rare
# Android 15 device: exercise the FGS timeout path
adb shell am compat enable FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS com.example.app

Use WorkManager's work-testing: TestWorkerBuilder for Worker logic and WorkManagerTestInitHelper/TestDriver for delays, periods, and constraints. On devices, assert database transitions, idempotency keys, retry classification, duplicate enqueue, constraint loss during a run, cancellation cleanup, process kill, reboot/reschedule, denied exact-alarm access, Doze/standby, and notification stop actions—not merely “the callback happened.” Restore device state after manual power tests.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Why is a Service not a background thread? It is a component and lifecycle entry point; callbacks normally use the hosting process main thread. Threading and cancellation are separate design choices.
  2. Started versus bound Service? A started Service follows explicit stop policy independently of the caller; a bound Service serves clients. Both lifetimes may coexist and both must end before destruction.
  3. When should a receiver use goAsync()? For brief asynchronous completion within roughly a ten-second budget and with finish() guaranteed. Enqueue long durable work.
  4. What does WorkManager guarantee? Persistent scheduling and execution when constraints and the system permit—not exact timing or an exactly-once external effect.
  5. Why unique work if the Worker is idempotent? Unique work controls scheduler duplication and chain policy; idempotency separately protects domain effects and crash windows. Both layers matter.
  6. Retry or failure? Retry transient conditions with backoff; fail permanent input/domain errors. Authentication can require refresh or user action rather than infinite retry.
  7. Expedited work versus FGS? Expedited work is short, latency-sensitive queued work under quota; an FGS is ongoing user-visible work with notification, type, permissions, and start restrictions.
  8. When is an exact alarm justified? Only when a core user-facing function needs precise time. Otherwise an inexact alarm or WorkManager gives batching and better battery behavior.
  9. What survives reboot? A WorkManager request and your durable database state; AlarmManager alarms do not and must be reconstructed. An in-memory service or coroutine does not survive.
  10. How do you prevent duplicate execution? Stable operation identity, transactional state transitions, a server idempotency key or upsert, checkpoints, and reconciliation—without calling the scheduler formally exactly once.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. HTTP 200 arrived, then the process died before the DB commit. The next run can repeat the call; a server idempotency key returns the same result and the Worker reconciles the acknowledgement atomically.
  2. A network constraint disappears during upload. WorkManager's stop signal does not roll back the network. Abort cooperatively, store a resumable offset/session, close resources, and safely continue or restart.
  3. “Every day at 09:00” fires at 08:00 after DST. The implementation stored an elapsed or 24-hour interval rather than a civil-time rule. Store zone plus local time and recompute the next instant after each fire, time-zone change, and reboot.
  4. A foreground Worker on Android 16 stops starting under load. Long-running workers can exhaust job quota. Inspect stop reason and quota; use UIDT for a user-started transfer, a lawful typed FGS for a direct ongoing case, or chunk/defer the work.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Which durable record and idempotency key protect your most important background side effect?
  2. What happens if the process dies before start, during I/O, and after remote success?
  3. Which API fits the latency, durability, visibility, and clock precision of your case?
  4. How does your code react to constraint loss, cancellation, force-stop, reboot, and a time-zone change?
  5. Which dumpsys or test-driver assertions prove a state transition rather than merely a callback?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you choose and design reliable background execution on Android?

~30-second answer#

I separate process, component, and durable-work lifetimes. For deferrable work that must survive process death or reboot I default to WorkManager with constraints, unique-work policy, bounded retries, and idempotent effects. A service is not a thread; a foreground service is only for ongoing user-visible work and must satisfy start, type, permission, and notification rules. Broadcast receivers stay short and enqueue durable work. Alarms are for clock events, exact only when the user-facing requirement justifies special access. I test cancellation, duplicates, Doze, process death, and reboot.

~2-minute answer#

I begin with four requirements: latency, durability across process death or reboot, user visibility, and clock precision. UI-scoped work remains lifecycle-scoped. Deferrable persistent work goes to WorkManager; short important work may be expedited, but quota and out-of-quota behavior are explicit. Ongoing user-visible work may require a correctly typed foreground service or a purpose-built API such as a user-initiated data-transfer job.

A Service is an Android component, not a background thread. Its callbacks normally run on the process main thread. Started and bound lifetimes are independent, and neither makes the process immortal. A receiver is also a short entry point: goAsync extends the broadcast only briefly, so durable continuation is persisted and enqueued.

For WorkManager I model constraints, unique-work conflict policy, transient versus permanent failure, backoff, cooperative stop, and chain failure propagation. Data carries small IDs, not payloads. Persistence still does not make an external side effect exactly once: a crash after server success but before local commit can replay it. I use an operation ID, transactional outbox, server idempotency key, checkpoints, and reconciliation.

AlarmManager is for clock-driven delivery. I prefer inexact alarms, reserve exact alarms for justified user-facing precision, check special access, and rebuild schedules after reboot or civil-time changes. Finally, I verify DB transitions and stop reasons with WorkManager test drivers, adb and dumpsys under constraint loss, quota, Doze, cancellation, process death, reboot, and OEM-restricted conditions.
