Kotlin Flow: foundations, operators, and Android lifecycleexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to explain cold Flow as a sequential asynchronous contract, predict context, cancellation, and buffering along a pipeline, select operators by value-loss or work-cancellation semantics, adapt callbacks safely, bind collection to Android lifecycle, and test per-collector behavior. Deep treatment of StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel, stateIn, and shareIn is reserved for Stage 10; advanced combine, flattening, and retry composition is reserved for Stage 11.

Senior mental model#

A Flow is a recipe for an asynchronous sequence; collection executes that recipe in the collector coroutine. An ordinary flow is cold: its builder does not run until a terminal operator and runs again for every collector. Upstream and downstream are sequential in the collector context by default. Cold does not mean background, cached, or single execution.

  • Flow<T> has a suspending collection contract. Intermediate operators create another lazy pipeline; terminal operators execute it.
  • Sequential means that without an explicit concurrency or buffer boundary, the emitter waits for downstream handling. This is natural suspension, not a promise of Reactive Streams demand accounting.
  • Cancelling the collector coroutine cancels collection and cooperative upstream work. A blocking callback or CPU loop still needs its own cancellation and cleanup design.
  • Cold Flow differs from hot StateFlow/SharedFlow and a point-to-point Channel: it has no shared lifetime, replay/cache, or event ownership by default.

Internals / operator pipeline#

collector coroutine / downstream context
collect { render(it) }
        ↑ filter       sequential suspend calls unless a boundary is inserted
        ↑ map
-------- flowOn / buffer channel boundary --------
        ↑ flow { emit(load()) }  upstream context selected by flowOn

collection #1 → new builder execution → its own local state
collection #2 → new builder execution → its own local state

Most operators are flows that collect upstream and emit transformed values downstream. Without buffer, flowOn, channelFlow, or another concurrency boundary, one coroutine traverses the chain. A boundary introduces producer/consumer decoupling and a channel. Ordering remains operator-defined, while timing and in-flight cancellation become observable design concerns.

Builders, cold execution, and sequential collection#

  • flowOf(a, b) represents fixed values; supported values, Iterable, Sequence, and ranges can use asFlow(). flow { } is the general sequential builder with suspending emit.
  • Code inside flow { } executes for every collect. A network read, database query, or listener registration inside it repeats per collector unless cached or shared elsewhere.
  • take(n) completes early by aborting upstream collection through Flow machinery; upstream finally must still release resources. A finite flow can complete normally; an infinite flow needs cancellation or a limiting condition.
  • Terminal operators include collect, first, single, toList, reduce, and fold. Their empty and multiple-element contracts differ, so do not substitute one only for convenience.
fun observeOrders(): Flow<Order> = flow {
    repository.snapshot().forEach { emit(it) } // runs per collector
}

val labels = observeOrders()
    .filter { it.visible }
    .map { it.toLabel() }
    .take(20)

labels.collect { render(it) }                  // terminal, cancellable suspension

Context preservation, exception transparency, and flowOn#

  • The flow builder preserves context: do not emit from arbitrary withContext or a launched coroutine. Sequential emissions belong to the collection context. Use flowOn for upstream context or channelFlow for concurrent producers.
  • Exception transparency means an implementation stops emitting when emit or emitAll fails. Do not catch a downstream failure and emit a fallback from the same builder; handle only the boundary you own.
  • flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) changes only operators upstream of its position. It does not move downstream mapping or collector/UI rendering. The collector stays in its caller context.
  • When the dispatcher changes, flowOn commonly runs upstream in another coroutine and uses a channel with default buffering. Adjacent channelFlow, flowOn, and buffer boundaries can fuse; explicit buffer controls capacity. Cancellation can leave an already produced value undelivered, so do not infer exactly-once hand-off.

Intermediate and terminal operator semantics#

OperatorSemanticsSenior caveat
map / filterOne-to-one transformation / conditional forwarding.Sequential by default; expensive code runs in the context at that pipeline position.
transformCan emit zero, one, or many values for one input.Keep emission and error ownership explicit; it is not implicit parallelism.
collectProcesses every delivered value in order.A slow action suspends the pipeline unless a buffer boundary exists.
collectLatestA new value cancels the previous action and starts the new one.It cancels work; the action must be cancellable and safe to abandon.
debounceEmits after a quiet window; continuously changing input can postpone output.Time-based; every overload (Long, Duration, lambda) is currently @FlowPreview; not a durable event queue.
sampleEmits the latest available value at sampling ticks.Can omit the final and intermediate values; check current API status and version.
distinctUntilChangedSuppresses consecutive equal values.Equality quality matters; applying it to StateFlow has no effect because state is already distinct.

Rate mismatch: buffer, conflate, and latest families#

  • buffer(capacity) lets producer and consumer run concurrently up to capacity. It changes suspension, timing, and memory use, but with default overflow it does not intentionally discard values.
  • conflate() keeps the most recent value while the consumer is busy: the emitter is not suspended by that slow collector and intermediate values are dropped. This fits replaceable state or progress, not audit events or payments.
  • collectLatest, mapLatest, and transformLatest cancel prior work when a new input arrives. Cancellation is cooperative; non-cancellable blocking work may continue, and side effects are not rolled back.
  • Use “backpressure” only informally for producer/consumer rate mismatch and suspension or buffering policy. Kotlin Flow can interoperate with Reactive Streams, but ordinary Flow code should not claim Reactive Streams request accounting, delivery, or exactly-once guarantees.

callbackFlow, channelFlow, and cleanup races#

fun locations(): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val listener = LocationListener { value ->
        trySend(value).onFailure { cause -> logger.debug("location dropped", cause) }
    }
    client.register(listener)
    awaitClose { client.unregister(listener) }
}.buffer(capacity = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
  • Both builders expose a ProducerScope. channelFlow permits concurrent child coroutines and thread-safe sends, and completes after its block and children. callbackFlow is the callback adapter and must keep the channel open for multi-shot callbacks.
  • send suspends according to channel capacity; trySend immediately returns a ChannelResult. Ignoring failure silently loses data. The builder has a channel/buffer boundary; adjacent buffer configures capacity and overflow.
  • callbackFlow requires cleanup with awaitClose { unregister(...) }. Registration, callbacks, cancellation, and unregistration can race; external unregister must be safe from the required thread/context and ideally idempotent.
  • Handle registration failure before or around awaitClose, and do not assume one callback maps to one collector delivery. Buffer overflow, cancellation, and downstream policy can reject or drop values.

Android lifecycle and Compose collection#

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        launch { viewModel.ui.collect(::renderUi) }
        launch { viewModel.messages.collect(::showMessage) }
    }
}

// Compose UI boundary
val ui by viewModel.ui.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
  • repeatOnLifecycle launches its block at or above the target state, cancels below it, and re-launches on re-entry. To collect multiple flows in parallel, launch one child per flow; sequentially collecting an infinite flow never reaches the next collect.
  • flowWithLifecycle is convenient for one flow, but operator position affects which surrounding pipeline remains active. For multiple streams or explicit ownership, repeatOnLifecycle is clearer.
  • A lifecycle restart re-collects a cold flow and can repeat upstream network calls, registrations, or writes. Put side effects behind idempotent, cached, or explicitly shared ownership rather than accidentally in a UI collection recipe.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle is a Compose-to-State collection boundary, not a repository architecture or event-delivery guarantee. Keep domain and data APIs lifecycle-free where possible.

Safe exposure, completion, and error ownership#

  • A repository can expose Flow<DomainModel> while keeping mutable callback, channel, and source details private. A ViewModel exposes read-only streams or state and owns UI mapping; UI should not receive mutable producers.
  • Document whether a flow is finite or long-lived, what starts per collection, dispatcher and main-safety, cancellation and cleanup, error types, and who owns retry or fallback. Flow does not cache by default.
  • Normal completion is a valid outcome, not an error. onCompletion observes a completion cause but is not a universal catch; collector/action failures remain downstream ownership. Do not encode every failure as nullable data.
  • Cold versus hot does not define “event.” Neither Flow, Channel, nor lifecycle collection provides a blanket exactly-once UI or business event guarantee; durable effects need persisted identity, acknowledgement, and reconciliation.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

Safe claimDo not promise
A cold builder executes anew for every collector.Cold means background, cached, single-shot, or side-effect-free.
The default pipeline is sequential; collection is cancellable and context-preserving.Blocking work stops immediately, or flowOn moves the downstream collector.
conflate keeps the latest and drops intermediate values.Every emission is processed, or conflation fits non-replaceable events.
collectLatest cancels the prior action.Prior blocking work stops or external side effects roll back.
awaitClose supplies callback cleanup on close or cancellation.Registration and unregistration are race-free without explicit design.
A lifecycle restart can start a fresh cold collection.Upstream side effects run once or events are delivered exactly once.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Pin one consistent kotlinx-coroutines family and inspect the resolved API. debounce/sample overloads, annotations, default capacities, and fusion details can evolve.
  • flowOn channel behavior depends on whether the dispatcher actually changes and on adjacent fusible operators. Never derive a business invariant from a default buffer size.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle comes from AndroidX lifecycle-runtime-compose; overloads, supported platforms, and default lifecycle state depend on the resolved AndroidX version.
  • The lifecycle boundary is conceptually stable, but minimum active state and operator placement are code-level choices. Test the versions in the app, not a remembered blog sample.

Decision framework#

  1. Define the stream: finite or ongoing, cold recipe or truly shared state/event, and what every collector starts.
  2. Place ownership: source and cleanup in the repository, UI mapping in the ViewModel, lifecycle collection at the UI boundary.
  3. Draw contexts: collector context, upstream flowOn boundary, blocking calls, and allowed emission scope.
  4. Choose loss semantics: preserve each value with suspension/buffer, drop replaceable intermediate values with conflate/sample/debounce, or cancel obsolete work with latest operators.
  5. Specify completion and errors: normal completion, cancellation, source failure, downstream failure, and translation/retry owner.
  6. Audit restarts and races: multiple collectors, lifecycle restart, callback registration/unregistration, buffer overflow, and non-idempotent effects.
  7. Test the public contract: per-collector execution, ordering, cancellation and cleanup, exact operator semantics, and lifecycle integration separately.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A purely sequential flow is predictable and bounds production by suspension, but a slow collector increases end-to-end latency. Buffering improves overlap at the cost of memory and in-flight cancellation.
  • Conflation and latest operators reduce obsolete work but lose intermediate state or cancel actions. They are wrong when each item carries non-replaceable meaning.
  • Cold per-collector execution gives isolation, but duplicate collectors duplicate I/O and callback registrations. Do not “fix” this with a hidden global scope; choose explicit Stage 10/11 sharing when required.
  • Lifecycle-aware collection prevents off-screen UI updates, but restart can repeat upstream effects and lose transient non-durable events.
  • callbackFlow makes callbacks composable but adds buffer, close, and race semantics. Missing awaitClose leaks listeners; unchecked trySend hides loss.

Production scenario: search suggestions#

Hypothetically: the UI exposes query changes; the ViewModel trims and applies distinctUntilChanged, debounces deliberate typing bursts, and performs cancellable latest search work. The repository returns a cold main-safe flow; blocking SDK work is isolated upstream with flowOn(IO). Results are collected with lifecycle awareness. Recreation can re-collect, so cache and request deduplication belong to an owned data layer rather than an assumption about cold Flow.

A location callback for nearby suggestions is wrapped in callbackFlow. The trySend result is observed, buffer overflow policy is explicit, and awaitClose unregisters race-safely. Search results are replaceable, so cancellation or conflation may fit; analytics and purchase events are not, so they use a separate durable policy. Errors map at the repository or use-case boundary, while UI owns presentation and collector cancellation.

Code-review/debugging trap#

fun updates() = flow {
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(api.load()) } // violates flow context invariant
}.conflate()                                       // silently wrong for audit events

fun callbacks() = callbackFlow {
    sdk.register { trySend(it) }                   // result ignored
    // no awaitClose: registration leaks / builder contract fails
}

lifecycleScope.launch {
    flowA.collect(::renderA)
    flowB.collect(::renderB)                       // unreachable for infinite flowA
}

Review should move upstream work with flowOn or call a main-safe suspend API, preserve every audit event, inspect trySend, unregister in race-safe awaitClose, and collect independent infinite flows in sibling coroutines under repeatOnLifecycle. Debug by recording collector identity, context, emission and action timestamps, cancellation cause, buffer policy, and register/unregister counts. Never infer exactly-once from a clean log.

Testing cold Flow fundamentals#

  • For a finite flow under runTest, use toList() or first() and assert values, order, completion, and failure. For an ongoing flow, collect in backgroundScope and cancel or bound it with take.
  • Collect the same cold flow twice and assert two source invocations and isolated local state when that is its contract. This catches accidental caching or accidentally duplicated effects.
  • Use a shared TestCoroutineScheduler to drive debounce and sample delays. Test just before, at, and after boundaries without treating virtual scheduling as production thread ordering.
  • For callbackFlow, fake registration, trigger callbacks, cancel the collector, and assert unregister according to the adapter contract, including cancellation during registration and failed trySend. Add real-thread integration or stress coverage for thread-safety races.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. What does cold Flow mean? Its builder starts at a terminal operator and executes independently for every collector. It does not imply background execution, caching, or absence of side effects.
  2. Is collection sequential? By default, yes: emit waits through downstream processing. Explicit buffer or concurrency boundaries decouple producer and consumer.
  3. Where does a flow execute? In the collector context unless an operator such as flowOn changes its upstream segment. flowOn never moves the downstream collector.
  4. Why context preservation and exception transparency? They support local reasoning: emission cannot jump arbitrary context, and a failed emit cannot be followed by hidden fallback emissions.
  5. collect or collectLatest? Collect handles every delivered value; collectLatest cancels the prior action for a new one. Use latest only when obsolete work is cancellable and safe to abandon.
  6. buffer or conflate? Buffer overlaps producer and consumer and normally preserves queued values; conflate keeps the latest and drops intermediate values.
  7. How do debounce and sample differ? Debounce waits for quiet; sample emits the latest at periodic ticks. Both can omit inputs and do not provide durable event delivery.
  8. When should you use callbackFlow? For a multi-shot callback adapter with explicit send-result and capacity policy plus mandatory race-safe awaitClose cleanup.
  9. How do you collect in a Fragment or Compose? Views use repeatOnLifecycle; Compose commonly uses collectAsStateWithLifecycle for state. Multiple infinite flows need parallel child collection.
  10. What delivery guarantee does Flow provide? Only its documented operator, context, and cancellation contract. It has no blanket caching or exactly-once business/event delivery guarantee.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Two screens collect the same repository cold flow. Expect two executions and possibly two registrations or I/O calls. Decide whether isolation is desired; otherwise define owned sharing in Stage 10/11 rather than assuming cache.
  2. A value disappears around flowOn cancellation. A dispatcher-changing flowOn uses a channel boundary; cancellation can prevent in-flight delivery. A business-critical transfer needs durable identity and reconciliation, not timing assumptions.
  3. collectLatest starts duplicate server writes. Cancellation does not roll back a write, and blocking code may ignore it. Do not use latest for non-idempotent effects; use operation IDs and explicit serialization or status.
  4. Lifecycle restart registers the listener twice. Verify prior awaitClose unregister, the race-safe SDK contract, and collector ownership. A new cold collection legitimately registers again after cleanup.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Which operations in your pipeline execute per collector, and in which context?
  2. Where can values buffer or drop, and where can prior work be cancelled?
  3. Which lifecycle restarts repeat upstream side effects, and are they safe?
  4. Does the callback adapter inspect trySend and unregister race-safely?
  5. Which layer owns normal completion, source error, downstream error, and cancellation?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do Kotlin Flow execution, context, rate mismatch, and Android lifecycle collection work?

~30-second answer#

A normal Flow is a cold recipe: each terminal collection runs its builder again. The pipeline is sequential in the collector context unless I add a boundary. flowOn moves only its upstream segment and may introduce a buffered channel; it never moves downstream UI collection. Buffer overlaps work, conflate drops intermediate values, and collectLatest cancels the previous action. callbackFlow needs checked sends and race-safe awaitClose cleanup. On Android I collect at the UI lifecycle boundary and remember that a restart can rerun cold upstream effects. Flow itself provides neither caching nor blanket exactly-once delivery.

~2-minute answer#

I model Flow as a suspending asynchronous sequence contract. flowOf and asFlow cover fixed sources, while flow builds a sequential producer. Intermediate operators are lazy and a terminal operator starts collection. A cold flow runs independently for every collector, so it is not automatically background, shared, or cached.

By default, emit and downstream operators form a sequential call chain in the collector coroutine. Context preservation prevents arbitrary cross-context emit, and exception transparency prevents continuing with hidden emissions after emit fails. I use flowOn only to change the upstream segment. If it changes dispatcher, it normally creates an upstream coroutine and channel boundary, so capacity and in-flight cancellation matter rather than assumed delivery.

For rate mismatch I choose semantics explicitly. Buffer overlaps producer and consumer while normally retaining queued values; conflate drops intermediate values and retains the latest; latest operators cancel obsolete work. Cancellation is cooperative and never rolls back an external effect. Debounce, sample, and distinctUntilChanged suppress values under different time or equality rules, so they fit replaceable inputs, not durable events.

For callbacks I use callbackFlow or channelFlow with ProducerScope, inspect trySend or use suspending send deliberately, configure the buffer, and always use race-safe awaitClose unregister. On Android, repeatOnLifecycle restarts collection and parallel flows need child coroutines; flowWithLifecycle is convenient for one chain, while collectAsStateWithLifecycle is only the Compose state boundary. A restart can repeat cold upstream effects. Repositories expose read-only, main-safe contracts and document completion and errors; tests verify per-collector execution, order, cancellation, timing policy, and cleanup. Hot state, sharing, flattening, retry, and combine require separate design rather than being implied by Flow.

  • callbackFlow, channelFlow, and awaitClose

StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel, and Android UI state/eventsexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to distinguish replaceable state, a transient effect, and a durable outcome; explain the exact contracts of StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel, stateIn, and shareIn; choose lifecycle and persistence boundaries; find races and lost updates; and test replay, buffering, and subscriber timing. This stage does not repeat Stage 9 cold Flow basics or Stage 11 advanced operator composition.

Senior mental model#

Classify the information before choosing a primitive. State answers “what is true now?” and a new UI can render it. An effect is a short-lived presentation command whose loss and repetition policy must be explicit. A durable outcome is a business fact with persisted identity, status, and reconciliation; an in-memory stream does not make it durable.

  • StateFlow is a hot conflated state holder with a current value; SharedFlow is a configurable hot broadcast; Channel is a send/receive queue and ownership hand-off, not UI acknowledgement.
  • A hot object exists independently of collectors, but an owner scope determines producer lifetime. The UI lifecycle should control collection, not the lifetime of a business operation.
  • Navigation, a snackbar, and payment completion have different significance. No primitive alone guarantees exactly-once user-visible handling across inactivity, recreation, and process death.

Internals and contracts#

durable source / SavedStateHandle / repository
                 ↓ reducer (serialized or atomic transition)
MutableStateFlow<UiState> ── latest state ──► lifecycle-aware UI
                 │
                 └─ optional transient-effect policy ─► SharedFlow or Channel

Cold upstream ── stateIn/shareIn(ownerScope, started, replay/initial) ──► subscribers

StateFlow: state, equality, and atomic updates#

  • MutableStateFlow(initialValue) requires an initial value; value synchronously reads current state. It is a hot holder that replays the latest value to a new collector.
  • Updates are conflated using Any.equals: assigning an equal value emits nothing, and a slow collector can skip fast intermediate values and observe the latest. StateFlow is therefore not an event queue; behavior is unspecified when equality is broken by mutable models.
  • value, methods, and atomic helpers are thread-safe. For read-modify-write, use update, updateAndGet, or getAndUpdate. Their lambda can run more than once under contention, so it must have no side effects.
  • _state.value = _state.value.copy(count = _state.value.count + 1) has a lost-update race between concurrent writers. Atomic update protects one holder transition, not a multi-store transaction or external side effect.
  • Collecting StateFlow never completes normally; failure and completion must be materialized in state. Expose asStateFlow(), not the mutable producer.

SharedFlow: replay, buffer, and subscribers#

  • MutableSharedFlow(replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow) broadcasts each accepted value to all active subscribers. The replay cache gives the latest replay values to new collectors; extra capacity supports lagging active subscribers.
  • A non-default onBufferOverflow is allowed only when replay + extraBufferCapacity > 0. Overflow occurs only with a slow subscriber. With no subscribers, only replay values are retained; overflow has no effect and extra capacity does not accumulate an offline backlog.
  • emit can suspend only with SUSPEND and active slow subscribers. tryEmit is non-suspending and can return false only in that situation. On an unbuffered flow with no subscribers, tryEmit returns true but the value is discarded immediately.
  • subscriptionCount is a StateFlow of active collector count for resource policy, not acknowledgement of a specific event. A check-then-emit sequence races with subscription changes.
  • resetReplayCache() is experimental: it clears replay for future subscribers, while current subscribers retain already buffered values. It is not erasure, a transaction, or durable deletion.
  • SharedFlow never completes normally and does not represent failure itself; materialize completion or error. Replay is an in-memory cache, not durable storage.

stateIn, shareIn, and SharingStarted#

  • stateIn turns a cold upstream into shared StateFlow with an initial/latest value; shareIn creates SharedFlow with specified replay. The sharing coroutine belongs to the supplied scope, so that scope must match the data lifetime.
  • Eagerly starts immediately; values beyond replay can be lost before subscribers. Lazily starts at the first subscriber and never stops. WhileSubscribed starts and stops with subscribers, so upstream can restart and repeat I/O or side effects.
  • WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis, replayExpirationMillis) can delay stopping and resetting the cache. Expiration empties shareIn replay or resets stateIn to its original initial value. Check defaults and version-specific overloads in the resolved API.
  • Normal upstream completion does not complete subscribers; the sharing coroutine follows its strategy and can restart with WhileSubscribed. An upstream exception terminates the sharing coroutine and is handled by the owner scope, not automatically by collectors. Materialize, catch, or retry before the boundary according to contract.

Channel and Channel-to-Flow boundaries#

CapacitySemanticsRisk
RENDEZVOUSZero buffer; send meets receive.Sender suspension couples lifetimes.
BUFFEREDDefault-sized buffer determined by library/configuration.Do not derive business guarantees from its size.
CONFLATEDAt most the latest element; older values are lost.Wrong for non-replaceable work.
UNLIMITEDSender does not suspend for capacity.Unbounded memory with a stalled receiver.
  • send suspends as capacity requires; trySend returns ChannelResult; receive suspends for an element. Always inspect failed non-suspending operations.
  • close rejects new sends and lets buffered elements drain; normal close eventually ends receiving. cancel removes remaining elements and cancels waiters. Producer and consumer ownership must define who closes or cancels and why.
  • One channel element is received by one receiver. Multiple receivers compete, creating fan-out/work distribution; one receiver provides single-consumer ordering. A Channel is not broadcast.
  • Prompt cancellation creates a hand-off caveat: cancellation can happen after an element is obtained but before caller processing starts. onUndeliveredElement enables synchronous resource cleanup, not business exactly-once.
  • receiveAsFlow() supports multiple collectors competing for elements, and collector failure does not cancel the source channel. consumeAsFlow() is single-collection and consumes or cancels the source on collector failure. Neither makes receipt equivalent to handled UI effect.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

GuaranteeNon-guarantee
StateFlow has a current value, required initial state, equality conflation, and thread-safe atomic-update APIs.It records every transition, queues events, completes, or persists across process death.
SharedFlow broadcasts accepted values under its configured replay and buffer policy.It represents completion/failure, replay is durable storage, or inactive collectors receive replay=0 events.
Channel defines queue, capacity, close/cancel, and receive ownership.Delivery equals UI handling, cancellation cannot lose a hand-off, or memory survives process death.
Lifecycle APIs stop and restart collection at the UI boundary.They make transient effects exactly once or prevent WhileSubscribed upstream restart.
Persistence plus IDs and acknowledgement can support retry and reconciliation.No primitive alone guarantees exactly-once user-visible handling.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Pin one kotlinx-coroutines family and inspect signatures. resetReplayCache is experimental; Duration/millisecond WhileSubscribed overloads and annotations vary by release.
  • Channel.BUFFERED capacity can be changed by JVM property; never depend on a remembered numeric default. Prompt-cancellation and onUndeliveredElement behavior belongs to the resolved library contract.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle comes from AndroidX lifecycle-runtime-compose; overloads, platform support, and default lifecycle state depend on the resolved version.
  • SavedStateHandle provides Bundle-compatible, size-bounded restoration semantics, not arbitrary durable business storage. API integrations differ by AndroidX version.

Decision matrix#

NeedPrimary modelRequired policy
Renderable latest screen stateImmutable StateFlow<UiState>Initial value, reducer, equality, lifecycle collection.
Replaceable shared signal or tickSharedFlowReplay, buffer, overflow, and subscriber absence explicitly accepted.
In-memory work hand-off to one consumerChannelCapacity, ownership, close/cancel, undelivered policy.
Expensive cold source shared in an owner scopestateIn/shareInScope, start strategy, replay expiration, restart/error policy.
Payment or order completionPersisted operation/result as source of truthStable ID, idempotency, status query, acknowledgement/reconciliation; UI derives state.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A one-off event wrapper in state can replay an already “consumed” event to another collector or lose it through a consume race. Mutable consumed flags also violate immutable state.
  • SharedFlow(replay=0) misses an inactive UI; replay=1 can repeat stale navigation or a snackbar after recreation and sends it to every collector.
  • A Channel can retain an effect during short UI inactivity within ViewModel lifetime, but competing collectors split events, recreation timing races, and process death clears the queue. Receive does not mean navigation or a snackbar was shown.
  • Modeling an effect as state enables replay and recovery, but needs idempotent acknowledgement or a clear transition; state conflation can suppress an equal repeat.
  • A mutable object or list inside StateFlow can change in place without a new unequal value; Compose has no reliable immutable snapshot boundary. Emit immutable copies.
  • WhileSubscribed saves resources, but stop/restart churn can duplicate expensive setup. Choose a timeout and idempotent upstream.

Production scenario: checkout outcome, navigation, and snackbar#

Hypothetically: a checkout ViewModel reducer updates immutable CheckoutUiState with update. Form, loading, and error information that must survive recreation is state. A draft ID and minimal restorable input can live in SavedStateHandle; the cart, payment operation, and completion are persisted by the repository, database, or server. stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(...), initial) has an explicit restart and error policy.

A successful payment is not an ephemeral “navigate now.” The repository records operation ID and status; UI state exposes completion, and navigation is an idempotent presentation reaction keyed by destination or handled ID before acknowledgement updates state. A low-value hint can be a documented best-effort SharedFlow snackbar; an actionable error stays state until user action. This is not an exactly-once claim: a crash can happen between display and acknowledgement, so critical outcome reconciles from durable truth.

private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CheckoutUiState())
val state = _state.asStateFlow()
private val _effects = MutableSharedFlow<UiEffect>(
    replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST
)

fun quantityChanged(delta: Int) {
    _state.update { old -> old.copy(quantity = old.quantity + delta) }
}

// Best effort only; payment completion is persisted and reduced into state.
fun hint(text: String) { _effects.tryEmit(UiEffect.Snackbar(text)) }

Code-review/debugging trap#

_state.value = _state.value.copy(count = _state.value.count + 1) // lost update
_events.emit(NavigateToReceipt)                                  // replay=0; no collector
if (_events.subscriptionCount.value > 0) _events.emit(effect)     // check/emit race
val effects = Channel<UiEffect>(Channel.UNLIMITED)                // hidden memory growth
orders.stateIn(GlobalScope)                                       // wrong lifetime/defaults

Review should require an atomic reducer, explicit scope/start/replay/buffer/overflow, read-only exposure, immutable state, lifecycle collection, and a durable boundary. Debug producer scope, subscription-count transitions, replay cache, buffer result, collector identity and lifecycle, operation IDs, and timestamps. Do not “fix” a race by enlarging a buffer without defining delivery requirements.

Testing timing, replay, and concurrency#

  • In runTest, start the collector before emission when the contract requires it; a hot flow does not save everything automatically. Use backgroundScope, runCurrent, advanceTimeBy/advanceUntilIdle, and one shared scheduler.
  • StateFlow: assert initial/current value, equal suppression, slow-collector conflation, and concurrent update. Do not expect every intermediate value.
  • SharedFlow: cover before/after subscribe, zero/multiple subscribers, replay 0/N, full buffer, each overflow mode, emit suspension, tryEmit result, and replay reset for a future collector.
  • stateIn/shareIn: count upstream starts/stops, test stop timeout and replay expiration around exact virtual-time boundaries, and assert WhileSubscribed restart and owner-scope cancellation.
  • Channel: test every capacity, competing receivers, close versus cancel, failed send/receive, and onUndeliveredElement. Add lifecycle, recreation, and process-restoration integration tests plus real-thread stress tests; virtual time is not proof of thread ordering.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Why does StateFlow fit UI state? It has an initial/current value, latest replay, equality conflation, and thread-safe updates, so UI can render a snapshot. It is not an event queue.
  2. Why is a value++-style update unsafe? Read-modify-write is not atomic. Use update, updateAndGet, or getAndUpdate with a side-effect-free lambda.
  3. What does SharedFlow retain without subscribers? Only its replay cache; extra capacity and overflow do not create an offline queue. tryEmit can succeed while the value is discarded.
  4. emit or tryEmit? Emit can suspend under SUSPEND and a slow subscriber; tryEmit immediately reports its result. Success means contract acceptance, not UI handling.
  5. When does WhileSubscribed restart upstream? After it stops for lack of subscribers, a new subscription starts upstream again. Effects must be restart-safe and replay expiration explicit.
  6. Channel or SharedFlow? Channel distributes one item to one receiver; SharedFlow broadcasts to active subscribers. Both are in-memory and neither gives UI exactly-once.
  7. How do receiveAsFlow and consumeAsFlow differ? The first permits competing collectors and does not consume the source on collector failure; the second collects once and consumes or cancels the source.
  8. How should navigation and snackbars be modeled? Use requirements: a best-effort hint can be transient; a required next action should be state with idempotent handling and acknowledgement. Document loss and replay, not exactly-once.
  9. How should payment completion be modeled? Persist operation ID and status, make the server action idempotent, reconcile, and derive UI state. Channel or SharedFlow can only signal refresh.
  10. How should Android UI collect? Views use repeatOnLifecycle; Compose state uses collectAsStateWithLifecycle. Immutable state is the recomposition boundary; lifecycle restart cannot recover in-memory effects.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Two collectors received the same navigation effect. SharedFlow is broadcast. If one UI owner owns the action, enforce ownership or idempotent destination state rather than relying on a collector race.
  2. The same snackbar text is sent twice. StateFlow suppresses equal values; an event wrapper does not add durability. Add identity and state acknowledgement or accept best-effort SharedFlow behavior.
  3. Upstream reconnects repeatedly on rotation. Audit owner scope, lifecycle subscribers, WhileSubscribed timeout, and restart semantics; make setup idempotent and test start count.
  4. Channel send succeeded, but UI did not navigate. Receipt and handling differ; cancellation or a crash can occur between them. Critical navigation derives from durable, idempotent state and reconciles.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. What in your model is current state, a transient presentation effect, and a durable business outcome?
  2. What happens to an emission with no subscribers, a slow subscriber, and buffer overflow?
  3. Who owns the sharing or channel scope, close/cancel, and upstream restart?
  4. Which transitions are atomic, and which need a transaction or idempotency beyond StateFlow?
  5. What survives recreation and process death, and how does UI acknowledgement reconcile?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you choose among StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel, and durable UI state?

~30-second answer#

I classify the data first. StateFlow is for a current, replaceable value: it needs an initial value, exposes the latest value, conflates by equality, and should be updated atomically. SharedFlow is a configurable broadcast with replay and buffer policy, while Channel is a one-receiver hand-off queue. None is durable and none means the UI handled an effect. I collect state with the Android lifecycle, expose immutable state, and model critical outcomes such as payment completion in persisted state with identity and reconciliation rather than claiming exactly-once navigation.

~2-minute answer#

I start with semantics, not the API. Renderable UI state answers what is true now, so I expose an immutable StateFlow from a ViewModel. It has a required initial and current value, equality-based conflation, and never completes normally. Concurrent read-modify-write must use update, updateAndGet, or getAndUpdate; the lambda is side-effect free because it can be retried.

SharedFlow is hot broadcast. I specify replay, extra capacity, overflow, and behavior with no subscribers. Extra capacity is not an offline queue; without subscribers only replay is retained. emit can suspend for slow subscribers, while tryEmit reports immediate acceptance, not UI handling. Channel gives queue and one-receiver ownership with explicit capacity, close, cancellation, and undelivered-element policy. Multiple receivers compete. receiveAsFlow preserves that fan-out; consumeAsFlow is single-use and consumes the source.

For cold-source sharing, stateIn and shareIn belong to an owner scope. Eagerly, Lazily, and WhileSubscribed differ in start and stop lifetime. WhileSubscribed can stop, reset replay after expiration, and restart upstream, so setup and effects must tolerate restarts. Upstream errors need an explicit policy before the sharing boundary.

On Android, repeatOnLifecycle and collectAsStateWithLifecycle define collection boundaries, not delivery guarantees. Compose receives immutable snapshots and recomposes readers. A snackbar may be documented best effort, navigation should usually be idempotent state-driven when it matters, and payment completion must be persisted with an operation ID, status, acknowledgement, and reconciliation. SavedStateHandle restores small UI/process state, not durable business truth. Tests place subscribers before and after emissions, fill buffers, advance virtual time around sharing timeouts, race atomic updates, and verify recreation and process-restoration behavior. No primitive alone provides exactly-once user-visible handling.
