Advanced Kotlin Flow in productionexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage you should be able to design a production Flow topology: select timing, order, and completion semantics for composition and flattening; build latest-wins search without stale state; localize failure and retry; own sharing lifecycle and cache boundaries; integrate callbacks; and prove timing, cancellation, retry, and sharing with deterministic tests. Stage 9 basics and Stage 10 primitives appear only as comparative context.

Senior mental model#

A Flow topology is executable policy. For every edge, name ownership, ordering, concurrency, buffering, cancellation, failure, restart, and durability. An operator cannot repair the wrong business contract: latest-wins, all-results, paired-results, and durable work are different requirements.

  • A cold chain runs per collector; a hot boundary moves execution into its owner scope. Collector lifecycle and producer lifecycle are separate decisions.
  • Cancellation is control flow, not rollback. latest operators cancel cooperatively and cannot retract an HTTP request, database commit, or other external side effect.
  • Errors either terminate a stream or become typed domain values. Choose explicitly at a layer boundary.

Internals and operator topology#

source(s) → admission/rate policy → composition/flattening → error policy
          → context/buffer boundary → domain state → stateIn/shareIn(owner scope)
          → repeatOnLifecycle collector → render

Sequential operators normally execute in the collector coroutine. buffer, flowOn, flattening, channelFlow, and sharing may introduce channels or coroutines. Read data left-to-right, cancellation and failures right-to-left, and mark every external effect.

combine vs zip vs merge; flattening and latest transforms#

OperatorTiming/orderCompletion/failure
combineAfter its initial barrier, transforms latest values whenever any input changes.combine waits for the first value from every input. A completed input can retain its latest value while others emit; a failure terminates composition.
zipPairs the n-th values; a faster side waits/buffers under the contract.Completes when one side can form no more pairs and cancels remaining collection; failures propagate.
mergeCollects inputs concurrently and interleaves ready values without cross-input order.Normally completes after all inputs; an unhandled failure terminates merge and cancels siblings.
  • flatMapConcat collects inner flows sequentially and preserves outer order, with head-of-line blocking.
  • flatMapMerge(concurrency = n) collects up to n inners; output ordering follows timing. The limit is resource policy, not a business order or rate limit.
  • flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner; mapLatest cancels its previous transform; transformLatest can emit multiple values and cancels the whole previous block.
  • Use latest only when old work is obsolete. Use concat or bounded merge when every result matters.

Search pipeline: latest cancellation and stale-result protection#

val results: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = query
    .map(String::trim).debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { q ->
        if (q.length < 2) flowOf(SearchUiState.Idle)
        else flow<SearchUiState> {
            emit(SearchUiState.Loading(q))
            emit(SearchUiState.Content(q, repository.search(q)))
        }.catch { e ->
            if (e is CancellationException) throw e
            emit(SearchUiState.Error(q, e.toDomainError()))
        }
    }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState.Idle)
  • debounce is quiet-time admission; distinctUntilChanged removes adjacent equal normalized queries. Neither is caching.
  • For a blocking, uncancellable, or detached API, carry a request generation/query key into the reducer and reject a mismatched result.
  • Cancellation cannot undo a server mutation; writes need idempotency and reconciliation, not latest-wins.

Multi-source UI state and initial-emission traps#

  • Use combine for latest account, rows, and filter state when any source should rerender. Model initial/loading/absent/error explicitly.
  • A change-only callback, filtered source, or SharedFlow(replay=0) may never provide the first value, so combine may emit nothing. Seed only with a truthful initial state.
  • Independent latest values are not an atomic multi-source transaction. Read a database transaction or one versioned aggregate when consistency requires it.
  • One unhandled input failure terminates the aggregate. Materialize recoverable per-source errors before combine only when partial UI is required.

Exception transparency, completion, and retry boundaries#

  • catch handles upstream exceptions and preserves cancellation; catch does not catch downstream collector failures. An onEach before catch is in its recovery scope; one after catch is downstream.
  • onCompletion { cause } observes normal completion, failure, or cancellation and does not suppress failure. It is not catch.
  • retry/retryWhen re-subscribes and may repeat builders, calls, and side effects. Retry only typed transient failures with bounded attempts; never retry cancellation, programmer defects, authentication/authorization, validation, or deterministic client errors.
  • Use capped exponential backoff, jitter, connectivity policy, and a total deadline. Inject clock/randomness in tests and honor bounded server retry guidance.
  • Rethrow CancellationException. Materialize expected domain failures as sealed values if the stream should continue; terminate on invariants/programmer errors.

stateIn/shareIn lifecycle, cache, and single source of truth#

  • The supplied scope owns stateIn/shareIn. Match it to data lifetime; do not hide it in a global scope.
  • Eagerly starts now, Lazily starts once, and WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis, replayExpirationMillis) can stop, expire state/replay, and restart. Subscriber gaps can repeat setup or side effects.
  • Place catch/retry/completion policy before sharing. Normal upstream completion does not complete hot subscribers; an upstream exception is handled by the owner scope.
  • Hot-sharing replay is not a durable cache. It does not define freshness, persistence, invalidation, or the repository/database single source of truth.
  • Sharing provides no exactly-once network/database effect. Use idempotency, transactions/outbox, operation IDs, and reconciliation.

Context, fusion, buffers, concurrency, and partial results#

  • flowOn changes upstream context only and may create a channel across dispatchers; it cannot change collector context.
  • Adjacent channelFlow/callbackFlow, flowOn, buffer, and produceIn may fuse. Capacity, overflow, and placement change suspension, loss, and cancellation windows.
  • buffer overlaps producer and consumer; conflate drops intermediate values; latest cancels work. Place expensive transforms deliberately.
  • flatMapMerge bounds active inner collections, not all work those inners may spawn. Output order is not input order.
  • For independent partial failure, use supervisorScope outside Flow to create typed outcomes, then emit them. Merge is not a supervisor boundary.

callbackFlow and Android lifecycle re-subscription#

  • callbackFlow registers per collector, uses thread-safe trySend, and must unregister in awaitClose. Set buffering for the callback rate and inspect failed sends.
  • Make close/unregister races safe under the callback API. Cancellation cleans up but cannot undo callback side effects.
  • repeatOnLifecycle cancels and relaunches collection. A cold callback re-registers, and WhileSubscribed may restart after its timeout. Test start/stop counts.
  • Share in a longer owner only when multiple collectors should truly reuse one registration.

Guarantees vs non-guarantees#

GuaranteeNon-guarantee
combine uses latest after all first values; zip pairs; merge interleaves.Universal ordering, atomic snapshots, or an emission when a combine input never emits.
Latest requests cancellation of previous work.Preemption of blocking code or rollback of external effects.
Retry can re-subscribe conditionally.Safe repeats or exactly-once effects.
catch sees upstream non-cancellation failures.Downstream failures or cancellation are caught.
Sharing can replay in-memory values within its scope.Durable caching, invisible restart, or exactly-once network/database effects.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Latest/flattening/dynamic debounce and sharing APIs may have experimental or preview annotations in a resolved release. Inspect the pinned API.
  • Default merge concurrency and channel capacity can be library/property-sensitive; pass explicit values when operationally relevant.
  • WhileSubscribed overloads, Duration support, and replay-expiration annotations vary by release. Pin one coroutines family and test boundaries.
  • AndroidX lifecycle and Compose collection signatures/default states depend on the resolved AndroidX version; lifecycle is not durability.

Decision framework#

  1. Name the requirement: paired, latest snapshot, concurrent all-results, latest-wins, ordered work, or durable work.
  2. Write initial, completion, and failure behavior for every source.
  3. Choose cancellation/concurrency and classify every effect as idempotent, transactional, compensatable, or unsafe to repeat.
  4. Place context, buffers, catch/retry, and sharing; assign owner/start/expiration.
  5. Define source of truth, freshness, lifecycle re-subscription, telemetry, and a deterministic test timeline.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • combine is responsive but can recompute or wait forever; zip preserves pairing but stalls; merge improves concurrency with nondeterministic interleaving.
  • Latest removes stale cooperative work but drops progress; concat preserves order with latency; merge adds load, memory, and ordering costs.
  • Broad fallback catch hides incidents. Infinite broad retry amplifies outages and resource use.
  • Wrong sharing scope leaks; short timeout thrashes; long timeout retains resources; replay can be stale.
  • Lifecycle collection, retry, and sharing restart can multiply effects. Observe starts, attempts, cancellation, and operation IDs.

Production scenario: offline-first search#

Hypothetically: normalized query, account, and filters combine into a versioned request. Debounce/distinct/latest controls search. A database Flow is the single source of truth; refresh transactionally writes keyed network results. A generation guard rejects stale uncancellable completions. Bounded jittered retry handles transient I/O; auth and validation become domain state; cancellation is rethrown.

combine(query, filters, account) { q, f, a -> RequestKey(q.trim(), f, a.id) }
    .debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { key ->
        repository.observeRows(key)
            .onStart { repository.refresh(key) } // repeat-safe boundary required
            .retryWhen { e, attempt ->
                val retry = e is IOException && attempt < 3
                if (retry) delay(backoffWithJitter(attempt))
                retry
            }.catch { e ->
                if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                emit(emptyList()) // real code maps a typed domain error
            }
    }

The onStart refresh can repeat after retry or restart; production repository deduplication/idempotency owns it. There is no exactly-once network/database effect.

Code-review/debugging trap#

query.flatMapMerge { api.search(it) }          // stale results, unclear concurrency
    .catch { emit(emptyList()) }               // hides domain/programmer failures
    .retryWhen { _, _ -> true }                // repeats forever
    .shareIn(GlobalScope, Eagerly, replay = 1) // leaked owner; not persistence

Ask which result wins, what happens before first values, what can repeat, whether cancellation is preserved, who owns sharing, and where durable truth lives. Trace request ID, key, attempt, upstream start/stop, subscriber count, cancellation cause, latency, drops, and lifecycle state without logging secrets.

Deterministic testing and observability#

  • Use one runTest and shared TestCoroutineScheduler across injected test dispatchers; advance exact virtual-time boundaries.
  • Assert combine's barrier/latest snapshots, zip pairing/early completion, merge membership without false global order, and failure cancellation.
  • Make the old latest inner suspend, observe its finally, advance debounce exactly, reject stale output, and count retry subscriptions/effects/backoff.
  • For sharing, count starts/stops, cross timeout and replayExpirationMillis, resubscribe, cancel owner, and verify callback cleanup under lifecycle.
  • Telemetry distinguishes requested, admitted, started, cancelled, retried, succeeded, materialized error, stale-rejected, dropped, and rendered.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. combine, zip, or merge? combine produces latest snapshots after all first values; zip forms positional pairs and ends with the shorter side; merge interleaves concurrent inputs.
  2. Which flattening operator? concat for ordered all-results, bounded merge for concurrent all-results, latest when previous intent is obsolete.
  3. Why can search still become stale? Blocking, uncancellable, or detached work can complete externally; carry a generation/key and reject mismatches.
  4. Where should catch go? After the operators it owns and before its materialization/sharing boundary; it does not catch downstream collectors.
  5. What does onCompletion do? Observes normal, failed, or cancelled termination; it does not recover failure.
  6. When is retry safe? For classified transient failures with bounded backoff/jitter/deadline and repeat-safe upstream, never auth/validation/bugs/cancellation.
  7. Why can WhileSubscribed duplicate I/O? A new subscriber restarts a stopped cold upstream; choose owner/timeout and idempotent setup.
  8. Is replay a cache? It is only in-memory replay, not durable storage, freshness policy, or source of truth.
  9. How do partial results work? Materialize per-source outcomes; use supervisorScope outside Flow for independent concurrent failure isolation.
  10. How do you test timing? runTest with one scheduler, controlled fakes, explicit virtual-time steps, and cancellation/subscription/attempt assertions.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. A combine input completed after a value. Its latest can continue combining with other inputs; decide whether that stale completed dimension is acceptable.
  2. One user action caused three POSTs. Retry re-subscribed. Use an idempotency key and reconciliation or retry only a safe read.
  3. Rotation reconnects a callback twice. Trace repeatOnLifecycle, stop timeout, and owner; make register/unregister symmetric and test subscribers.
  4. You need input order and concurrency. Add sequence IDs and an explicit reordering aggregator, or use concat when latency permits.

5 unanswered self-checks#

  1. What are each source's initial, completion, and error contracts if it never emits?
  2. Where does cooperative cancellation end, and what stale guard remains?
  3. Which effects can retry, re-subscription, or sharing restart repeat?
  4. Who owns hot scope, replay lifetime, source of truth, and invalidation?
  5. What virtual timeline proves debounce, cancellation, retry, and replay expiration?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you design a production Kotlin Flow pipeline?

~30-second answer#

I treat a Flow chain as an execution policy. I use combine for latest snapshots after every input emits, zip for pairs, and merge for unordered concurrent values. Search normalizes, debounces, deduplicates, and uses flatMapLatest plus a stale request guard because cancellation is cooperative. I classify failures before bounded retry, preserve cancellation, and scope catch upstream. Sharing has an explicit owner and start strategy; replay is not durable cache. runTest with one scheduler verifies timing, cancellation, retries, restart, and lifecycle re-subscription.

~2-minute answer#

I first name the required semantics: positional pairs, latest snapshot, concurrent all-results, latest-wins, ordered work, or durable work. combine waits for every first value, zip pairs and ends with the shorter side, and merge interleaves. flatMapConcat preserves order, flatMapMerge bounds concurrent inner flows, and latest variants cooperatively cancel old work.

For search I normalize, debounce, deduplicate, and flatMapLatest. Cancellation cannot roll back a request, commit, blocking call, or detached job, so I carry a request key and reject stale completion. Multi-source UI models truthful initial/loading/error values; independent latest values are not an atomic transaction.

catch handles upstream non-cancellation failures, not downstream collectors. onCompletion observes but does not recover. retryWhen re-subscribes and can repeat effects, so only typed transient failures receive bounded capped backoff, jitter, and a total deadline; cancellation, auth, validation, and programmer errors do not. Expected domain errors may become values.

stateIn/shareIn belongs to a named scope. Eagerly, Lazily, and WhileSubscribed differ in start, stop, replay expiration, and restart, so upstream setup must tolerate repetition. Replay is memory, not durable cache or source of truth. flowOn and buffer placement changes concurrency and may fuse with callbackFlow; awaitClose owns callback cleanup. repeatOnLifecycle re-subscribes. Tests use one TestCoroutineScheduler and assert exact emissions, cancellation, attempts, starts/stops, replay reset, and callback cleanup. Observability records request IDs, attempts, cancellation causes, and lifecycle. Exactly-once network/database effects require idempotency and transactional reconciliation outside Flow.

Official references#

  • Kotlin Flow guide and kotlinx.coroutines Flow API
  • combine, zip, merge
  • flatMapLatest, flatMapMerge, flatMapConcat, transformLatest, mapLatest
  • catch, onCompletion, retryWhen
  • stateIn, shareIn, SharingStarted
  • buffer та operator fusion, flowOn, callbackFlow
  • StateFlow and SharedFlow on Android, Lifecycle-aware Flow collection, Testing Kotlin flows on Android
  • kotlinx-coroutines-test, runTest, TestCoroutineScheduler
Android UI architecture and state modeling: MVVM, MVI, UDFexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should design UI architecture through ownership, sources of truth, data flow, and failure semantics rather than an MVVM/MVI label: classify state by lifetime and durability, set ViewModel/state-holder boundaries, model loading/content/empty/error/stale/refresh/pagination without hidden combinations, separate effects from durable outcomes, protect asynchronous transitions from stale results, and test reducers, lifecycle, and integration boundaries. Stage 10 already covers hot-stream primitives; Stage 13 covers layering and modularization, so this stage stays at the UI boundary.

Senior mental model#

UI architecture is a map of ownership and causality. For every value, name the authoritative owner, lifetime, restore/persistence policy, writers, readers, and legal transitions. For every action, identify who accepts the intent, where business logic runs, how its result becomes state, and what happens on repetition, cancellation, or process death.

  • MVVM describes View/ViewModel/model roles; reducer-style MVI emphasizes intents and centralized transitions; UDF defines event → business logic → state → UI. They can overlap, and pattern names do not guarantee separation or testability.
  • The UI renders snapshots and sends semantic events. A screen holder coordinates app data and business rules. A local holder owns UI mechanics. Repositories remain data boundaries; use cases earn their place through reused or complex rules, not ceremony.
  • Ask which invariants, concurrency, effect delivery, restoration, and observability the screen needs—not only “MVVM or MVI?”

State taxonomy, internals, and data flow#

CategoryExampleTypical owner / lifetime
Domain/app dataOrder, catalog, payment statusRepository/database/server source of truth, independent of one UI.
Screen UI stateDisplay rows, access rules, load/refresh/paging statusScreen holder, often a ViewModel; derived from authoritative data and input.
Ephemeral widget stateFocus, drawer, animation, uncommitted text, scroll mechanicsComposable/View/Fragment or plain UI holder; hoist only to the lowest common owner.
Restorable stateSelected tab, query, item IDrememberSaveable, saved instance state, or SavedStateHandle for small reconstruction input.
Durable business stateSubmitted order, completed payment, queued uploadDatabase/server/transactional work—not a ViewModel, Bundle, or in-memory Flow.
UI event → screen state holder → business/data boundary → authoritative outcome
   ↑                                                       │
   └──────────── render(immutable UI state) ← derive/map ───┘

Side-effect request → lifecycle-aware UI handler
Durable outcome     → source of truth → UI state after recreation

A source of truth is the authority for a fact, not necessarily one object for the entire screen. A database can own order status, SavedStateHandle a query input, and a local holder focus. Derive state from owners instead of maintaining unsynchronized duplicate copies.

State shape: sealed phases, orthogonal fields, and atomic updates#

  • Sealed phases fit mutually exclusive states such as InitialLoading | Content | BlockingError. Orthogonal fields fit content plus refreshing, stale metadata, a non-blocking error, or a pagination footer.
  • A loose isLoading + data? + error? admits impossible or ambiguous combinations. One giant sealed tree can instead create combinatorial explosion and hide independent owners.
  • Empty means a successful zero result, not “not loaded.” Stale content remains renderable with freshness/retry metadata. Initial failure can block; refresh failure with cached content is usually non-blocking. Pagination distinguishes initial load, append in flight, end reached, and append error.
  • Publish immutable snapshots and use pure atomic MutableStateFlow.update transforms. val and copy do not make nested mutable lists, maps, or elements safe.
sealed interface Body {
    data object InitialLoading : Body
    data class Content(val rows: List<RowUi>, val isEmpty: Boolean) : Body
    data class BlockingError(val error: UiError) : Body
}
data class FeedUiState(
    val body: Body = Body.InitialLoading,
    val isRefreshing: Boolean = false,
    val freshness: Freshness = Freshness.Unknown,
    val append: AppendState = AppendState.Idle,
    val notice: Notice? = null,
    val requestId: Long = 0,
)
private val _state = MutableStateFlow(FeedUiState())
fun reduce(result: Result, id: Long) = _state.update { old ->
    if (id != old.requestId) old else old.reduce(result)
}

State holder versus ViewModel; Compose and XML parity#

  • Keep simple element state local and hoist it to the lowest common reader/writer. Extract a plain holder for cohesive focus, scroll, sheet, or selection logic. Use a ViewModel/screen holder for app data, business rules, repositories, or configuration-change retention.
  • A ViewModel must not retain an Activity, Fragment, View, NavController, Composer, focus/scroll runtime object, or callback. Create it through its owner/factory/DI path and scope it deliberately to a destination, graph, Activity, or another ViewModelStoreOwner.
  • Compose: a stateful route uses collectAsStateWithLifecycle() and passes plain state/callbacks to stateless content. remember survives recomposition only; rememberSaveable restores saveable UI input but is not durable storage. Frame-clock UI operations do not belong in viewModelScope.
  • XML/Fragment uses the same architecture: collect with viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.repeatOnLifecycle, render Views, send semantic callbacks, and never outlive the Fragment view. UDF does not require Compose.

UDF loop, events, effects, commands, and durable outcomes#

  • Events describe what happened, such as RetryClicked or AddressChanged, rather than exposing setters for every field. The handler validates the intent, invokes business/data work, and reduces typed results.
  • An effect/command asks an imperative boundary to act: open a picker, focus a field, show a disposable snackbar, or navigate. Define loss, replay, buffering, idempotency, and consumer count. StateFlow is not an event queue: equal values conflate and new collectors see current state, not every occurrence.
  • Navigation after validation may be an effect, but “checkout complete” must be a durable repository/server outcome so recreation derives the correct destination. A snackbar may be best effort; required acknowledgement belongs in state. Payment completion must not live only in a consumed event.
  • Exactly-once behavior is normally a business protocol using a stable operation/idempotency key, persisted status, and reconciliation. Channel or SharedFlow alone cannot make an external payment or navigation history exactly once.

Concurrency, stale results, and race prevention#

  • UDF does not inherently serialize async effects. Events can launch overlapping work that completes out of order. Choose latest-wins, queue-all, deduplication, a mutex/actor, or independent-key concurrency per operation.
  • Cancel obsolete cooperative jobs and also carry request identity/generation, because cancellation cannot undo blocking calls, detached work, or committed effects.
  • Atomic update prevents lost read-modify-write state updates; it does not make network + database + state transactional. Its reducer must remain pure because it may retry.
  • Disabling repeated submit helps UX; correctness still requires repository/server idempotency and persisted operation status.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

Guarantee / useful contractNon-guarantee
UDF makes direction and write boundaries explicit.UDF does not inherently serialize async effects or prevent races.
Immutable outer snapshots support predictable reducers.Immutable data does not make nested mutable members safe.
ViewModel is retained across configuration changes by its owner.ViewModel survives process death or is a durable store.
SavedStateHandle retains small restorable values through saved state.It is durable database/business storage or a large-object cache.
StateFlow exposes current conflated state.StateFlow is an event queue or delivers every occurrence.
A cohesive aggregate can support atomic screen transitions.One UI state object is always superior to smaller owned state holders.
MVVM/MVI names provide vocabulary.Architecture pattern names guarantee separation, correctness, or testability.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle(), lifecycle-runtime-compose artifacts, overloads, and default lifecycle behavior depend on resolved AndroidX versions. Pin versions and consult current API docs.
  • Compose saveability depends on SaveableStateRegistry, navigation integration, supported types, and platform Bundle limits. Test real recreation/process restoration.
  • ViewModel creation extras, factories, Navigation graph scoping, and SavedStateHandle integration have evolved across Lifecycle/Navigation releases. Verify the actual owner and dependency versions.
  • Do not derive semantics from Flow sharing/buffering defaults; Stage 10 covers those version-sensitive primitives. State the required architecture contract independently.

Decision matrix#

DecisionPreferWhen / cost
Local vs hoistedLowest owner needing read/writeLocal reduces coupling; hoist for coordination and a testable contract.
Plain holder vs ViewModelPlain for UI mechanics; ViewModel for screen/business dataViewModel adds an owner lifecycle and saved-state integration.
MVVM-style methods vs reducer/MVIFew independent actions vs many coupled transitionsA reducer improves auditability but can add boilerplate or become a god reducer.
Sealed phase vs fieldsSealed for exclusivity; validated fields for orthogonal dimensionsA hybrid often models refresh/paging best.
Effect vs stateEffect for disposable requests; state/durable source for required outcomesIf loss after recreation is a bug, transient-only is wrong.
Aggregate vs smaller holdersAggregate atomic invariants; split independent owners/lifetimesAvoid both duplicated facts and unrelated monoliths.
  1. Write user-visible invariants and classify each fact by owner, lifetime, and durability.
  2. Choose the source of truth and derived UI state; identify every writer and transition.
  3. Choose exclusive phases versus orthogonal metadata; define stale, empty, refresh, and append behavior.
  4. Define event admission, asynchronous ordering/cancellation, request identity, effect delivery, and process-death recovery.
  5. Choose the least ceremonial pattern that makes these contracts observable and testable.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Dogmatic MVI can route every edit, animation, and navigation through one global reducer, coupling unrelated lifetimes. Casual MVVM can scatter writes and expose mutable state.
  • A giant UiState hides ownership and causes broad updates; too many independent flows create torn combinations. Split by ownership and aggregate where transitions must be atomic.
  • Replacing cached content with full-screen loading during refresh flickers and loses context; treating initial empty as content before load hides latency and failure.
  • A transient navigation/payment-success event can be lost while inactive or repeated after recreation. Durable outcome plus idempotent UI reaction is safer.
  • Saving full responses in SavedStateHandle risks size/schema failures and duplicate truth. Save identifiers or input and reload authoritative data.
  • Launching per-click jobs without an operation policy allows stale overwrite, duplicate payments, and a spinner cleared by the wrong request.

Production scenario: checkout and payment#

Hypothetically: a checkout screen keeps focus/sheet mechanics locally, cart ID and uncommitted promo input in SavedStateHandle, screen state in a ViewModel, and cart/payment operation truth in a repository/database. Submit creates a stable idempotency key; the repository persists the operation and calls the backend. The UI observes durable Pending | Succeeded | Failed rather than treating a transient effect as proof of payment. After process death, a new ViewModel restores IDs, reads the operation, and shows a receipt or retry-safe failure.

fun submit() {
    val snapshot = state.value
    if (!snapshot.canSubmit) return
    val operationId = snapshot.operationId ?: ids.newStableId()
    _state.update { it.copy(isSubmitting = true, operationId = operationId) }
    submitJob?.cancel()
    submitJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        repository.submitPayment(snapshot.cartId, operationId)
        // The repository persists outcome; UI observes that source of truth.
    }
}

Double-tap and retry reuse the operation ID. Stale validation carries request identity and cannot overwrite a newer address. Receipt navigation derives from succeeded status; a snackbar can remain best effort. Telemetry uses redacted operation/request IDs, prior→next state, latency, cancellation, and stale rejection—not card data.

Code-review/debugging trap#

data class UiState(
    val loading: Boolean,
    val items: MutableList<Item>,
    val error: String?,
    val navigateAfterPayment: Boolean,
)
fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.value = _state.value.copy(loading = true)
    val rows = repo.load()                 // an older request can finish last
    _state.value.items.clear()             // mutates a published snapshot
    _state.value.items.addAll(rows)
    _state.value = _state.value.copy(loading = false)
}

The review trap is believing that ViewModel, UiState, and “MVI” naming imply safe ownership. Ask which combinations are legal, who writes, whether refresh preserves content, which request owns the spinner, whether nested data is mutable, what survives rotation/process death, and whether payment truth is durable. Debug with typed previousState → event/result → nextState, correlation/request ID, owner/lifecycle, active operations, and stale rejection. Redact payloads; transition logs complement repository traces.

Testing reducers, holders, and integration boundaries#

  • Pure reducer table/property tests cover each event/result × phase, invariants, empty/stale/refresh/append behavior, stale rejection, and forbidden combinations.
  • ViewModel tests inject fake repositories, IDs, and dispatchers; virtual time scripts out-of-order completion, cancellation, duplicate submit, and operation recovery. Test public transitions, not private Flow details.
  • Plain state-driven Compose/View tests render loading/content/empty/blocking/non-blocking error and callbacks. Add a small wiring test for lifecycle collection and effects.
  • Integration tests prove repository source-of-truth writes, SavedStateHandle reconstruction, graph scoping, Fragment view recreation, and critical process-recreation paths.
  • Observability uses stable state/event names, correlation/request generation, transition latency, effect enqueue/handle/drop reason, retries, and rejected stale results without PII or secrets.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. MVVM, MVI, or UDF? They are not exclusive brands. Choose explicit ownership and flow; reducers help coupled transitions, while direct ViewModel methods fit a few independent actions.
  2. What is UI state? A renderable snapshot including phase and metadata; domain data and widget mechanics can have different owners.
  3. Is one UiState always better? No. Aggregates support atomic invariants; independent owners and lifetimes should often remain separate.
  4. Sealed state or data class? Sealed for mutually exclusive phases, fields for orthogonal dimensions, and a hybrid to avoid both boolean soup and a combinatorial tree.
  5. How do you model refresh failure with cache? Keep content, end refreshing, expose freshness/non-blocking error and retry; block only without renderable content.
  6. State or event for navigation? Imperative navigation can be an effect; required business outcomes must be state or durable truth so recreation cannot lose them.
  7. Does ViewModel survive process death? No. It survives owner-retained configuration changes; restore minimal inputs and reload durable truth after death.
  8. What is SavedStateHandle for? Small restorable screen inputs/keys, not database or payment/order truth.
  9. How do you prevent stale results? Cancel obsolete cooperative work and validate request generation at reduction; writes also need idempotency and reconciliation.
  10. How do you test the architecture? Pure transitions, ViewModel race tests, plain UI render/callback tests, and focused lifecycle/persistence integration tests.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. The collector was STOPPED during a snackbar. Define the contract: best-effort can be lost; required acknowledgement is state. “Single event” does not resolve delivery semantics.
  2. Two refreshes complete in reverse. The latest request owns refresh metadata and result reduction; compare generation. Cancellation alone is insufficient.
  3. A screen has an editor, list, and bottom sheet. Split editor/sheet mechanics from screen data; aggregate only facts requiring an atomic invariant.
  4. Payment succeeded and the app died before navigation. Persist server/database status, restore operation ID, observe success, and derive receipt navigation idempotently.

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. Who owns, writes, restores, and outlives each state field?
  2. Which impossible or hidden loading, stale, refresh, and pagination combinations does the model admit?
  3. What is each asynchronous operation policy, and how does the reducer reject stale completion?
  4. Which apparent “events” are actually durable business outcomes that must not be lost?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you design Android UI architecture and state?

~30-second answer#

I treat MVVM and MVI as vocabulary, not guarantees. I assign every fact an owner, lifetime, source of truth, and durability. The UI sends semantic events and renders immutable state; a screen holder coordinates business data, while widget mechanics stay in the lowest UI owner. I use sealed types for exclusive phases and separate refresh or paging metadata. UDF does not serialize asynchronous work, so I define cancellation and request identity. Required outcomes such as payment completion are persisted, and I test reducers, races, recreation, and repository boundaries.

~2-minute answer#

I start with ownership and data flow rather than a pattern name. Domain data belongs to a repository or durable source of truth. A screen holder, often a ViewModel, combines it with screen input and exposes renderable UI state. Focus, scroll, animation, and similar mechanics stay local or in a plain UI holder unless business logic needs them. In Compose, a route collects lifecycle-aware state and passes values and callbacks to stateless content; Fragments use the same boundary with repeatOnLifecycle.

I use sealed phases for mutually exclusive initial loading, content, and blocking error. Refresh, stale status, non-blocking errors, and pagination are often orthogonal, so a hybrid avoids both boolean soup and an enormous sealed hierarchy. Snapshots are immutable, nested collections have controlled ownership, and atomic reducers are pure.

Events describe intent; the holder invokes business/data work and reduces typed results. Imperative focus, disposable snackbar, or navigation requests can be effects, but StateFlow is not an event queue. If losing an outcome after recreation is wrong—payment completion, order submission, or required acknowledgement—I persist it. A ViewModel survives configuration change, not process death, and SavedStateHandle stores reconstruction inputs rather than business truth.

Finally, UDF does not serialize concurrency. I define latest-wins, queueing, deduplication, or independent-key work, cancel obsolete jobs, and reject stale request IDs. Writes use idempotency and reconciliation. Tests cover reducers, out-of-order results, duplicate submit, lifecycle collection, saved-state reconstruction, and source-of-truth integration. Whether the team calls the result MVVM or MVI is secondary.

Official references#

  • Android: Guide to app architecture

  • Android: Saved state module for ViewModel

  • Compose: lifecycle-aware streams

Clean Architecture and Android modularizationexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should design boundaries around direction of change, ownership, and dependencies rather than folder names: apply the dependency rule, separate policy from mechanism, decide whether a domain layer, use case, repository interface, or model mapping earns its cost, move from logical packages to Gradle modules only for measurable value, and migrate a monolith incrementally with dependency fitness rules. This section avoids Stage 12 UI-state detail and Stage 17 DI-framework detail.

Senior mental model#

Architecture is controlled coupling. Clean Architecture is the dependency rule, not rings, presentation/domain/data names, or a fixed layer count. High-level policy should not know a volatile mechanism. Source dependencies point toward stable policy, although runtime control can call outward through an implementation selected at the composition root.

  • Policy is a business decision or invariant such as eligibility, pricing, or failure classification. Mechanism is Android, HTTP, SQL, analytics, or a clock. Volatility and ownership matter more than package names.
  • A boundary earns its cost when it localizes change, defines an independently testable contract, or supports ownership. An interface, mapper, or module without that reason is ceremony.
  • Keep two graphs visible: compile-time dependencies and runtime calls/data flow. Dependency inversion changes the first; it does not deny the second.

Dependency graph and internals#

compile time:
:app ──> :feature:checkout ──> :feature:checkout:api (owns port/policy)
  │                                             ▲
  ├──> :data:orders ────────────────────────────┘ (implements port)
  └──> :core:navigation-api

runtime:
UI → CheckoutPolicy → OrderRepository(port) → Sql/HttpOrderRepository(adapter)

Forbidden: :core:domain → Android/Retrofit/Room/feature implementation
Risk: feature A ↔ feature B cycle; shared module with unbounded fan-out

Gradle has a directed project graph and derives task execution from it. A dependency cycle is not healthy collaboration; extract a small contract, move orchestration upward, reverse an edge, or reunite code that changes together. High fan-out gives a consumer many reasons to change; high fan-in makes a boundary stable and expensive to break. Stable dependencies should point from volatile features toward stable contracts, where stable means costly to change, not frozen forever.

Presentation, domain, data, and model boundaries#

  • Presentation adapts interaction and results to a UI contract. Data coordinates sources, cache, freshness/conflicts, and persistence. An optional domain layer concentrates reusable or complex policy. There is no mandated layer count: simple CRUD may call a data boundary directly, while pricing or entitlement policy benefits from a pure domain.
  • A domain layer helps when rules serve several callers, combine repositories, enforce non-trivial invariants, or need platform-free tests. It hurts when every class delegates one method, duplicates names and types, and stretches traces.
  • A DTO mirrors a wire schema; a persistence entity mirrors tables, indexes, and relations; a domain model carries validated business meaning; a UI model carries formatted display needs. A Room entity is not a domain entity because of its name.
  • Mapping isolates schema evolution and invalid input, but costs allocations, boilerplate, defaults, lost fields, and debugging hops. Map at real trust/change boundaries. Do not create four identical models by default; a small stable internal value can honestly be shared.

Repository ownership, inversion, and useful use cases#

A repository is not automatically a domain abstraction. A CRUD façade that leaks paging or HTTP DTOs remains a data gateway. A repository interface belongs to the policy-side consumer when that consumer defines a narrow capability and adapters or substitutes vary. A broadly shared data capability can instead be owned by a stable data API. Avoid one god repository.

Interfaces alone do not decouple. The consumer still depends on semantics, models, errors, threading, versioning, and lifetime. An interface is valuable when it protects a volatile implementation or defines a consumer-owned port; one interface per concrete class only adds navigation cost.

A use case earns its place by naming a business operation, coordinating ports, enforcing policy/transaction rules, or supporting reuse. GetUserUseCase.invoke() = repository.getUser() with no distinct semantics is a pass-through layer. Keep a simple call on the repository until a policy seam appears.

Package-by-feature/layer; logical versus Gradle modules#

  • Package-by-layer shows technical roles but scatters a feature change and permits accidental cross-feature access. Package-by-feature colocates change and ownership; a large feature can have local layers. Packages provide logical organization and language visibility, not a separate compilation unit.
  • A Gradle module enforces project edges and adds compilation/cache/task/API and ownership boundaries, but also configuration, variants, plugins, resources, dependency wiring, and IDE/build overhead. Prove a seam with packages and internal first; extract for change cadence, reuse, build graph, delivery, or team ownership.
  • A common graph uses a thin :app composition/manifest entry, vertical :feature:*, narrow :core:*, concrete :data:*, an owned :design-system, and :testing or test fixtures for reusable test support. Do not turn :core:common into a dump.

Module types, api/implementation, and delivery#

  • implementation keeps a dependency off consumers' compile classpaths and reduces accidental API/fan-out. Use api when the module's intentional public signature exposes that dependency's type. This is a Gradle classpath contract, not a security boundary.
  • A Kotlin/JVM module suits pure policy and models without Android classes/resources and usually has a smaller variant/task surface. An Android library is required for resources, manifest, Android APIs, BuildConfig, or Android tests; AAR, namespace, resources, and variants cost more.
  • A dynamic feature is a Play Feature Delivery concern with install-time/on-demand/conditional delivery, a base-module relationship, install failures, and unavailable-code/resource states. It is not a synonym for an ordinary feature library, and a compile module is not automatically downloaded separately.

Navigation, DI, resource, and build contracts#

  • A feature should not import another feature's implementation. Expose a small navigation contract such as a typed destination, entry interface, or registrar; app-level composition connects the graph. Do not put internal screen classes or NavController in core. Navigation mechanics belong to Stage 4.
  • A DI contract is the required ports plus an exported entry point; the composition root selects implementations. Avoid bidirectional “DI module” edges and service locators in core. Scope and framework binding detail belongs to Stage 17.
  • Resources belong to the feature; the design system owns shared tokens/components/assets. Avoid accidental transitive R access. Namespace and non-transitive R behavior depend on AGP.
  • A convention plugin centralizes repeated build policy—toolchains, lint, test defaults, Android options—without copy/paste. Keep it small, versioned, and tested; do not apply every plugin and dependency to every module.

Build performance, ownership, blast radius, and testability#

Modules can enable parallelism, caching, and recompilation of affected projects, but graph shape, ABI changes, code generation, configuration, and the critical path decide the result. More modules are not always faster: a serial chain of tiny projects can increase configuration and task overhead. Measure clean build, incremental ABI and non-ABI edits, configuration time, cache hits, and critical path on CI and representative machines.

A boundary can support CODEOWNERS, local tests, smaller blast radius, and independent evolution. Conversely, a shared core with many consumers creates coordination, while mocks that restate implementation create false confidence. Test pure policy locally, adapters with contract/integration tests, features with fakes, and a few app composition paths.

Guarantees and explicit non-guarantees#

Useful contractNon-guarantee
The dependency rule prevents policy from compiling against a concrete mechanism.There is no mandated layer count, and names such as domain/data prove nothing.
A consumer-owned port permits an adapter to be substituted.A repository is not automatically a domain abstraction; Interfaces alone do not decouple.
A Gradle module enforces its declared compile dependency graph.Modules do not guarantee runtime isolation or security; code can share one process/APK.
implementation narrows compile exposure.Runtime isolation, semantic independence, or absence of transitive runtime code.
Measured seams can reduce change and test blast radius.Modularization does not guarantee quality or build speed.

Version/build-sensitive behavior#

  • AGP/Gradle/Kotlin compatibility, variant APIs, namespace, non-transitive/non-final R, test fixtures, configuration cache, and compiler behavior evolve. Pin toolchains, read release notes, and inspect the resolved graph.
  • api/implementation behavior depends on the applied library plugins and public signatures. Verify dependency reports and ABI rather than reasoning from a configuration name alone.
  • Dynamic delivery depends on App Bundles, Play/installer behavior, device/API, delivery conditions, and the Play Feature Delivery library version. Test install, cancellation, failure, update, and unavailable states.
  • A build-performance claim is valid only for its graph, hardware, cache, daemon, CI, and edit scenario. Keep before/after baselines.

Decision framework#

  1. Draw the current package/project graph, owners, cycles, fan-in/fan-out, and change hotspots.
  2. For a candidate boundary, name the policy, volatile mechanism, contract owner, allowed direction, and crossing data/errors.
  3. Score independent change/team/reuse/test/build/delivery benefit against mapping, API versioning, variants, resources, navigation, and DI wiring cost.
  4. Try the cheapest enforcement: package-by-feature, internal, lint, or an architecture test. Create a Gradle module when a compile/build/ownership boundary is needed.
  5. Record a fitness rule and before/after metrics; merge or remove a boundary whose cost exceeds its benefit.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Layer-first organization produces horizontal god modules and wide changes; feature-only organization can duplicate policy or create direct feature edges.
  • Excess models/mappers lose fields and add allocations; one shared DTO leaks transport schema into policy and widens backend-change blast radius.
  • Pass-through use cases/interfaces stretch traces; no seam binds policy to Retrofit, Room, or Android.
  • An unbounded common, design-system, or navigation module gains high fan-out and becomes a coordination bottleneck.
  • Tiny Gradle modules multiply plugin, configuration, variant, and task costs; one app module cannot enforce ownership and may invalidate a broad graph.
  • Cycles, reflection/service locators, and duplicate copied models bypass the intended graph. Successful compilation does not prove correct runtime composition.

Production migration: seams and strangler#

Hypothetically: checkout lives in monolithic :app; UI directly calls Retrofit, a Room DAO, and a pricing singleton. First capture checkout file/change coupling, build critical path, incremental edit time, flaky integration tests, cycles, and owners. Introduce package-by-feature plus narrow CheckoutPolicy and OrderRepository seams, adapt the legacy implementation, and switch one journey: a strangler rather than a big-bang rewrite.

Move pure pricing/order contracts to Kotlin/JVM :feature:checkout:api or domain only if reuse and ownership justify it. Keep Android UI/resources in an Android feature library, Retrofit/Room adapter in :data:orders, and composition in :app. Delete the old path after product conversion/error parity, contract tests, graph checks, and incremental/CI metrics pass. Each slice stays deployable; rollback changes composition rather than discarding a rewrite.

Code-review/debugging trap#

// :feature:checkout depends on :feature:catalog:impl
class CheckoutUseCase(private val repo: CheckoutRepositoryImpl) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String) = repo.loadDto(id) // pass-through + DTO leak
}
interface CheckoutRepository // next to implementation, no consumer capability

The diagram has clean boxes, but the source edge points to implementation, the use case has no policy, a DTO crosses every boundary, and catalog/checkout can cycle. Debug with Gradle dependencies/dependencyInsight and the project graph, then identify the public signature exposing the edge, contract owner, and runtime composition. Fix with a narrow consumer-owned port, explicit model/error mapping, app orchestration, or a neutral API—not another generic interface.

Dependency fitness rules in CI#

  • Fail CI for project/package cycles, forbidden edges such as domain → android.* or feature → feature:impl, and unexpected public-API growth. Every exception needs an owner and expiry.
  • Check graph snapshots, dependency locking/verification, lint or architecture tests, explicit API/API dumps for published contracts, and resource-prefix/namespace conventions.
  • Track fan-out/fan-in, changed modules per PR, ABI versus implementation invalidation, configuration and critical-path time, cache hits, flaky tests, and cross-team reviews. Thresholds should catch regression, not reward module count.
  • A CI rule must explain the violation and local reproduction command; version convention plugins and contract tests with the boundary.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. What is the essence of Clean Architecture? The dependency rule: policy does not compile against volatile mechanisms. Layer names and count are secondary.
  2. When does a domain layer help? For reused or complex policy, multi-repository orchestration, or platform-free invariants—not automatic one-line wrappers.
  3. Who owns a repository interface? The owner of the needed contract: often policy/consumer for inversion, sometimes a stable data API for a shared data capability.
  4. Do DTO, domain, persistence, and UI models always need separation? No. Separate differing schemas, trust, and change cadence; include mapping and debugging cost.
  5. Package-by-feature or package-by-layer? Feature usually localizes change and ownership; local layers inside it retain roles without horizontal god packages.
  6. Is a package the same as a Gradle module? No. A package organizes source and visibility; a Gradle project adds compilation, dependency, task, and API boundaries with overhead.
  7. api or implementation? Default to implementation; use api only for a dependency type intentionally exposed in the public consumer surface.
  8. Android library or Kotlin/JVM? Kotlin/JVM for pure code; Android library for resources, manifest, Android APIs, or Android-specific tests.
  9. Do more modules make builds faster? Not necessarily. Parallel/cache isolation can help, while configuration, variants, and a serial critical path can hurt. Measure scenarios.
  10. How do you migrate a monolith? Baseline metrics, create a logical seam and adapter, move one strangler slice, enforce the graph, and extract physically only for proven benefit.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Two features need to navigate to each other. Do not add a cycle; app-level orchestration depends on their destination contracts or a neutral navigation API.
  2. The build became slower after extraction. Compare configuration, task count, critical path, cache, and ABI invalidation; reduce plugin/variant surface or merge tiny serial modules.
  3. The domain model is almost the DTO. If trust, schema, and cadence truly match, sharing can be cheaper. Add mapping when the boundary diverges, not from a template.
  4. A dynamic feature failed to install. Base must work without its code/resources, retain route intent, and show retry/fallback. Test cancellation, failure, update, and unavailable states.

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. What are the three largest change hotspots, cycles, or fan-out edges in your current graph?
  2. Which policy currently knows an Android, network, or storage mechanism, and what narrow port does it need?
  3. Which mappings protect genuinely different schemas, and which merely copy identical fields?
  4. Which product, ownership, test, and build metrics would prove an extraction is worth its cost?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you apply Clean Architecture and modularization in an Android app?

~30-second answer#

I treat Clean Architecture as a dependency rule, not a mandated folder diagram. Stable business policy owns narrow contracts; Android, database, and network mechanisms implement them at the composition boundary. I add domain models, use cases, and mappers only when they protect real invariants or change boundaries. I start with package-by-feature and extract Gradle modules for measurable ownership, reuse, build, or delivery needs. I prevent cycles and implementation leaks in CI and compare incremental build, test, and change-blast-radius metrics, because more modules do not automatically improve quality or speed.

~2-minute answer#

I begin with policy and volatility. Business rules should not compile against Retrofit, Room, Android, or a feature implementation. A consumer-owned port describes the capability policy needs, an outer adapter implements it, and the app composition root connects them. Runtime calls can still go outward; inversion is about source dependencies.

I do not mandate presentation, domain, and data for every feature. A domain layer earns its cost when it centralizes reused or complex policy. A use case names an operation or coordinates rules rather than forwarding one call. DTOs, persistence entities, domain models, and UI models separate when schema, trust, or cadence differ; mapping also costs allocations, defaults, and debugging.

I prefer package-by-feature, then extract Gradle modules for an enforced boundary, ownership, reuse, cache isolation, or delivery. The app stays a thin composition root; features expose narrow APIs; core, data, design-system, and testing modules have explicit ownership. I default to implementation dependencies, use api only for intentional public types, and place pure policy in Kotlin/JVM. Dynamic features are delivery, not ordinary modules.

CI rejects cycles, feature-to-implementation edges, and unbounded shared APIs. Navigation and DI cross features through small contracts; resources retain an owner and convention plugins encode build policy. In a monolith, I baseline metrics, introduce a logical seam and legacy adapter, migrate one strangler slice, then extract physically. I verify product parity, fan-out, changed modules, and incremental/CI critical path. Modules enforce a build graph, not runtime isolation, security, quality, or guaranteed speed.
