Jetpack Compose runtime and stateexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should explain how composition and snapshot state construct and update UI; select an observable representation, owner, lifetime, and save boundary; distinguish invalidation, recomposition, skipping, and phase-specific work; use remember, rememberSaveable, snapshot collections, derivedStateOf, mutation policies, and key safely; and diagnose stale UI or lost identity. Stage 12 already covers screen-state architecture. snapshotFlow is comparative only; effects/navigation belong to Stage 15 and deep performance work to Stage 16.

Senior mental model#

Composition is incremental execution with identity and tracked dependencies, not repeated tree inflation. The compiler adds a runtime protocol; a Composer associates call sites and groups with a slot table; snapshot reads are tracked; and a change can invalidate a restart scope or a later phase. Invalidation makes work eligible—it does not promise execution.

  • Separate state write, invalidation, scheduled work, and the composition/layout/draw work that actually executes.
  • State must be observable, have one truthful owner, and match the required lifetime. remember provides only positional retention in composition.
  • A composable can rerun, run in a different order, be skipped, or be cancelled, so it must be idempotent and side-effect-free.

Runtime, internals, and topology#

@Composable source
  → compiler protocol (Composer + change/group metadata)
  → initial composition: execute calls, create groups/slots, emit UI tree
  → snapshot reads associate state with observing scopes/phases
state write → snapshot/apply → invalidate affected observations
  → recomposition may re-execute restart scopes and skip unchanged groups
  → apply changes → layout (measure/place) → draw

identity ≈ call-site/group position + explicit key where supplied
remembered value lives in its slot while that identity remains composed

The slot table is a runtime representation of composition groups and remembered slots, not a public DOM or durable storage format. Compiler/runtime protocol creates eligible group and restart boundaries. Positional memoization normally identifies an invocation by call site and relative execution position. Initial composition builds topology and values; recomposition revisits invalidated portions and records updates. Do not claim that every write reruns a whole function or tree: restartability, skipping eligibility, actual parameter comparisons, and observation location determine work.

Conditional calls alter positions. In loops or reordered siblings, key(item.id) gives stable local identity so remembered objects and lifecycle follow the logical item. A key must be stable and unique among siblings at that call site; an index preserves position, not item identity.

Snapshot reads, writes, mutable snapshots, and threads#

  • MutableState and snapshot collections participate in the snapshot system. Reads are observed in context; writes create state records and, when applied, notify relevant observers according to mutation policy.
  • A mutable snapshot isolates reads/writes until apply. Concurrent snapshots can conflict on incompatible writes; apply can fail, so low-level callers need an explicit retry, merge, or error policy. A snapshot is not a database transaction or global lock.
  • Visibility follows snapshot/apply semantics. Arbitrary cross-thread ordinary-field mutation is neither tracked nor made safe. Use supported snapshot APIs, clear ownership, correct publication/apply, and normal synchronization for non-snapshot data.
  • Atomic snapshot apply does not make external I/O atomic, serialize business operations, or guarantee rendering of every intermediate value.

Composition, layout, and draw phases#

Read locationDescribesTypical invalidation
CompositionWhat UI exists and its parameters/modifiersRecompose the observing scope; changes may then require layout/draw.
Layout: measure/placeSize and positionRemeasure or placement; measurement can propagate.
DrawPixels/graphicsRedraw without necessarily recomposing or laying out.

The runtime tracks the phase of a snapshot read. Moving a fast-changing read to placement or draw can narrow work only when structure does not depend on the value. It is not a universal optimization; correctness and measurement dependencies come first, and Stage 16 owns detailed profiling.

State authoring: observable values and collections#

@Composable
fun Filters(initial: Set<String>) {
    var query by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
    val selected = remember { mutableStateListOf<String>() }
    // Assigning query and selected.add/remove are observable snapshot writes.
}

val rows = remember { mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<Row>()) }
rows.value.add(newRow) // Hidden mutation: State's value reference did not change.
// Prefer mutableStateListOf<Row>() + add, or mutableStateOf(listOf<Row>()) with rows.value = rows.value + newRow.

remember { mutableStateOf(x) } retains the state holder while call identity remains and makes assignments observable. A plain local var resets on execution; a remembered ordinary mutable object survives but sends no notification. mutableStateListOf/mutableStateMapOf observe collection operations, not hidden mutation inside arbitrary element objects. Prefer immutable element replacement or explicitly owned observable fields.

remember(key1, key2) { build(...) } recreates the cached value when a key changes. A missing dependency creates a stale cache; a volatile key destroys retention. Its calculation should not perform external effects.

remember, rememberSaveable, ViewModel, and Saver#

MechanismLifetime / purposeBoundary
rememberRecomposition while identity remains composedDoes not survive leaving composition, Activity recreation, or process death.
rememberSaveableSmall UI element state through SaveableStateRegistryNeeds a Bundle-compatible value or custom Saver; it is not durable storage.
ViewModelScreen/business owner across configuration changesDoes not itself survive process death; use SavedStateHandle for minimal restoration input and a repository for durable truth.

Saver, mapSaver, and listSaver convert a holder to minimal saveable values and reconstruct it. Save a query, selected IDs, or a scroll key/index—not repositories, callbacks, coroutine scopes, huge object graphs, or duplicate server data. Validate missing/old restored values and rebuild runtime-only dependencies.

State hoisting and plain state holders#

  • Keep simple element state local when one composable owns it. Hoist value and events to the lowest common owner that must read or change them, not automatically to the screen root.
  • Extract a plain state holder when cohesive UI behavior coordinates several element states. Create it through a remember…State factory; if restoration matters, save minimal reconstructible values with a truthful Saver.
  • Business rules, repositories, and durable screen state belong to the Stage 12 screen owner such as a ViewModel/component. Feed observable immutable values and callbacks into stateless rendering.
  • A holder's lifetime must match the objects it owns. Do not leak a composition-owned holder into a longer-lived owner.

derivedStateOf and mutation policies#

derivedStateOf tracks snapshot reads and is useful when dependencies change more often than the meaningful derived result—for example, scroll index versus “show back to top”. It is not generic memoization and it is not free: observation, calculation, and equality bookkeeping have a cost. Calculate ordinary values directly, or use keyed remember only to avoid a proven expensive recalculation.

  • structuralEqualityPolicy(): values equal by == are not a change; the common default.
  • referentialEqualityPolicy(): only a different reference counts; use when identity is the semantic contract.
  • neverEqualPolicy(): every assignment counts; it can amplify invalidation and is not event-delivery semantics.

Choose the policy that matches semantic equality. snapshotFlow also observes snapshot reads but exports changes to Flow for effect/collection work; its cancellation and effect rules are reserved for Stage 15.

Identity, remembered-object lifecycle, and disposal#

A remembered value belongs to a composition location. If a branch disappears, a parent is removed, a key changes, or the host composition is disposed, its slots are forgotten and later entry creates new objects. Reordering unkeyed siblings can associate retained state with the wrong item; stable keys move identity with data. Cleanup aligns with leaving composition, but imperative registration/unregistration belongs to Stage 15 effect APIs, not a remember initializer.

Compiler protocol, stability, and non-Compose state interop#

The compiler transforms composable calls into a protocol conceptually involving a Composer, groups, changed metadata, restart scopes, and skipping. This is a mental model, not a generated-signature or representation contract. Stability helps compiler/runtime reasoning about changes and comparisons. @Stable/@Immutable are promises; an annotation does not freeze an object, observe hidden fields, or make mutable data safe. A false promise can cause stale UI. Strong-skipping defaults and comparisons are compiler-version-sensitive; Stage 16 covers reports and performance.

Flow/StateFlow, LiveData, RxJava, and custom observables are not automatically snapshot state. Adapt them with collectAsStateWithLifecycle, observeAsState, subscribeAsState, or a carefully implemented adapter. Collection lifetime, initial value, equality/conflation, thread, and error semantics remain part of the source/integration contract.

Guarantees versus explicit non-guarantees#

Useful contractDoes not guarantee
Observed snapshot reads establish dependencies; applied writes can invalidate observers.Every invalidation reruns the entire UI or every intermediate write is rendered.
remember retains a slot while identity stays composed.Survival after leaving composition, recreation, or process death.
rememberSaveable uses SaveableStateRegistry.Durable storage; only Bundle-compatible or custom-saved minimal values qualify.
Recomposition produces an updated description.A fixed execution time/order: it may happen at any time and be skipped, coalesced, or cancelled.
mutableStateOf observes writes to its value property.Observation of internal mutation of an arbitrary mutable object.
Stability metadata supports change/skipping reasoning.That @Stable makes mutable data immutable, observable, or thread-safe.

Composables must therefore be idempotent and side-effect-free. derivedStateOf is not free, snapshot apply is not persistence, and scheduled recomposition is not delivery acknowledgement.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Compose compiler plugin/Kotlin integration, strong-skipping defaults, stability inference, lambda memoization, and generated protocol evolve. Pin versions and inspect current release notes/reports before a performance claim.
  • Group, slot, and snapshot implementation details can change. Depend on public observable contracts, not group counts, generated parameter layouts, or slot-table shape.
  • Saveable types and registry integration depend on host/platform/library version. Test custom Saver round trips and recreation on supported Android versions.
  • Snapshot APIs can be experimental or evolve conflict behavior. Check the exact runtime API and never infer general thread safety from one successful test.

Decision framework#

  1. Name the fact and owner: UI element, shared UI behavior, screen/business state, or durable data.
  2. Choose observable representation: immutable replacement, MutableState, snapshot list/map, or lifecycle-aware adapter from external state.
  3. Choose lifetime: local execution, composition identity, saveable recreation, ViewModel screen lifetime, or durable repository; save only minimal reconstruction input.
  4. Mark each snapshot read by phase and every mutable boundary. Check whether hidden mutation bypasses the State setter and snapshot collection operations.
  5. Check identity under conditions/reordering, use stable keys, and enumerate when remembered objects leave composition.
  6. Only then consider derivedStateOf, a custom policy, or phase deferral; reserve measured, version-specific performance work for Stage 16.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Local state minimizes coupling, but duplicate owners diverge; over-hoisting creates broad APIs and broad invalidation.
  • Immutable replacement gives clear snapshots/equality but allocates; snapshot collections give granular operations but expose mutable ownership and do not observe mutable element internals.
  • rememberSaveable improves recreation UX, but Bundle size/schema and Saver defects matter; saving whole models duplicates durable truth.
  • Structural equality can suppress equivalent assignments but costly/broken equality hurts; referential policy misses in-place semantic changes; never-equal amplifies work.
  • Missing remember keys retain stale dependencies; excessive keys recreate holders. Missing item keys transfer state after reorder; unstable keys reset it.
  • Fast state read in composition can broaden work; a draw read is incorrect when the value changes structure or measurement.

Production scenario: reorderable product filters#

Hypothetical: a ViewModel exposes immutable product/filter results as StateFlow, collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle. A query that drives repository search belongs to the ViewModel; expanded chips and draft selection stay at the lowest UI owner. A plain FilterPanelState coordinates UI behavior by stable category ID. Its Saver stores only selected IDs and query text and reconstructs runtime objects.

@Composable
fun ProductRows(products: List<ProductUi>, onOpen: (String) -> Unit) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(products, key = { it.id }) { product ->
            var expanded by rememberSaveable(product.id) { mutableStateOf(false) }
            ProductRow(product, expanded, { expanded = !expanded }) { onOpen(product.id) }
        }
    }
}

The stable item key keeps slots with product identity during sorting. A snapshot list is used only for UI-owned draft operations; repository results arrive as new immutable lists. derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } can justify its cost because index changes more frequently than the Boolean. Scroll effects belong to Stage 15.

Code-review/debug trap#

@Stable
class CartUiState(val lines: MutableList<Line>) // false stability promise

@Composable fun Cart(state: CartUiState, currency: Currency) {
    val total = remember { state.lines.sumOf { it.price } } // stale: missing keys
    state.lines.add(promoLine)                              // hidden write in composition
    state.lines.forEachIndexed { index, line ->
        key(index) { EditableLine(line) }                   // identity follows position
    }
}

The total is stale, mutation may not invalidate, another observed write could loop, and editor state moves after insertion. Debug ownership/lifetime first; identify exact snapshot reads, writes, and phases; verify setter/collection operations; inspect remember and sibling keys; remove false stability. Fix with immutable replacement or one-owner snapshot collection, pure composition, truthful cache keys only when caching is justified, and key(line.id). Reproduce reorder, recreation, and process restoration; reserve profiling for Stage 16.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. What does composition do? It executes composable calls, associates groups/slots with identity, and creates or updates a UI description; initial composition builds topology and recomposition revisits invalidated scopes.
  2. Does a state write recompose everything? No. Applied writes invalidate observed scopes/phases; work can be coalesced, skipped, or cancelled, and actual work depends on reads, restart scopes, and changed inputs.
  3. What does remember guarantee? Positional retention while the same identity remains composed—not leaving composition, recreation, or process death.
  4. Why can mutableStateOf(mutableListOf()) leave stale UI? add mutates internals without assigning State. Replace an immutable list or use a snapshot state list.
  5. When should you use rememberSaveable? For minimal UI element state restored through the registry; it is not durable storage.
  6. When is derivedStateOf appropriate? When dependencies change more frequently than the meaningful result, not around every expression and not for free.
  7. How does identity work in a reordered list? Position is the default; a stable unique key moves remembered state with the logical item, while index follows position.
  8. What does a mutation policy control? Whether an assignment counts as a change by structural, referential, or never-equal semantics; it cannot observe hidden mutation.
  9. Does @Stable make a class safe? No. It is a semantic promise; hidden mutable fields make that promise false and can produce stale UI.
  10. How should StateFlow or LiveData enter Compose? Through an appropriate lifecycle-aware State adapter while preserving source initial-value, lifetime, equality, thread, and error semantics.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Background threads simultaneously edit snapshot state. Define owner and mutable-snapshot boundaries, apply explicitly, handle conflicts/retry, and never mix unsynchronized ordinary fields. Validate the exact runtime version.
  2. Rows retain the wrong text after sorting. Positional identity followed index. Use stable unique business keys and put nested remembers inside that keyed identity.
  3. Saved state exceeds limits. Persist the durable model in a repository; save only IDs/query/position needed to rebuild, and test registry restoration/schema fallback.
  4. A draw-only animation triggers recomposition. Find the actual read. If structure is fixed, defer to draw/placement; if measurement or structure depends on it, the earlier phase is correct.

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. For every mutable value on your screen, who owns it, what observable write path does it use, and what lifetime does it require?
  2. Which remembered values can retain stale dependencies or move to another logical item after reorder?
  3. Which reads happen in composition, measure/place, and draw, and what is the earliest correct phase?
  4. What survives branch removal, Activity recreation, and process death, and what must be reconstructed from durable truth?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How does Compose runtime state drive recomposition, and how do you choose state ownership and retention?

~30-second answer#

Compose is an incremental runtime. The compiler makes composable calls participate in groups and restart scopes, while the slot table retains values by call-site identity. Snapshot reads register dependencies; applied writes invalidate the scopes or phases that observed them, but work can be coalesced, skipped, or cancelled. I use observable immutable replacement or snapshot collections, hoist to the lowest owner, use remember only for composition lifetime, and rememberSaveable only for minimal registry-saveable reconstruction data. Stable item keys preserve identity. Composables remain idempotent and side-effect-free.

~2-minute answer#

I model Compose as incremental tree construction and update. The compiler transforms composable calls into a runtime protocol conceptually involving a Composer, groups, change metadata, restart scopes, and skipping. The slot table stores group structure and remembered values by positional call-site identity. Initial composition creates that topology; recomposition revisits invalidated scopes. A stable explicit key is essential when conditional or reordered content must retain logical item identity.

Snapshot state records reads and writes. An applied write invalidates observers that read the changed value. That is not a promise that the whole tree reruns: invalidations can be coalesced, groups can be skipped, and work can be cancelled. Mutable snapshots isolate changes until apply and concurrent writes can conflict, so low-level users need explicit apply, conflict, and thread ownership rules. Ordinary mutable fields and a MutableList inside mutableStateOf are not observed when mutated internally.

I separate composition, layout, and draw reads because invalidation can restart only the relevant later phase. I author local state with remember plus mutableStateOf, or snapshot lists/maps, and replace immutable values at ownership boundaries. Missing remember keys create stale caches; volatile keys recreate state. I hoist only to the lowest common owner, extract a plain state holder for cohesive UI logic, and keep business/durable state in a ViewModel and repository.

Remember survives only while its identity remains composed. RememberSaveable uses the SaveableStateRegistry and Bundle-compatible or custom-Saver values; it is not durable storage. A Saver stores minimal IDs or input needed to rebuild objects. derivedStateOf is justified when dependencies change more often than the meaningful result, and it has overhead. Mutation policy must match semantic equality. Compiler stability and skipping behavior are version-sensitive, and Stable is a promise—not a mechanism that makes mutable data safe. Therefore composables are idempotent and side-effect-free; effects belong to the next stage and deep profiling to Stage 16.

Compose effects, navigation, and ViewModel integrationexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should keep composable bodies pure and idempotent; choose an effect API by work lifecycle; design semantic keys, cancellation, cleanup, and stale-capture policy; integrate lifecycle-aware state, stateless content, ViewModels, and Navigation Compose; model back stacks, deep links, and transient UI actions without a false exactly-once promise; and test each boundary. Stage 10 owns event primitives, Stage 12 architecture/state ownership, Stage 14 runtime, and Stage 17 full DI; this stage covers their Compose wiring.

Senior mental model#

Composition describes desired UI; an effect binds imperative work to a composition identity and lifecycle; a ViewModel owns screen state; a NavController owns a UI back stack, not domain truth. A composable body can rerun, be skipped, or be abandoned before commit, so external work in the body is invalid. An effect starts for a successfully composed instance, and its key defines restart identity, not business exactly-once execution.

  • Separate composition-driven synchronization, user-event work, and a durable business transition: each has a different trigger, lifetime, and delivery contract.
  • Draw the topology: producer → lifecycle gate → route/state holder → stateless content; effect source → collector → imperative UI target; and NavController → back stack separately.
  • Cancellation stops cooperative coroutine work; it cannot roll back an HTTP request, payment, or other external effect already accepted.

Effects, navigation, and ViewModel internals/topology#

repository/domain truth → ViewModel-owned StateFlow
    → collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in Route
    → immutable UiState + callbacks → stateless Content

composition identity + effect keys → effect instance/job/cleanup
user callback → rememberCoroutineScope job (UI-owned)

NavHost graph ↔ NavController ↔ back-stack entries
                               ↳ destination/graph ViewModelStoreOwner
deep link → parse + validate/authorize ID → repository truth

NavHost materializes graph destinations against a NavController. A back-stack entry can provide lifecycle, saved state, and a ViewModelStoreOwner; popping its owner clears scoped ViewModels. A nested graph entry can share a ViewModel across child destinations, while Activity scope intentionally outlives all destinations. Use the narrowest owner that must share the state rather than widening scope to avoid a proper contract.

Effect API selection and lifecycle#

APICorrect contractTypical trap
SideEffectPublish Compose state to non-Compose code after every successful recomposition.One-shot analytics repeats.
LaunchedEffect(keys)Composition-driven suspend work; cancel/restart when the instance leaves or a key changes.Unit captures a changing input, or a broad/volatile key churns.
DisposableEffect(keys)Paired registration/removal through onDispose.Treating disposal as a process-shutdown hook.
rememberCoroutineScope()Launch suspending UI work from a click/gesture; scope cancels when its owner leaves composition.Creating an event flag solely to trigger LaunchedEffect.
rememberUpdatedState(value)Read the latest callback/value from deferred code without restarting the long-lived effect.Hiding an input that should change work identity.
produceStateAdapt a suspend/callback producer into Compose State; producer follows keys and values conflate.Duplicating ViewModel state or omitting awaitDispose for a callback.
snapshotFlowTurn snapshot reads into a cold Flow inside a coroutine.Expecting every write, or building a chain with no terminal collection.

An abandoned composition must not leak an external effect: a body is not a committed lifecycle. Post-commit SideEffect and the setup/disposal boundary of DisposableEffect exist for this reason. A crash or process kill can still skip cleanup, so external correctness cannot depend only on onDispose.

Semantic keys, stale capture, and snapshotFlow topology#

@Composable
fun SearchRoute(queryId: String, onExpired: () -> Unit) {
    val latestOnExpired by rememberUpdatedState(onExpired)
    LaunchedEffect(queryId) {              // work identity follows queryId
        delay(30_000)
        latestOnExpired()                  // latest callback, timer not restarted
    }
}

LaunchedEffect(listState) {
    snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }
        .map { it > 0 }
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .collectLatest { visible -> analytics.setScrolled(visible) }
}
  • A key is semantic work identity: userId, queryId, or lifecycleOwner. A key change cancels/disposes the old instance and starts a new one; cancellation is cooperative.
  • Use rememberUpdatedState when effect lifetime stays fixed but a delayed callback must be current. If a new userId means a new source, make it a key.
  • snapshotFlow records snapshot reads in its block, reruns after relevant applied changes, and emits an unequal result, like distinctUntilChanged. It is observation, not an audit log; equal/intermediate values need not appear.
  • Backpressure remains Flow topology. debounce, buffer, conflate, and collectLatest intentionally change latency, cancellation, or loss. A slow collector can suspend progress, and no operator creates external exactly-once delivery.

Lifecycle-aware collection and duplicate collectors#

An Android route normally reads render state with collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). Collection is active only at the configured minimum lifecycle and can unsubscribe and re-subscribe. That saves work, but a cold upstream can restart, current/replayed state can be read again, and transient emissions while inactive can be lost. Use an appropriate collectAsState contract where Android Lifecycle is unavailable. Do not collect the same UI effect independently in both an Activity and route: lifecycle re-entry or duplicate composition creates duplicate handlers.

Lifecycle collection is not acknowledgement. A completed payment belongs in durable order/payment state so resubscription can reconstruct UI; a completion snackbar may be best-effort. SharedFlow and Channel are in-memory coordination mechanisms, not durable exactly-once queues.

Stateless content + route/state-holder wiring#

@Composable
fun CheckoutRoute(
    onReceipt: (String) -> Unit,
    viewModel: CheckoutViewModel = viewModel(),
) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    CheckoutContent(
        state = state,
        onPay = viewModel::pay,
        onReceipt = { onReceipt(state.orderId) },
    )
}

@Composable
fun CheckoutContent(
    state: CheckoutUiState,
    onPay: () -> Unit,
    onReceipt: () -> Unit,
) { /* layout only; preview/test with plain values */ }

The route obtains the ViewModel/controller, collects state, and turns navigation into callbacks. Content accepts an immutable UI contract and user-event lambdas; it knows nothing about DI, repositories, NavController, or lifecycle. Avoid passing a controller down the tree: onProductClick(id) is easier to test and reuse.

ViewModel ownership, factories, and scoping#

  • A destination-scoped ViewModel lives while its back-stack entry remains. A graph-scoped ViewModel intentionally shares flow state across nested destinations. An Activity-scoped one survives destination pops and is appropriate only for genuinely Activity-wide state.
  • viewModel() uses the nearest ViewModelStoreOwner. For a parent graph, explicitly obtain its stable entry with getBackStackEntry(graphRoute) and use that owner. Scope must be a visible design decision.
  • A ViewModel survives configuration change of its owner, not process death. A new instance after recreation rebuilds from minimal saved input and durable repository truth.
  • Constructor dependencies come from ViewModelProvider.Factory/CreationExtras; createSavedStateHandle() derives a handle from extras. Hilt can generate the factory and provide hiltViewModel(). The concern here is owner/extras integration, not Stage 17 container setup.

SavedStateHandle, arguments, and recreation boundaries#

SavedStateHandle is key/value state for ViewModel recreation, not durable business storage. Navigation arguments can be present in the handle; compatible type-safe route APIs can decode them with toRoute<T>(). Pass stable identifiers and primitives such as productId or orderId, not domain objects. The destination reloads authoritative data from a repository. After process death, server/database truth may have changed and an argument can be missing or old, so parse, validate, and handle not-found explicitly.

Navigation graph, type-safe routes, and back-stack policy#

@Serializable data object Home
@Serializable data class Receipt(val orderId: String)

NavHost(navController, startDestination = Home) {
    composable<Home> { HomeRoute(onReceipt = { navController.navigate(Receipt(it)) }) }
    composable<Receipt> { entry ->
        val route = entry.toRoute<Receipt>()
        ReceiptRoute(orderId = route.orderId)
    }
}

navController.navigate(Home) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
    restoreState = true
}
  • popUpTo removes entries up to a target; inclusive = true removes the target too. A wrong target or inclusive flag destroys expected Back history.
  • launchSingleTop avoids another instance only when the target is already on top; it is not global deduplication.
  • saveState/restoreState can preserve navigator destination state for tab-like flows. Multiple back stacks require deliberate top-level route policy and tests; they are not domain persistence.
  • Deep links are untrusted input. Restrict scheme/host/path, decode safely, validate format/range, authorize access, and load by ID. A syntactically valid route grants no domain permission.

Navigation/UI actions versus durable outcomes#

Direct click navigation is a UI action: a callback can invoke a navigator for that click. Composition-driven navigation needs explicit consumption or idempotency semantics. if (state.paid) navController.navigate(...) in the body, or a naive LaunchedEffect(state.paid), can repeat after recreation or resubscription. A key controls restart, not “handled once forever.”

FactModelTrade-off
Payment/order completedDurable repository status and idempotent command/request ID.Survives process death; UI can derive a safe destination, but transition policy must prevent loops.
Navigate after clickUI callback/navigator contract.Simple; debounce double taps and define stack options.
SnackbarBest-effort effect, or durable message state with explicit acknowledgement if loss is unacceptable.SharedFlow/Channel can lose or duplicate around lifecycle/process boundaries.

Never turn the current NavController destination into the source of truth for payment or auth. The domain outcome exists authoritatively outside navigation; route selection is only a projection. When an effect stream is used, document loss, replay, duplicate collection, and acknowledgement policy without durable exactly-once claims.

Guarantees versus explicit non-guarantees#

Useful contractDoes not guarantee
A LaunchedEffect job is cancelled when its key/instance leaves.Preemption of non-cooperative code, rollback of external effects, or exactly-once execution.
An effect key defines restart identity.One execution per process, session, or business operation.
rememberCoroutineScope cancels when its composition owner leaves.Completion after navigation away or durable business delivery.
DisposableEffect.onDispose runs when the key/instance leaves composition.Cleanup on process crash or shutdown.
A ViewModel survives its owner's configuration change.Survival after process death or after its owner is cleared.
SavedStateHandle supports recreation.Durable, large, or authoritative business storage.
Lifecycle-aware collection stops and starts with lifecycle.Continuous subscription or delivery while inactive.
SharedFlow/Channel coordinate in-memory consumers.A durable exactly-once queue.
NavController manages a UI stack.A domain source of truth.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Generic type-safe Navigation Compose routes—composable<T>, object/data-class routes, toRoute<T>, typed navigate/popUpTo—are Navigation 2.8-era APIs and evolve with Navigation and Kotlin serialization. Pin artifacts/plugins, read current release notes, and do not treat legacy string routes as identical.
  • Navigation 3 is a separate evolving Compose-first library with different back-stack ownership and APIs; do not mix its contracts into Navigation 2 examples.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle is in androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose; overloads, minimum-lifecycle constraints, and platform availability depend on Lifecycle version. Compose Multiplatform can require another collector.
  • viewModel(), hiltViewModel(), CreationExtras/default factories, and SavedState integration depend on Activity/Lifecycle/Navigation/Hilt versions. Verify the owner and factory in the pinned graph.
  • Follow current Compose runtime documentation for effect semantics; scheduling implementation is not a public exactly-once protocol.

Decision framework#

  1. Name the trigger: successful composition, key identity, user event, lifecycle visibility, or durable domain transition.
  2. Name the owner/lifetime: composition instance, destination, nested graph, Activity, ViewModel, or repository.
  3. Choose the narrowest API: body for description; SideEffect to publish; DisposableEffect to pair; LaunchedEffect for keyed suspend work; remembered scope for callbacks; produceState for an adapter; snapshotFlow for snapshot observation.
  4. Write down semantic keys, stale-value policy, cooperative cancellation points, cleanup, and external idempotency.
  5. For state, choose a lifecycle collector; for an action/event, specify loss, duplication, replay, and acknowledgement semantics.
  6. For navigation, define ID validation, owner scope, stack transform, deep-link trust boundary, and post-process-death reconstruction.
  7. Test pure content, effect contract, ViewModel state/recreation, and graph/back-stack behavior at their respective boundaries.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A broad key restarts an expensive collector; a constant key captures a stale dependency; a random key destroys lifecycle.
  • rememberUpdatedState keeps a callback current without restart, but hides a defect if the source itself should change.
  • collectLatest reduces lag by cancelling prior handling; non-idempotent external writes can be left partially complete.
  • Activity-scoped ViewModels simplify sharing but retain stale cross-screen state after a graph exit.
  • Passing a domain object creates a stale, oversized, serialization-coupled route snapshot; an ID requires reload but preserves truth and authorization.
  • launchSingleTop and multiple-stack restoration improve tabs, but a wrong popUpTo loses history or accumulates duplicate entries.
  • Lifecycle resubscription can restart cold upstreams; duplicate route/effect collectors can show a snackbar or navigate twice.

Production scenario: payment completion#

Hypothetical: the user taps Pay; the ViewModel sends a command with an idempotency key, the repository persists order/payment status, and a StateFlow exposes Processing/Completed. The route uses collectAsStateWithLifecycle; stateless content only calls onPay. Navigation to Receipt(orderId) is a guarded/consumed UI policy, and the receipt reloads the order by ID. After process death, the app reads durable Completed state and chooses a safe destination; a SharedFlow completion is not the sole proof.

A “Payment complete” snackbar is best-effort: it can be lost in background or repeat after collector restart. If the message is legally or operationally important, model acknowledged durable notification state instead. Bottom tabs use popUpTo(start) { saveState = true }, launchSingleTop, and restoreState; a deep-linked orderId is format-checked and authorized before display.

Code-review/debug trap#

@Composable
fun Checkout(vm: CheckoutViewModel, nav: NavController) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    if (state.paid) nav.navigate("receipt/${state.order}") // side effect in body
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.events.collect { nav.navigate(it.route) } }
    DisposableEffect(Unit) {
        gateway.addListener { vm.refresh() }
        onDispose { } // leaked listener
    }
}

Navigation in the body can repeat; a Unit collector can retain the wrong VM/nav owner and duplicate another collector; a domain object/string route is stale or untrusted; and listener cleanup is missing. Debug with effect-instance logs for key, owner, start/cancel/dispose; back-stack snapshots; collector counts; and lifecycle/process recreation. Fix with route/content separation, a typed stable orderId, direct click navigation or explicit outcome consumption, semantic keys/latest callbacks, symmetric cleanup, durable payment truth, and an idempotent command.

Testing effects, navigation, and ViewModel boundaries#

  • Pure Compose tests render Content(state, callbacks) and assert semantics and callback IDs without a real ViewModel or NavController.
  • Effect tests control keys and composition presence: assert restart cancellation, latest callback, listener registration/removal, and absence of body effects; use deterministic coroutine time where relevant.
  • ViewModel unit tests cover state transitions, idempotency/retry, and reconstruction from minimal SavedStateHandle. A configuration-change test is not proof of process-death safety.
  • Graph integration can use TestNavHostController plus ComposeNavigator to verify start destination, typed destination/back stack, popUpTo, and restoration policy. Use a small Navigator contract fake for route callbacks and test deep-link validation/authorization separately.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Why not run an effect in a composable body? The body can rerun, skip, or be abandoned and has no committed external lifecycle. Use a post-commit/keyed effect or user callback.
  2. How do you choose a LaunchedEffect key? Use semantic source/work identity. Change means cancel old and start new; it does not mean exactly-once.
  3. LaunchedEffect or rememberCoroutineScope? The former is composition-driven and keyed; the latter starts suspending UI work from a user callback and cancels with its owner.
  4. When should you use rememberUpdatedState? When a long-lived effect must not restart but deferred code needs the latest callback/value, not for source identity.
  5. What does DisposableEffect guarantee? Paired disposal when the key/instance leaves composition, not cleanup after process kill.
  6. What does snapshotFlow do? It observes snapshot reads and emits unequal results into a cold Flow; it is not a log of every write, and downstream operators define backpressure/loss.
  7. How do you scope a ViewModel? To the narrowest ViewModelStoreOwner: destination, intentionally shared nested graph, or genuinely Activity-wide owner.
  8. What belongs in a route or SavedStateHandle? Minimal stable IDs/primitives needed for reconstruction, not domain objects or durable truth.
  9. Does SharedFlow guarantee navigation once? No. Lifecycle/process gaps and duplicate collectors permit loss or duplication; model durable outcomes as state with an idempotent policy.
  10. How do you test Navigation Compose? Test content callbacks directly; test the graph with TestNavHostController/ComposeNavigator or a navigator contract fake and assert stack options.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. An effect was cancelled after HTTP submit. Cancellation cannot undo the server effect. Use an idempotency key, query durable status, and reconcile an unknown outcome.
  2. Bottom-tab state sometimes disappears. Verify a stable top-level route, popUpTo(findStartDestination()), paired saveState/restoreState, singleTop, and version-specific navigator restoration tests.
  3. A graph-shared ViewModel is created twice. Both destinations must explicitly use the same parent graph back-stack entry as owner; log owner and entry lifecycle, not only class name.
  4. Completion navigation duplicates after rotation. Do not use Boolean state as a one-time command. Keep completion durable and make route transition guarded, acknowledged, or an idempotent stack transform; test recreation.

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. For every effect, what are its trigger, semantic key, cancellation points, stale-capture policy, and cleanup?
  2. What happens to each state/effect collector across STOP→START, duplicate destination, pop, and process death?
  3. What exact owner holds each ViewModel, when is it cleared, and what reconstructs it after process recreation?
  4. Which navigation inputs are untrusted, what stack transform is expected, and where does durable domain truth live?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you integrate Compose effects, Navigation, and ViewModels without duplicate work or lost outcomes?

~30-second answer#

I keep composable bodies pure and choose an effect by ownership: SideEffect for post-commit publishing, DisposableEffect for paired registration, LaunchedEffect for composition-driven keyed work, and a remembered scope for user events. Keys define restart identity, not exactly-once delivery, and cancellation cannot undo external effects. A route collects ViewModel state with lifecycle awareness and passes immutable state and callbacks to stateless content. I scope ViewModels to the narrowest destination, graph, or Activity owner, pass stable IDs through typed routes, treat deep links as untrusted, and keep durable outcomes in repositories rather than SharedFlow, SavedStateHandle, or NavController.

~2-minute answer#

My starting rule is that composition describes UI and can rerun, skip, or be abandoned, so it cannot perform external work. I use SideEffect to publish after successful recomposition, DisposableEffect for symmetric setup and cleanup, LaunchedEffect for suspend work whose lifetime follows semantic keys, and rememberCoroutineScope when a click starts UI-owned suspend work. rememberUpdatedState keeps a callback fresh without restarting a long-lived effect; produceState adapts an external producer to State; snapshotFlow observes snapshot reads as a cold Flow. Effect cancellation is cooperative, disposal is not a process-shutdown hook, and no key gives business exactly-once.

On Android, the route layer collects StateFlow with collectAsStateWithLifecycle and passes plain immutable state and callbacks to stateless content. Collection can stop and restart with lifecycle, so cold upstreams may restart and transient emissions may be lost. I avoid duplicate collectors and treat SharedFlow or Channel as in-memory delivery, not durable queues. A completed payment or order is repository state with idempotent commands; a snackbar is usually best-effort.

I scope a ViewModel to the narrowest ViewModelStoreOwner: a destination by default, a nested graph for intentional sharing, or the Activity only for Activity-wide state. It survives configuration change, not process death. Factories and CreationExtras reconstruct dependencies and SavedStateHandle; Hilt can generate that wiring, but scope remains explicit. SavedStateHandle stores minimal restorable input, not authoritative business data.

Navigation Compose owns a UI graph and back stack. I prefer version-compatible typed serializable routes, pass stable IDs rather than objects, validate and authorize deep links, and reload truth from a repository. I specify popUpTo and inclusive carefully; launchSingleTop only deduplicates the top; saveState and restoreState support deliberate multiple-back-stack policies. NavController is never my domain source of truth. I test pure content with callbacks, ViewModel state and recreation separately, effects by key/disposal, and graph behavior with TestNavHostController or a navigator contract fake.

Jetpack Compose performanceexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should diagnose Compose jank evidence-first from a frame symptom through composition, layout, draw, GPU, and I/O; choose Macrobenchmark or Microbenchmark; interpret Perfetto/System Trace, Layout Inspector counters, and Compose compiler reports; fix a demonstrated stability, state-read phase, lazy identity, allocation, image, or animation problem; and re-measure a regression budget with representative data. The focus is rendering and interaction; broad startup optimization and the full Baseline Profile workflow are reserved for Stage 25.

Senior mental model#

Optimize the missed frame, not a proxy metric. A state change can invalidate a restart scope; runtime can execute recomposition or skip it; measure/layout, draw recording, and GPU work are separate. Recomposition is a normal update mechanism, not a defect. Fewer recompositions do not necessarily mean faster frames: one image decode, intrinsic pass, or overdraw hotspot can cost more than many cheap skips.

  • First pin down the user journey, frame deadline, and trace; then locate CPU/GPU/I/O work, phase, and owner.
  • Separate startup from steady-state rendering. Macrobenchmark can measure both, but this stage optimizes scroll, animation, and screen rendering; broad startup belongs to Stage 25.
  • Every change should explain the trace: which work moved or disappeared, from which phase, and at what correctness, memory, or readability cost.

Runtime/performance topology#

input / State write
  → snapshot invalidation of scopes that read it
  → recomposition execution or skipping
  → node changes / measure → layout → draw recording
  → RenderThread / GPU composition → displayed frame

release/profileable app + representative dataset
  → Macrobenchmark/JankStats symptom
  → Perfetto/System Trace attribution
  → Layout Inspector counters + compiler reports as supporting evidence
  → one targeted change → same benchmark and regression budget

Frame timing is end-to-end: UI thread, RenderThread, GPU, binder, decoding, GC, and scheduling can all be the critical path. JankStats adds per-frame timing and UI-state observability, but does not identify root cause by itself.

Performance pipeline and evidence tools#

ToolCorrect questionBoundary
MacrobenchmarkDoes a real startup/scroll/navigation journey meet frame or startup metrics?End-to-end and device-sensitive; broad startup is reserved for Stage 25.
MicrobenchmarkIs an isolated pure function or layout primitive faster?Does not model full UI, scheduler, GPU, or end-to-end UX.
Perfetto / System TraceWhere is the critical path for a long frame: main, RenderThread, GC, decode?Correlate the trace with the interaction and app markers.
Layout InspectorWhich composables recompose or skip during one controlled action?Counters are a lead, not a frame-time verdict; tooling adds overhead.
Compose compiler reportsWhat is restartable/skippable, and what stability did the compiler infer?A build-time model, not runtime proof of jank.
JankStats/frame metricsWhich frames are janky, and which UI state was active?Observability/field signal, not automatic attribution.

Make final conclusions on a release-like non-debuggable or controlled profileable build; debug builds are unsuitable for final performance conclusions. Baseline Profiles can change compilation state and startup/rendering numbers, so record their mode, while leaving the full profile workflow to Stage 25.

Recomposition, skipping, stability, and churn#

  • Restartable means runtime can restart a scope; skippable means its body can be omitted for unchanged inputs under the applicable contract/compiler mode. Invalidation is not execution, and execution does not imply full layout/draw.
  • Under strong skipping, restartable composables with unstable parameters are generally skippable; stable parameters compare by equality and unstable parameters by instance identity. A fresh unstable instance on every recomposition still defeats comparison.
  • @Immutable promises observable public state never changes; @Stable promises stable equality and observable changes. These are compiler contracts, not runtime enforcement. A false annotation can leave stale UI; stable annotations do not make mutable data safe.
  • Kotlin List/Set/Map interfaces do not prove immutability. Prefer truly immutable UI models/immutable collections; stability configuration is a promise for external types, not a suppression file.
  • Inspect call-site instance and lambda churn. Strong skipping can automatically memoize lambdas, but version/mode and capture keys matter; do not add manual remember without evidence and correct keys.
@Immutable
data class FeedUi(val items: ImmutableList<FeedItemUi>)

// Truthful only if FeedItemUi and every reachable value are immutable.
@Composable
fun FeedRow(item: FeedItemUi, onOpen: (Long) -> Unit) { /* cheap UI */ }

State-read phases, deferred reads, caching, and backwards writes#

val offset = animateIntOffsetAsState(targetValue, label = "cardOffset")
Box(Modifier.offset { offset.value }) // layout-phase read

val color = animateColorAsState(targetColor, label = "cardColor")
Box(Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(color.value) }) // draw-phase read
  • A state read in composition invalidates composition; a read in a layout/draw block can invalidate only that later phase. Pass a provider lambda and use block-form offset { }, graphicsLayer { }, or drawBehind when a fast value does not change tree shape.
  • Do not back-write observable state composition→composition. Likewise, onSizeChanged in layout writing a value read by a sibling in composition creates a layout→composition loop; keep the measurement in constraint/placement work where possible.
  • derivedStateOf has observation/calculation cost. Use it when inputs change more often than a derived threshold/result, such as showing a scroll-to-top control; not for cheap concatenation that legitimately changes with every input.
  • remember(keys) caches within composition identity, but remember does not make expensive work free: first calculation, invalid keys, retention, and main-thread cost remain. Missing keys produce stale data; heavy CPU work often belongs outside composition.

Lazy lists, item identity, and layout cost#

  • Provide stable unique key values so identity/state move with items during insert/reorder; keys preserve identity but do not guarantee zero recomposition. Avoid positions when order can change.
  • contentType helps reuse compatible item compositions in heterogeneous feeds. Keep it semantically stable and do not group incompatible layouts.
  • Paging reduces the resident dataset, but placeholders need realistic size, IDs must remain stable, and load/error rows need distinct keys; otherwise a viewport can request pages repeatedly or identity can jump.
  • Avoid same-direction nested lazy containers without bounded size and clear ownership; flatten sections into one parent lazy DSL. Nested horizontal carousels can be valid, but measure composition/reuse.
  • SubcomposeLayout/BoxWithConstraints are appropriate when composition depends on constraints, but subcomposition adds work. Intrinsic measurement can add passes. A custom layout only earns its complexity when a trace proves layout is the bottleneck.

Modifiers, drawing, images, overdraw, and animation#

  • Hoist/reuse long modifier chains only when allocation churn is demonstrated or the chain is stable; modifier order and correctness come first. Use caching draw APIs such as drawWithCache for size/state-dependent brushes or paths instead of allocating each frame.
  • graphicsLayer can move translation/alpha/scale to a layer and avoid composition/layout, but layers cost memory, recording, and sometimes offscreen compositing. Do not add them prophylactically.
  • Request/decode images near display size, use thumbnail/cache policy, and avoid decoding a huge bitmap for a small cell. Check placeholder→image size stability and main-thread work.
  • Remove redundant opaque backgrounds, clipping/offscreen buffers, and invisible layers; skipping cannot cure overdraw or a GPU bottleneck.
  • Read frame-rate animation state in layout/draw when tree shape is unchanged; limit animated area/effects and verify frame pacing. Do not reduce refresh rate or visual quality without a product/accessibility decision.

Guarantees versus explicit non-guarantees#

Useful contractDoes not guarantee
Skipping can avoid a restartable body for unchanged inputs.Fewer recompositions mean faster frames, or no layout/draw/GPU cost.
A truthful stability contract enables defined comparison/skipping.@Stable/@Immutable make mutable data safe.
remember(keys) reuses a value for an identity and keys.Expensive work becomes free, background, or immune to stale data.
A lazy key preserves logical identity through moves.Zero recomposition, measurement, or allocation.
A Microbenchmark measures its hot loop under stated conditions.End-to-end UX, scroll jank, or production scheduler/GPU behavior.
A Macrobenchmark/trace gives evidence for one build/device/journey.Universal speed across every device and dataset.
Modules and abstractions can improve ownership/build isolation.Rendering speed; more modules/abstractions are irrelevant without evidence.
Debug tooling can expose a lead.A final verdict: debug builds are unsuitable for final conclusions.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Strong skipping is enabled by default in Kotlin 2.0.20+ Compose compiler setups, but that is not universal for older compiler versions, disabled mode, or pinned toolchains. Record Kotlin/Compose compiler versions and flags.
  • Automatic lambda memoization and stable/unstable comparison rules depend on strong-skipping mode; use the current compiler documentation and reports for the shipped variant.
  • Compiler-report Gradle configuration changed with the Kotlin Compose compiler plugin; do not copy old flags without checking.
  • Layout Inspector counters, trace labels, Macrobenchmark/JankStats metrics, and Baseline Profile behavior vary with Android Studio, device API, and library versions. Pin versions and retain raw results.

Diagnosis/decision framework#

  1. Name the visible symptom, journey, device class, dataset, frame/startup metric, and budget.
  2. Reproduce on a release/profileable build; warm up for the scenario, repeat iterations, and retain a distribution plus noisy-environment notes.
  3. Use Macrobenchmark for the journey and Microbenchmark only for an isolated suspect. Correlate a slow iteration with Perfetto/System Trace.
  4. Classify the critical path: composition/skipping, layout/intrinsics/subcomposition, draw/allocation, image/I/O, RenderThread/GPU, GC, or unrelated work.
  5. Use Layout Inspector and compiler reports to test a concrete Compose hypothesis, not as the goal.
  6. Make one minimal correctness-preserving change; repeat the identical measurement and compare percentiles/distribution against the regression budget.
  7. Add a benchmark/observability guard and verify accessibility, visual fidelity, memory, and representative worst-case data.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A false stability annotation improves a report and breaks updates; immutable copies reduce mutation risk but can add allocations.
  • Excess caching retains memory or stale values; missing keys break correctness and broad keys miss the cache.
  • A deferred read avoids composition but adds a callback/provider contract; use it for measured hot state, not UI branching.
  • derivedStateOf reduces downstream invalidation only when the result changes less often; otherwise it adds overhead.
  • A layer/cache can help repeated transform/draw but costs memory/offscreen work; a custom layout saves nodes at a complexity cost.
  • A tiny dataset, one flagship device, or one lucky iteration hides tail latency; thermal throttling, background work, and compilation mode add noise.

Production optimization scenario: janky product feed#

Before. A 500-card mixed feed janks during fling: positions are keys, there is no contentType, images are full resolution, toolbar scroll offset is read in composition, rows create lists/lambdas, and nested vertical lazy sections have unclear reuse.

Measure. A release/profileable Macrobenchmark uses the same seeded dataset and scripted fling after warmup. JankStats/frame metrics establish the symptom; Perfetto shows main-thread composition/layout plus image decode; Layout Inspector shows visible-row churn; the compiler report shows fresh unstable wrapper instances. Record median/tail, janky frames, and the regression budget—not one run.

Change. Add stable item IDs and semantic contentType, flatten the vertical lazy DSL, request thumbnail-sized images, make the per-item model immutable, and remove call-site instance churn. Pass a scroll provider to the toolbar and read it in graphicsLayer { }. Do not add an annotation until its contract is truthful.

Re-measure. The same device/build/profile state/dataset/journey shows fewer long frames and shorter decode/layout slices without memory or visual regression. Reports and counters support the explanation, but acceptance is the frame distribution within budget. Record startup as a guard and defer broad startup/Baseline Profile tuning to Stage 25.

Code-review/debug trap#

@Immutable // false: mutable list can change invisibly
class FeedState(val items: MutableList<Item>)

@Composable
fun Feed(state: FeedState, listState: LazyListState) {
    val y = listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset // frame-rate composition read
    val visible = remember { expensiveFilter(state.items) } // stale: missing key
    LazyColumn {
        itemsIndexed(visible, key = { index, _ -> index }) { _, item ->
            Card(Modifier.graphicsLayer(translationY = -y.toFloat()))
        }
    }
}

The annotation lies; in-place mutation can be skipped incorrectly; the cache is stale; a position key loses identity; scroll crosses every row boundary as a composition value; and the value-form layer cannot defer the read. Do not “fix” this with modules, more annotations, or a lower recomposition count. Trace one fling, make model and identity truthful, move the read to a provider/block layer, size images, and rerun the benchmark.

Testability and observability#

  • Inject deterministic representative datasets, fake image sources, and controllable clocks/animation where possible; benchmark production-like paths.
  • Keep semantics/correctness Compose tests separate from performance tests. Output/identity tests protect refactors; Macrobenchmark guards a frame journey; Microbenchmark guards a proven isolated primitive.
  • Add trace sections around app work, stable scenario labels, and JankStats state so a field/session signal maps to screen mode without PII.
  • Store raw Perfetto traces, build SHA, device/API, thermal/compilation/Baseline Profile mode, iterations, and distributions. CI budgets should tolerate known noise but fail a sustained regression, not one outlier.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Macrobenchmark or Microbenchmark? Macro measures a user journey, frames/startup, and system interaction; Micro measures isolated hot code. A Microbenchmark does not predict end-to-end UX.
  2. Is recomposition bad? No. It is the expected update mechanism; only unnecessary or expensive work on a measured critical path is a problem.
  3. Restartable versus skippable? A restartable scope can be re-entered; a skippable body can be omitted for unchanged inputs under the applicable compiler mode.
  4. What did strong skipping change? In Kotlin 2.0.20+ it is default: unstable parameters do not automatically prevent skipping, but compare by identity; verify version/mode.
  5. When should you add @Immutable? Only when the whole observable contract is truly immutable; the annotation is a promise, not a repair for mutable state.
  6. When is derivedStateOf useful? When a frequently changing input changes a derived result/threshold less often, not for every cheap derivation.
  7. Why defer a state read? So a frame-rate value invalidates layout/draw rather than composition when it does not alter the emitted tree.
  8. What do lazy key and contentType provide? Stable move identity and compatible item reuse, not zero recomposition.
  9. Why not measure a debug build? Debug, tooling, and compiler behavior distort timings; final conclusions require a release/profileable representative setup.
  10. How do you prove an optimization? Same journey/build mode/device/dataset: before trace/distribution, one explained change, re-measurement, and a budget/regression guard.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. Counters fell, but jank did not. Inspect layout/draw/GPU/decode/GC critical path; a count does not contain cost.
  2. A stable model still recomposes. Check truly changed parameters, parent execution, lambda/instance churn, strong-skipping mode, and the compiler report; legitimate state can require execution.
  3. The fling benchmark is noisy. Seed data, fix the gesture, control warmup/iterations/device thermal/background state, analyze distributions/traces, and never cherry-pick.
  4. graphicsLayer improved CPU but memory rose. Measure layer size, offscreen, and GPU cost; bound its area/lifetime or return to direct draw if total frame performance is worse.

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. Which exact frame journey, percentile, and device-class budget does your benchmark protect?
  2. Where is each fast-changing state read—composition, measure, placement, or draw—and why?
  3. Which stability annotations/config entries are evidenced contracts, and which merely hide mutable data?
  4. Does the representative dataset include paging, mixed content types, large images, reorder, and worst-case animation?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you diagnose and optimize Jetpack Compose performance?

~30-second answer#

I optimize frame time, not recomposition counts. I reproduce a representative journey in a release or profileable build, use Macrobenchmark and frame metrics for the symptom, and Perfetto for attribution. Layout Inspector counters and compiler reports test a specific Compose hypothesis. I then fix the proven phase—stability or instance churn, deferred state reads, lazy identity, layout, drawing, images, or animation—and rerun the same benchmark. Fewer recompositions, stable annotations, remember, keys, and microbenchmarks are not end-to-end guarantees.

~2-minute answer#

I start with a user-visible journey and a budget: for example, tail frame time during a fling on a mid-tier device with a seeded production-sized feed. I measure a release or profileable build with Macrobenchmark, control warmup, compilation and Baseline Profile state, retain distributions and traces, and use JankStats or frame metrics for observability. Microbenchmark is only for an isolated primitive; it cannot predict full UX.

In Perfetto I locate the critical path across the UI thread, RenderThread, GPU, decoding, GC, and scheduling. If composition is implicated, I use Layout Inspector counters and Compose compiler reports to distinguish invalidation, execution, and skipping. Restartability is not skippability. With Kotlin 2.0.20+ strong skipping is default, unstable parameters can still be skippable but compare by identity, so fresh instances still churn. I make data truly immutable or configure external stable types truthfully; annotations never make mutation safe.

I then target the phase. Fast scroll or animation values that do not change tree shape can be read in block-form layout/draw modifiers or provider lambdas. I avoid backwards writes, use derivedStateOf only when the result changes less often, and key remember correctly. Lazy lists get stable keys, content types, and realistic paging placeholders. I inspect subcomposition, intrinsics, modifier/draw allocations, layer trade-offs, image decode size, and overdraw.

Finally I make one change and rerun the identical benchmark against a regression budget, checking memory, visuals, and correctness. Fewer recompositions are supporting evidence, not success. Broad startup and the full Baseline Profile strategy belong to the later startup stage.

  • Macrobenchmark overview, Microbenchmark overview, Macrobenchmark metrics
  • Overview of system tracing, Perfetto documentation, JankStats
