Dependency injection on Androidexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should distinguish dependency inversion, dependency injection, and service locator; design constructor injection and a composition root manually or with Dagger/Hilt; explain generated graphs, bindings, scopes, and Android lifecycle topology; diagnose missing or duplicate bindings, scope mismatch, cycles, and generated-code build failures; and choose testing seams, runtime parameters, and an incremental migration path. This does not repeat Stage 13 layering or Stage 15 ViewModel mechanics: the focus is object-graph ownership and lifetime.

Senior mental model#

DI assembles an object graph at a boundary; it is not architecture. Dependency inversion is a policy: high-level behavior should not depend directly on volatile implementation details. Dependency injection is a mechanism: a caller or composition root supplies a dependency. A service locator is hidden pull: an object asks a global registry, so it is not DI because the dependency is absent from its constructor/API.

  • Constructor injection is the default choice: dependencies are explicit, the object is valid after construction, and a unit test creates the SUT without a container.
  • Manual DI is sufficient for a small, stable graph: one composition root creates objects and owns cleanup. A framework earns its cost when graph scale, Android entry points, variants, and repeated lifetime wiring dominate.
  • Interfaces belong at real volatility or ownership seams; interfaces do not decouple components that change together. A wrapper for every class only enlarges the graph.
  • DI does not create architectural separation or testability automatically: hidden I/O, global state, and broad contracts remain coupled inside a neatly generated graph.
ApproachStrengthCost / poor fit
Manual DITransparent Kotlin, minimal build/tooling cost, direct debugging.Boilerplate and manual lifecycle/variant wiring grow with the graph.
Dagger/HiltCompile-time graph validation and generated wiring; Hilt supplies Android lifecycle components.Code generation, build integration, annotation model, and generated error traces.
Koin (optional trade-off)Runtime DSL and straightforward incremental adoption.A different validation/debugging model where some wiring failures occur at runtime; assess the current version, startup, and tooling in your own project without blanket claims.

Graph, Dagger internals, and ownership#

composition root / generated component
  request CheckoutViewModel
    → CheckoutViewModel_Factory
      → Provider<PlaceOrder>
      → PlaceOrder_Factory
        → qualified PaymentGateway binding
          → @Provides SDK factory

key = type + optional qualifier
binding = construction rule
component instance = graph owner/cache boundary
scope = reuse rule inside compatible component lifetime

Dagger reads @Inject constructors and modules, validates the reachable binding graph, then emits components, generated factories, and Provider wiring; reflection-based runtime lookup is not its core model. An unscoped binding is normally created per request, while a scoped binding is cached by a component instance. A component entry point is an explicit provision/injection boundary, not permission for business code to use a locator.

Lazy<T> memoizes the first T for that injected Lazy; Provider<T> requests a value later or repeatedly according to binding scope. Lazy/Provider break eager construction but can hide cycles; redesign bidirectional responsibility or add an event/callback boundary instead of defaulting to Lazy.

Hilt component/lifecycle topology#

Generated componentAndroid owner/lifetimeCompatible scope
SingletonComponentApplication component instance; process lifetime@Singleton
ActivityRetainedComponentOne logical Activity across configuration changes@ActivityRetainedScoped
ViewModelComponentOne Hilt ViewModel instance@ViewModelScoped
ActivityComponentOne concrete Activity instance@ActivityScoped
FragmentComponentOne concrete Fragment instance@FragmentScoped
ViewComponent/ViewWithFragmentComponentOne injected View, optionally with Fragment bindings@ViewScoped
ServiceComponentOne Service instance@ServiceScoped

In Hilt, a child can see ancestor bindings, not the reverse. Component lifetime and scoped-object lifetime are connected: a scoped instance lives while its component instance lives unless an outside reference leaks it longer. Scope annotation controls graph reuse/lifetime, not thread safety or durability. A short-lived context/object captured by a long-lived binding is a captive dependency and likely leak; an application dependency consumed by a short-lived object is usually the safe direction.

An @Singleton singleton is per generated component/process instance, not a cross-process or durable global singleton. Every app process has a separate graph, and process death removes memory. A mutable singleton still needs synchronization or serialization and an explicit consistency model: scope does not provide thread safety.

Constructor injection, modules, and qualifiers#

class PlaceOrder @Inject constructor(
    private val orders: Orders,
    @IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
)

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class OrdersBindings {
    @Binds abstract fun bindOrders(impl: SqlOrders): Orders
}

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object SdkModule {
    @Provides @Singleton
    fun paymentSdk(@ApplicationContext context: Context): PaymentSdk =
        PaymentSdk.create(context)
}
  • Use an @Inject constructor for an owned constructible type; the graph sees dependencies directly. Do not introduce an interface solely for Dagger.
  • @Binds is an abstract implementation-to-API alias with no custom construction; @Provides handles factory logic, third-party types, builders, or derived values. A provider method should be deterministic with respect to declared inputs.
  • A qualifier is part of the binding key. Prefer a semantic qualifier such as @IoDispatcher or @AuthenticatedClient over a fragile string, and audit every injection site when qualified and unqualified instances coexist.

Multibindings, optional bindings, and deferred access#

  • Set/map multibinding aggregates plugins or handlers from separate modules without a central switch. Map keys must be stable and unique; contribution iteration order must not become a business contract.
  • An optional binding models an absent capability/default more clearly than a nullable locator. Availability may differ between parent and subcomponent graphs.
  • Inject Provider<T> for repeated/on-demand requests and Lazy<T> for deferred memoized access. These control construction, not lifecycle cancellation or automatic background execution.
  • A cycle signals confused ownership/responsibility. Break it with a command/event interface, split state owner, or higher-level coordinator; Lazy as a default only postpones the failure.

Hilt ViewModel, SavedStateHandle, and Compose#

@HiltViewModel with an @Inject constructor supplies ViewModel dependencies from ViewModelComponent; the default SavedStateHandle binding belongs to that ViewModel creation context. Hilt ViewModel scope follows the ViewModel instance, not a navigation destination by magic: the owner/store/back-stack entry, key, and navigation scoping API determine reuse. SavedStateHandle is for small restorable state/arguments, not an object store or durable repository.

In Compose, obtain a Hilt ViewModel with hiltViewModel() from androidx.hilt:hilt-lifecycle-viewmodel-compose (Hilt 1.3.0+; it works with or without Navigation and, inside a NavHost, scopes to the back-stack entry) at a screen boundary, then pass state and actions down. Do not query a generated component/entry point in leaf composables. Hilt entry points exist for a framework-created or non-Hilt-owned boundary that cannot use constructor injection; keep them narrow so they do not become a service locator.

Gradle/feature modules and graph ownership#

Graph ownership should follow deployment and lifetime boundaries rather than merely the package tree. A feature/API module exposes a minimal contract or factory; the app/composition module selects the implementation. Hilt code generation must see transitive modules in app compilation; a dynamic feature or separate compilation boundary can require explicit Dagger component dependencies. Plain Dagger subcomponents inherit a parent graph and lifecycle ownership; component dependencies consume only an exposed dependency API. These are composition mechanics, not a repeat of Stage 13 layer/module taxonomy.

  • Do not expose concrete generated types between Gradle modules; stable API contracts should remain source-level.
  • Avoid a mega-module that knows every feature or a reverse dependency added only to install one binding. Multibindings or a feature-owned factory can reduce central coupling.
  • Sharing a scope annotation without sharing a component owner does not share an instance; the annotation is not a bridge between unrelated components.

Testing seams and production wiring#

  • Test a constructor-injected class directly with fake dependencies; most unit tests need no Dagger/Hilt. This explicit constructor seam is why constructor injection reduces DI-framework testing.
  • Separately keep a graph/component smoke test for production bindings and an Android integration test. Pure unit tests prove behavior, not wiring.
  • Hilt tests can use test module replacement with @TestInstallIn, remove a production module via @UninstallModules, or contribute a per-test binding; generated test components isolate the graph.
  • Test module replacement does not prove production wiring: the replacement deliberately bypasses the production provider, qualifier, and configuration. Retain a production graph build/smoke path.

Runtime parameters and assisted injection#

Graph-owned stable dependencies and runtime values are different inputs. An order ID, parsed deep link, or opened file should not become a global binding. Pass it as a method/factory parameter; when a generated factory must combine runtime arguments with injected dependencies, use a supported assisted injection pattern. For a ViewModel, verify current Hilt assisted APIs and versions; navigation arguments through SavedStateHandle are often simpler when the value is restorable. Never add a scope merely to transport a parameter.

Startup, eager work, and external resources#

  • Building a graph does not instantiate every object, but an entry-point request can transitively run eager constructors/providers. Constructors should not start network, disk, or coroutine side effects.
  • Lazy/Provider defer construction but retain first-use latency. Eager initialization needs an explicit startup owner, ordering, failure/timeout policy, and measurement; do not hide it in a singleton constructor.
  • Wrap a third-party SDK with an adapter/factory: explicit application Context, credential/config validation, init/shutdown, and callback/thread policy. An AutoCloseable resource needs an owner that calls close; a DI scope does not perform cleanup by itself.

Guarantees vs explicit non-guarantees#

What it providesWhat it does not guarantee
An explicit constructor dependency.DI does not create architectural separation or testability automatically.
An interface can define a replaceable contract.Interfaces do not decouple components that change together.
Scope reuse inside a compatible component.Scope annotation controls graph reuse/lifetime, not thread safety or durability.
@ViewModelScoped reuse in a ViewModelComponent.Hilt ViewModel scope follows the ViewModel instance, not a navigation destination by magic.
@Singleton reuse in SingletonComponent.A singleton is per generated component/process instance, not a cross-process or durable global singleton.
Deferred construction.Lazy/Provider break eager construction but can hide cycles.
Dagger validates type/key reachability.Compile-time graph validation does not validate runtime business configuration.
A replaced test graph.Test module replacement does not prove production wiring.

Version/build-sensitive behavior#

  • Hilt/Dagger, Android Gradle Plugin, Kotlin, Compose navigation integration, and the KSP plugin form a compatibility matrix. Pin versions, read current release notes, and do not copy old Gradle DSL blindly.
  • KSP analyzes Kotlin symbols without Java stubs; KAPT generates stubs and runs Java annotation processing. Processor support for KSP is library/version-specific. A module-by-module migration can temporarily run KSP/KAPT together; do not migrate an unsupported processor.
  • Generated source paths, aggregating options, error wording, and assisted/ViewModel APIs are version-sensitive. Never make generated class names part of a production API.
  • Measure build performance with a Gradle Build Scan/profile: clean versus incremental, processor task time, cacheability, and invalidation fan-out. “KSP is always faster” is not project-specific evidence.

Decision framework#

  1. Draw graph roots, owners, runtime parameters, and cleanup; mark Android-created entry points.
  2. Make constructor injection the default, use a factory for runtime arguments, and add a narrow interface only at a real seam.
  3. For a small stable graph, use a manual composition root. When Android entry points, variants, and graph scale dominate, choose Hilt; use plain Dagger for custom component topology.
  4. Choose the shortest valid scope; verify that each dependency lives at least as long as its consumer without capturing a UI owner.
  5. Define eager/lazy policy, thread safety, startup budget, resource-close owner, and failure behavior.
  6. Separate behavior tests, graph validation, and production-wiring smoke tests; measure build impact.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Over-scoping causes stale shared state or leaks; under-scoping duplicates a connection, cache, or work. A classic captive dependency is a singleton holding an Activity, Fragment, View, or other short-lived collaborator.
  • A mutable singleton can race: one instance does not mean serialized access, atomic compound operations, or process durability.
  • Locator/entry-point creep hides dependencies. A large constructor may accurately reveal too many responsibilities; do not hide that signal with a locator.
  • A duplicate/missing qualifier, wrong @InstallIn, inaccessible feature binding, or scope mismatch breaks the graph; credentials and other runtime configuration can still fail after successful compilation.
  • A repository/manager cycle usually means bidirectional ownership. Lazy changes construction timing, not the design.

Production migration scenario: locator to Hilt#

Before. AppServices.get() returns mutable auth, Retrofit, a database, and analytics; ViewModels pull dependencies, a singleton SDK receives an Activity, and tests mutate the global registry.

Seam first. Add constructors to use cases/repositories and a manual composition root, wrap the third-party SDK with an application-Context adapter, and use a factory for a session runtime value. The old locator temporarily delegates to the new graph only at the legacy boundary; new code never reads it.

Incremental Hilt. Add @HiltAndroidApp and migrate one Android entry point at a time. Move constructible types to @Inject, implementation aliases to @Binds, and SDK builders to qualified @Provides. Auth state gets a thread-safe application owner; Activity callbacks remain short-lived adapters. Feature APIs expose no generated types.

Verify and remove. Pure unit tests instantiate constructors with fakes; a production graph smoke test creates the real component with safe configuration; instrumentation verifies ViewModel ownership/recreation. Startup traces and a Gradle profile catch regressions. Remove the locator and global test reset after the final consumer migrates.

Code-review/debug trap#

@Singleton
class CheckoutManager @Inject constructor(
    private val activity: Activity,
    private val payment: Lazy<PaymentManager>,
) { var currentOrder: Order? = null }

class PaymentManager @Inject constructor(
    private val checkout: Provider<CheckoutManager>,
)

Trap: in Hilt this does not even compile—Activity is a default binding only in ActivityComponent, so SingletonComponent reports [Dagger/MissingBinding]. The real leak happens when an Activity/Fragment/View reaches a long-lived object through a setter, method, callback, third-party SDK, or a manual Dagger graph (@BindsInstance into an app component). Also, mutable state is neither thread-safe nor durable, and Lazy/Provider hid a cycle. Debug from the first Dagger error path and binding key (type plus qualifier): locate the requesting entry point, component/@InstallIn, scope, and shortest-to-longest lifetime chain; inspect a generated factory only to confirm wiring. Fix it by giving a flow/ViewModel coordinator ownership of the order, making payment depend on a narrow command/port, and giving the SDK application Context—not by adding another scope or Lazy.

Graph observability and diagnostics#

  • For a missing binding, read the full dependency trace from the entry point and check exact generic type, qualifier, visibility, module inclusion, and variant. For a duplicate binding, find every contributor rather than suppressing the error.
  • For a scope error, draw the component hierarchy and requested/scoped owner. Generated *_Factory/*Component code is evidence, not a stable API; run a clean build only after checking version/cache inputs.
  • Log graph-safe events: SDK initialization duration/result, first-use latency, and component-owner IDs in debug builds, with no secrets or PII. Add startup trace sections and crash metadata for app/library versions.
  • Compile-time graph validation does not validate runtime business configuration: separately validate base URLs, credentials, manifest metadata, remote flags, and multi-process behavior.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Dependency inversion, DI, or service locator? Inversion is the dependency policy; DI means the caller supplies a dependency; a locator hides a pull from a registry and is not DI.
  2. Why default to constructor injection? It makes the API explicit, creates valid objects immediately, supports immutable dependencies, and enables framework-free unit tests; use a factory for runtime arguments.
  3. When is manual DI sufficient? A small, stable graph with a few roots and simple lifetimes, where an explicit composition root stays readable and testable.
  4. What does Dagger generate? Factories/providers and a component implementation that connects keys and validates the reachable graph at compile time.
  5. @Binds or @Provides? Binds for an implementation-to-API alias; Provides for custom construction, a third-party builder, or a derived value.
  6. What does a scope mean? Reuse in a compatible component instance/lifetime—not thread safety, persistence, or cross-process identity.
  7. ActivityRetained versus ViewModel? ActivityRetained can be shared by ViewModels of one retained Activity; ViewModelScoped is shared only inside one ViewModelComponent.
  8. Provider versus Lazy? Provider performs on-demand/repeated requests under scope rules; Lazy locally memoizes its first value. Both can hide a cycle.
  9. How do you test DI? Test behavior directly through constructors/fakes, then separately smoke-test the production graph and minimal Hilt Android integration.
  10. How do you debug a missing binding? Walk the trace from the entry point and verify exact type plus qualifier, module visibility/@InstallIn, variant, and generated factory.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. A singleton requests an Activity. That is lifetime inversion/a captive dependency. Supply an application-safe adapter or pass a short-lived callback to a method, not an Activity to the singleton.
  2. A dynamic feature cannot see an app Hilt binding. Treat it as a compilation/graph visibility boundary: expose a narrow dependency API and use the documented component-dependency pattern, not a reverse module dependency.
  3. A KSP migration made builds slower. Check compatible processor versions, mixed KAPT/KSP tasks, clean versus incremental profiles, aggregating invalidation, and caches; one clean build proves little.
  4. Production crashes despite a valid graph. Inspect runtime configuration, manifest/process state, SDK initialization, and first-use failures; compile-time types do not prove business configuration.

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. Draw every component and object lifetime in a checkout flow; where can a captive dependency arise?
  2. Which bindings truly need an interface, qualifier, or scope, and which are accidental abstraction?
  3. Which test proves behavior, which proves production wiring, and what remains a runtime-only configuration risk?
  4. Where are first-use latency, cleanup, and thread-safety contracts for the SDK, cache, and session state?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you design and debug dependency injection on Android?

~30-second answer#

I treat DI as object-graph assembly, not architecture. Constructor injection is my default, with a composition root owning creation and cleanup. Manual DI is enough for a small stable graph; Dagger adds compile-time generated wiring, and Hilt maps components to Android lifecycles. I choose the shortest valid scope, keep runtime values in factories, and test classes directly with fakes plus a separate production-graph smoke test. A scope controls reuse, not thread safety or persistence, and Provider or Lazy should not hide a design cycle.

~2-minute answer#

I first separate dependency inversion, dependency injection, and service location. Inversion is the policy that stable behavior should not depend directly on volatile details. Injection means the composition root supplies dependencies; a locator hides them behind global lookup. I default to constructor injection because it produces valid objects and framework-free unit-test seams.

For a small graph I use manual DI. At scale, Dagger validates reachable type-plus-qualifier keys and generates factories, providers, and component implementations. Hilt standardizes roots for Singleton, activity-retained, ViewModel, activity, fragment, view, and service lifetimes. I scope only when instance sharing is required and ensure a long-lived object never captures a shorter-lived Android owner. Singleton means one per component and process, not thread safety, persistence, or cross-process identity.

I use @Inject for owned constructible types, @Binds for aliases, @Provides for third-party construction, qualifiers for same-type semantics, and multibindings for plugin sets/maps. Provider and Lazy defer access but are not my default cycle breaker. Runtime values use factory or assisted inputs; ViewModel SavedStateHandle is for small restorable values, and ViewModel scope follows the actual owner and instance.

Finally, I keep constructors free of eager I/O, give SDK resources explicit init/close owners, profile KSP/KAPT and generated tasks with pinned versions, and debug errors from the requesting entry point through the full binding trace. Unit tests use fakes directly; Hilt replacement tests cover test graphs, while a separate production graph smoke test catches real wiring. Compile-time validation still cannot validate credentials, flags, or other runtime business configuration.

Android networking fundamentalsexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to trace a request from a Retrofit declaration to bytes on a socket and back; distinguish transport, HTTP, parsing, and domain failures; place interceptors, cache, timeouts, retries, cancellation, and observability at the correct boundaries; design evolvable serialization and pagination contracts; and verify them with MockWebServer, fakes, and contract tests. Token refresh, certificate pinning, and secrets belong to Stage 19; a durable offline-first source of truth belongs to Stage 21.

Senior mental model#

Networking is a chain of independent contracts, not one “API call.” Retrofit describes and adapts an endpoint; OkHttp executes the HTTP exchange; DNS/TCP/TLS transport bytes; a converter transforms a representation; the data layer interprets the application contract. Every boundary has its own failure, lifetime, cancellation, and observability semantics.

  • HTTP success, parse success, and domain success are separate axes. A 2xx response may still contain a domain failure in a valid envelope.
  • A network-availability signal, DNS resolution, socket connection, and reachability of a specific backend are not equivalent.
  • A retry is a new attempt with a possibly unknown prior outcome; it guarantees neither success nor exactly-once processing.
  • An HTTP cache, repository persistence, and a durable domain source of truth have different policies and owners.

Internals: request/response topology#

Retrofit interface + annotations
  → ServiceMethod parses metadata
  → request Converter (model → RequestBody)
  → CallAdapter (Call / suspend / custom return type)
  → OkHttpClient.newCall(Request) → RealCall
  → execute() caller thread OR enqueue()/suspend async path
  → Dispatcher admission (async global/per-host limits)
  → application interceptors (once per logical call)
  → retry/follow-up + bridge + HTTP cache + connect internals
  → DNS → candidate routes/proxy → connection pool or new socket
  → TCP socket → TLS handshake/hostname verification for HTTPS
  → network interceptors (per network exchange)
  → HTTP codec writes request / reads status, headers, body
  → response Converter (ResponseBody → DTO)
  → CallAdapter/coroutine resumes → repository maps DTO/domain result

RealCall represents one prepared OkHttp call and can be executed once. A connection is reused from the pool when address, route, and protocol constraints allow it; otherwise route selection tries viable proxy/address paths and opens a socket. HTTP/2 can multiplex exchanges. Internal class names and ordering are implementation details: explain the responsibilities and inspect the pinned OkHttp source/version instead of coupling application code to internals.

Retrofit resolves annotations, parameter handlers, a converter, and a call adapter for a service method. Converter ordering matters because the first capable factory wins. The call adapter shapes execution and the return type; it does not redefine HTTP success. Retrofit does not move work off the main thread by magic for every adapter or arbitrary custom code. A synchronous Call.execute() runs on its caller thread, and custom adapters/converters can also execute work where invoked.

interface CatalogApi {
    @GET("v1/items")
    suspend fun page(
        @Query("cursor") cursor: String?,
        @Header("If-None-Match") etag: String? = null,
    ): Response<ItemPageDto>
}

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .callTimeout(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .connectTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .writeTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .addInterceptor(CorrelationIdInterceptor()) // application
    .eventListenerFactory(TimingEventListener.factory())
    .cache(Cache(cacheDir.resolve("http"), 20L * 1024 * 1024))
    .build()

Application vs network interceptors#

TypeWhat it observesCorrect responsibilities
Application interceptorOne logical call; may receive a cached response; does not observe every redirect/retry exchange.Stable request headers, correlation IDs, coarse logging/metrics, and application-wide request policy. Call proceed() according to an explicit contract.
Network interceptorEvery real network exchange and its connection; not invoked when the cache fully satisfies a response.Wire-level headers/metrics and diagnostics for a specific exchange; application code needs these less often.

Ordering matters: interceptors observe requests in registration order and responses in reverse order. Do not parse business envelopes, manage repository persistence, or run an arbitrary retry loop inside an interceptor. An OkHttp Authenticator is a specialized follow-up mechanism after an authentication challenge; that comparison is sufficient here, while token refresh, concurrency, and loop prevention are reserved for Stage 19.

Synchronous, suspend, cancellation, and Dispatcher#

  • execute() blocks its caller thread until a response or failure; the response body must be closed. enqueue() performs an asynchronous call through the Dispatcher and delivers a callback.
  • Retrofit's suspend integration awaits the OkHttp call asynchronously and cancels the underlying Call when the coroutine is cancelled. Cancellation is cooperative and can end socket/read work, but cannot undo a request that the server has already processed.
  • The OkHttp Dispatcher controls admission and running asynchronous calls, including global and per-host limits. Exact defaults, host accounting, WebSocket treatment, executor behavior, and APIs vary by version; synchronous calls use a different scheduling path. Do not treat a memorized number as an architecture guarantee—inspect the pinned version.
  • The queue protects client resources, but it is not a product-priority queue or a server rate limiter. Excessive limits raise contention; limits that are too small introduce head-of-line delay.

HTTP semantics: methods, status, and headers#

  • A safe method has read-only intended semantics; idempotent means that one or multiple identical requests have the same intended effect. GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/TRACE are safe; safe methods are idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST/PATCH are not generally idempotent. GET safety and idempotency are protocol semantics, not proof that a backend is correct.
  • 2xx represents HTTP-level success, 3xx redirection/selection, 4xx a client-side contract/request outcome, and 5xx a server-side failure class. Interpret the API contract: 404 may mean expected absence, 409 conflict, and 429 rate limiting. Never flatten every non-2xx response into “no internet.”
  • An application envelope such as {"ok":false,"error":...} can arrive with 200. The repository must validate status, media type, schema, and domain invariants; Retrofit's Response.isSuccessful only checks for 2xx.
  • Accept describes acceptable response representations; Content-Type identifies the media type of the actual request or response body. Charset, encoding, locale, API version, authorization, and correlation headers need explicit ownership. Do not log sensitive headers or bodies.

HTTP caching and validation#

OkHttp Cache applies HTTP cache rules; it does not merely “save the last JSON.” Freshness follows response directives and metadata: Cache-Control: max-age, s-maxage for shared caches, Expires, and heuristic rules. no-cache means revalidate before reuse, not “do not store”; no-store forbids storage. Request directives can require validation or constrain stale reuse.

  • Once stale, a cache can issue a conditional request: If-None-Match with an ETag, or If-Modified-Since with Last-Modified. A 304 Not Modified has no new representation body; the cache combines its metadata with the stored response.
  • Vary adds named request headers to cache-key matching. Vary: * is not reusable. An incorrect Vary can mix locale, encoding, or tenant representations.
  • Cacheability depends on method, status, and directives; authenticated responses have additional rules. Assert networkResponse/cacheResponse in tests instead of assuming the source.
  • OkHttp cache obeys HTTP rules and is not repository persistence: entries can be evicted, the key is URL plus Vary, and it offers no domain queries, transactions, or migrations; the origin controls freshness. It is not a durable domain SSOT and is not the Stage 21 offline-first design.

Timeouts, deadlines, and retry boundaries#

ControlBoundary
connect timeoutEstablishing one socket connection; DNS/TLS/fallback details depend on the implementation.
read timeoutLack of progress during a socket read, not the maximum total download duration.
write timeoutLack of progress during a socket write.
call timeoutBounds the whole call once it starts executing: DNS, connect, TLS, write, server processing, read, and all redirects/retries. Time spent waiting in the async Dispatcher queue is not included, so use a caller-side deadline (for example withTimeout) for an end-to-end budget.
coroutine timeout/deadlineThe caller's budget; it should cancel the child call but is not a distributed business deadline without propagation to downstream hops.

Timeouts are not end-to-end business deadlines automatically. A budget must account for the UI/workflow SLA, queueing, retries, and server deadline propagation. The meaning of “0 = infinite” and per-call overrides is version/API-sensitive, so inspect the pinned client documentation.

Retry only selected transient failures for idempotent operations, or a non-idempotent operation with an explicit idempotency-key/deduplication contract. Consider request-body replayability, whether bytes may have been sent, the status contract (often 408/429/selected 5xx), Retry-After, exponential backoff, jitter, maximum attempts, total time budget, and cancellation. Do not retry parsing, domain, or TLS trust failures. Backoff must not outlive the caller scope. A retry guarantees neither success nor exactly-once processing.

Bodies, streaming, and schema evolution#

  • A request/response body is a byte stream with a media type and lifetime. Buffering an entire payload is simpler but risks memory spikes; streaming enables incremental work but holds a connection and requires explicit ownership.
  • ResponseBody is one-shot: consume it once and close it with use/close; otherwise a leak exhausts the pool or sockets. Do not pass a streaming response across layers without an owner that always closes it.
  • A streaming upload can be one-shot and non-replayable. Retry, redirect, or authentication follow-up may be impossible after a partial write; model replayability rather than assuming it.
  • Unknown JSON fields should usually be ignored for additive evolution; a missing field, explicit null, and a default value are three different states. A nullable Kotlin type does not define the wire contract by itself. Validate required fields and invariants at the DTO-to-domain boundary.
  • For schema evolution, additive optional fields are safer; an unknown enum value needs a fallback or explicit failure; changing a type, meaning, or requiredness is breaking. Contract tests need old/new schema fixtures, malformed JSON, and an unexpected media type.

Pagination, connectivity, and TLS basics#

  • Offset pagination is simple, but concurrent inserts/deletes produce duplicate or missing items. Cursor/keyset contracts preserve position better, but a cursor is opaque, can expire, and depends on stable ordering.
  • Specify deterministic sort plus tie-breaker, page boundary, end signal, duplicate identity policy, refresh anchor, filter/version binding, and mutation behavior. Client deduplication prevents duplicate rendering but cannot restore missing items or prove snapshot consistency.
  • ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback, capabilities, and a validated network are useful UX and scheduling hints. A DNS result or connectivity callback does not guarantee internet or backend reachability: a captive portal, split DNS, firewall, stale validation, or backend outage remains possible. The concrete request outcome is the truth; do not reject requests solely because of a stale “offline” Boolean.
  • For HTTPS, DNS finds an address, TCP establishes transport, and TLS verifies the certificate chain/hostname and negotiates crypto/protocol before HTTP. Network Security Config declaratively controls trust anchors, cleartext policy, and debug overrides. Disable cleartext for production domains.
  • A TLS failure is not generic offline and is normally not a retry-loop target. Certificate pinning, token lifecycle, and secret storage are intentionally reserved for Stage 19.

Error taxonomy and observability#

CategoryExample / policy
TransportDNS, refused/reset socket, unreachable route; may be transient, but the write outcome can be unknown.
TLSHandshake, trust, or hostname; a separate security/configuration category.
TimeoutCall/connect/read/write/caller deadline; preserve the boundary in telemetry.
ProtocolMalformed HTTP, unexpected redirect, or HTTP/2 stream/protocol issue.
HTTPNon-2xx status plus bounded/redacted error body, headers, and request ID.
ParsingWrong media type or malformed/incompatible schema.
DomainA 2xx envelope failure or violated invariant.
CancellationExpected control flow; do not present it as a network error or retry it.

Capture a redacted method, route template rather than a raw PII URL, outcome taxonomy, status, byte counts, cache/network source, attempt, timings, and correlation/request ID. EventListener exposes DNS, connect, TLS, connection acquisition, and call-phase awareness; it observes but does not define business success. Never log Authorization, Cookie, tokens, secrets, or unbounded bodies. A correlation ID connects client/server traces, but it is not an idempotency key.

Guarantees vs non-guarantees#

  • Guarantee: closing a response body returns client resources; non-guarantee: cancellation rolls back server state.
  • Guarantee: HTTP defines safe/idempotent semantics; non-guarantee: a concrete GET backend performs no mutation.
  • Guarantee: 2xx denotes successful HTTP semantics; non-guarantee: the payload satisfies domain rules.
  • Guarantee: the interceptor chain has a defined order; non-guarantee: arbitrary reordering of logging/cache/header/retry behavior is equivalent.
  • Guarantee: OkHttp cache follows the HTTP cache contract; non-guarantee: a durable, queryable domain SSOT.
  • Non-guarantees: retry success or exactly-once; connectivity/DNS as backend reachability; Retrofit as automatic off-main execution for every adapter/custom operation; a transport timeout as an end-to-end business deadline.

Version-sensitive behavior#

Pin Retrofit, OkHttp, converter, and serializer versions. Before making a design claim, inspect release documentation/source for Dispatcher defaults and per-host accounting; built-in retry/follow-up policy; route, DNS, TLS, and platform behavior; HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 support; one-shot/duplex body APIs; timeout defaults and overrides; suspend and nullable-body behavior; and MockWebServer package/API. Android API level, security provider, Network Security Config, and manifest cleartext defaults also matter. Document measured behavior instead of copying constants from another major version.

Decision framework#

  1. Write the endpoint contract: method semantics, media types, statuses/envelope, pagination, cache validators, idempotency, and schema compatibility.
  2. Allocate budgets: payload/memory, concurrency, call latency, business deadline, retry attempts, and server rate limits.
  3. Assign ownership to the Retrofit declaration/converter, application or network interceptor, repository mapper, HTTP cache, or durable storage—without duplicating policy.
  4. Build a typed error taxonomy and cancellation path to the underlying call; decide what is user-facing, retryable, and observable.
  5. Verify success and deterministic failures on pinned versions, including leak, cancellation, cache, and concurrency behavior; add redacted production signals.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Aggressive concurrency lowers queue time for one workload but raises contention, radio/server load, and 429 responses; conservative limits can delay unrelated calls to one host.
  • A longer timeout tolerates slow networks but retains resources and stale UI; a short one creates false failures. One global timeout ignores endpoint and payload SLAs.
  • Automatic retry improves transient availability but multiplies load and side effects; without jitter it creates a retry storm, and without a total budget it hides latency.
  • A lenient parser survives additive fields, but defaults can hide a contract break; a strict parser detects drift sooner but hurts forward compatibility.
  • HTTP caching saves latency and bandwidth, but freshness is not domain consistency; manually rewriting headers can violate the server contract.

Production scenario#

A catalog screen uses a cursor endpoint with stable (updatedAt,id) ordering. A Retrofit suspend method returns a DTO envelope; the converter tolerates unknown fields, while the mapper requires id/name and distinguishes missing from null. An application interceptor adds a correlation ID; EventListener measures DNS/connect/TLS/TTFB; a network interceptor only adds wire diagnostics in a debug build. The server returns Cache-Control, ETag, and a correct Vary: Accept-Language; OkHttp revalidates with If-None-Match/304, while Room remains a separate durable SSOT only in the Stage 21 design.

The retry policy permits at most two GET attempts for selected connection resets, 503, or 429; respects Retry-After; applies exponential backoff plus jitter; and shares a call budget. Parsing, TLS, and cancellation are not retried. Deduplication by item ID protects the UI from overlap, while telemetry separately counts duplicates, cursor expiry, and gaps. A network callback only changes a UX hint. MockWebServer reproduces 304, delayed headers/body, disconnect during a body, malformed JSON, 429, duplicate pages, and cancellation.

Code-review / debug trap#

suspend fun load(): Result<Payload> = runCatching {
    if (!connectivity.isOnline) error("offline")
    retry(3) { api.getPayload().body()!! }
}

Trap: the stale connectivity gate rejects a workable network; blanket retry ignores method, prior outcome, Retry-After, and body replayability; body()!! collapses empty, parsing, HTTP, and domain failures; runCatching can turn CancellationException into a failure; response/error-body ownership is invisible; and there is no deadline, redaction, or correlation. Start debugging with a request ID, phase timings, and a deterministic MockWebServer case—not “increase the timeout and retries.”

Testing strategy#

  • Pure fakes: repository/use-case tests for domain mapping, pagination merge/deduplication/order, retry decisions, and cancellation without imitating HTTP.
  • MockWebServer: assert method/path/query/headers/body and script 2xx domain errors, 304 validation, redirects, 404/409/429/503, malformed JSON, wrong content type, disconnect, throttled body, no response, and large/streaming bodies. Assert body closure and connection reuse where observable.
  • Contract tests: run consumer fixtures/schema against provider assumptions: unknown/missing/null fields, enum evolution, error envelopes, cursor expiry, and ordering. They do not replace integration/E2E tests.
  • Determinism: inject a clock, seeded jitter/random source, fake sleeper, bounded virtual time, and fixed dispatcher limits where supported; assert attempts and total budget instead of relying on wall-clock luck.

Likely practice questions and answers#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. 1. How does a request travel through Retrofit and OkHttp? Retrofit parses the declaration, parameter handlers, converter, and call adapter. An OkHttp RealCall traverses Dispatcher admission, ordered application/internal/network interceptors, cache, route/DNS/pool/socket/TLS, and the codec; a response converter creates a DTO and the repository maps a domain result.
  2. 2. Application versus network interceptor? An application interceptor sees one logical call and cached responses; a network interceptor sees each wire exchange and connection. Headers/correlation/coarse policy normally belong to application interceptors; exchange diagnostics belong to network interceptors. Ordering changes behavior.
  3. 3. What does suspend cancellation guarantee? Retrofit cancels the underlying OkHttp Call and does not resume a cancelled continuation as success. This releases client work, but it cannot undo a side effect already processed by the server.
  4. 4. Are safe and idempotent the same? No. Safe means no intended mutation; idempotent means repeated identical requests have the same intended effect. PUT/DELETE are idempotent but not safe. These are protocol contracts, not proof of backend implementation.
  5. 5. Why is 200 not always success? It is HTTP-level success; the payload can contain an application error envelope, incompatible schema, or violated domain invariant.
  6. 6. How does ETag revalidation work? A stale cached response with an ETag leads to If-None-Match; a 304 permits reuse of the stored body with updated metadata. Vary specifies which request headers must match.
  7. 7. What are the timeout boundaries? Connect/read/write govern distinct I/O phases, while call timeout covers nearly the complete OkHttp call. None automatically forms a distributed business deadline; design caller budgets and propagation separately.
  8. 8. When is retry acceptable? For a selected transient failure, replayable body, and idempotent operation or explicit idempotency-key contract, with Retry-After, backoff, jitter, attempt/total budgets, and cancellation. It does not guarantee success or exactly-once.
  9. 9. Why is a connectivity callback not a gate? It reports a network and capabilities at an observation point, not the DNS/TLS/backend result. A real request can succeed or fail contrary to a stale flag.
  10. 10. How do you test a network layer? Use fakes for domain policy, MockWebServer for HTTP bytes, timing, and failures, and contract tests for schema/provider assumptions, with deterministic clocks/jitter and explicit cancellation/resource assertions.

Follow-up questions#

  1. How would the retry design change for a POST with a server-supported idempotency key?
  2. How would you distinguish queue delay, DNS, connect, TLS, TTFB, and body download in a production trace?
  3. Which cache headers are required for a localized, authenticated catalog response?
  4. How should cursor pagination behave when filters and concurrent updates change?

Unanswered self-checks#

  1. Draw the exact topology of your pinned stack and mark thread, coroutine, and resource ownership at every boundary.
  2. Classify ten real failures from your API and assign retry, user message, and telemetry without a catch-all “network error.”
  3. Prove with a test that 304, Vary, and stale revalidation work without turning the HTTP cache into the SSOT.
  4. Show where one-shot bodies are closed and what happens when cancellation arrives after the server commits.

English answer skeletons#

~30-second answer#

I treat networking as layered contracts. Retrofit turns a declaration into a request using converters and a call adapter; OkHttp owns the call, interceptor chain, cache, route, pooled connection, socket and TLS exchange; the repository maps the parsed DTO into a domain result. I separate transport, TLS, timeout, protocol, HTTP, parsing, domain and cancellation failures. Retries are bounded and only for selected transient, idempotent or explicitly deduplicated operations. Cancellation releases client work but cannot undo a server-side commit, and HTTP cache is not a durable domain source of truth.

~2-minute answer#

I start with topology. Retrofit parses the annotated service method, chooses parameter and body converters, and applies a call adapter. The resulting OkHttp RealCall is admitted by the asynchronous Dispatcher, traverses application interceptors, internal retry/bridge/cache/connect stages and network interceptors, then uses DNS and route selection to reuse a pooled connection or establish a socket and TLS session. The response status, headers and one-shot body return through the chain, then the converter produces a DTO and the repository validates the application envelope and domain invariants.

I keep semantics explicit. A 2xx response can still be a domain failure. GET being safe and idempotent is a protocol contract, not proof of a correct backend. Suspend cancellation propagates to the Call, but cannot undo a request already processed. Connect, read, write and call timeouts protect different boundaries and are not automatically an end-to-end business deadline. Retries require a selected transient failure, replayable body, idempotency or an idempotency-key contract, Retry-After handling, exponential backoff with jitter, attempt and total budgets.

Application interceptors own logical-call concerns such as correlation headers; network interceptors observe each wire exchange, and ordering matters. HTTP caching follows freshness, validators, Vary and 304 rules; it is not repository persistence. I test domain policy with fakes, protocol and deterministic failure cases with MockWebServer, and schema evolution with contract fixtures. In production I redact sensitive data and use correlation IDs plus EventListener phase timings. Authentication refresh, pinning and secrets are a separate security design.

Official references#

  • Retrofit documentation and Retrofit API
  • OkHttp Calls, Interceptors, Connections, HTTPS, and Caching

  • Android network operations, Connectivity monitoring, and Network Security Configuration
