Authentication, token refresh, and Android mobile securityexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage you should be able to design native OAuth 2.x/OIDC sign-in, carry credentials across Android and OkHttp boundaries, serialize concurrent refresh without races or deadlocks, and build defense-in-depth for token storage, transport, IPC, observability, and incident response. This continues Stage 18 rather than repeating networking basics, and it avoids the future persistence deep dive.

Senior threat / mental model#

A mobile app is a public client in a hostile environment, and authentication is a distributed state machine. Separate the browser authorization session, app session, resource-server access, local key use, and device/app integrity signal. For each boundary identify the attacker, asset, trust root, lifetime, replay surface, cancellation, and recovery path.

  • Threats include a malicious app, link hijacking, phishing, stolen device or backup, proxy/CA compromise, a rooted or instrumented process, telemetry leakage, replay, and a compromised backend account.
  • The authorization server authenticates the user and issues grants/tokens; the client initiates; the resource owner delegates; the resource server validates access. OIDC adds an identity layer, not permission to treat an access token as a profile object.
  • A mobile client cannot safely embed a universal secret. Obfuscation, NDK storage, or remote config raises extraction cost but a shared secret in a distributed binary does not authenticate that client instance.
  • Defense-in-depth reduces blast radius. No Keystore key, biometric prompt, certificate pin, root check, or integrity verdict makes a compromised process trusted.

Authentication / refresh / security topology and internals#

App → external user-agent (browser / Custom Tabs)
  → authorization server: authentication + consent
  → exact redirect URI / verified App Link → callback
  → validate state + issuer + transaction
  → token endpoint: authorization code + PKCE verifier
  → access token → resource server
  → validate ID token → local identity assertion
  → refresh token rotation → new refresh token in the same token family / session state

Request → credential Interceptor reads atomic session snapshot
  → resource server → 401 challenge
  → OkHttp Authenticator → RefreshCoordinator single-flight
  → dedicated refresh client (no resource Authenticator)
  → compare generation/version → install or discard
  → one replayable follow-up request with new access token

The session owner holds an immutable snapshot containing sessionId/generation, token values, access expiry, refresh-family/version, and subject/issuer metadata. An atomic read gives each request a coherent version; compare-and-set prevents an old refresh response overwriting logout or a newer login.

OAuth 2.x / OIDC roles and token semantics#

ArtifactAudience / purposeClient policy
Authorization codeShort-lived one-time grant for the token endpoint.Not an API credential; bind it to client/redirect and PKCE verifier, then exchange promptly.
Access tokenAuthorization at the resource server: audience, scopes, expiry.Send only to the intended API over HTTPS; do not use as a profile unless a contract explicitly says so.
Refresh tokenObtains new access tokens from the authorization server.Never send to a resource API; define rotation, reuse detection, revocation, and at-rest policy.
ID tokenOIDC assertion about an authentication event for the client.Validate signature, issuer, audience/authorized party, expiry, and nonce; it is not an access token.

Opaque and JWT tokens have different server validation paths. The mobile client usually is not the authority for access-token validity; the resource server performs signature validation or introspection and authorization. Decoding a JWT without validating its signature and claims creates no trust. Scope is delegated capability, while subject, tenant, and object-level authorization still apply.

Authorization Code + PKCE for a native app#

  1. Generate a high-entropy code_verifier, S256 code_challenge, random state, and OIDC nonce; bind them to one pending transaction.
  2. Open the authorization endpoint in an external user-agent—the system browser or Custom Tabs—to preserve origin UI and a shared security context. Do not collect the password in the app.
  3. Accept only a registered exact redirect URI. Verify domain association for an HTTPS App Link; a custom scheme can be claimed by another app and therefore still needs PKCE and strict routing.
  4. On callback, validate the pending transaction, state, scheme/host/path, and expected issuer before exchanging the code once with the original verifier.
  5. For OIDC validate the ID token and nonce, establish a new local session generation, and erase pending artifacts.

PKCE mitigates authorization-code interception but not all phishing or device compromise. An external user-agent reduces password exposure to the app, but fake UI/browser surfaces, malicious accessibility, account takeover, and authorization-server defects remain.

Redirect, deep-link, App Link, state, and nonce boundaries#

  • state correlates the authorization response with a browser transaction and protects the CSRF/session-swap boundary. nonce binds an ID token to an OIDC request/replay context. They are not interchangeable.
  • Exact redirect matching covers scheme, normalized host, port, path, and allowed query contract. Reject wildcard hosts, open redirects, arbitrary nested URLs, and callbacks without an outstanding transaction.
  • A verified HTTPS App Link gives stronger app ownership than a custom scheme, but association, configuration, and OS behavior can fail. Intent data is still untrusted input inside the app.
  • The transaction is single-use, expiring, and bound to issuer/client. Never place verifier/state in logs, analytics, or a process-global mutable singleton without session ownership.

Token lifetime, rotation, revocation, and session state#

  • A short access lifetime narrows the theft window but increases refresh load and clock sensitivity. Refresh token rotation issues a replacement and invalidates or marks the previous token; reuse detection may revoke the family.
  • Client expiry is a scheduling hint with bounded skew, not a final verdict. The server can revoke earlier, the device clock can be wrong, and opaque policy can change.
  • Specify revocation endpoint, server logout, password/device-change, and remote revocation propagation. An offline device may not learn immediately; the resource server must enforce session state.
  • Session state includes subject/tenant, issuer, generation, refresh family, and credential version. Account switch creates a new generation, so a response from the old generation cannot commit.

Interceptor versus OkHttp Authenticator#

BoundaryResponsibilityAvoid
Application InterceptorRead the current immutable snapshot and attach Authorization: Bearer … only to allowlisted origins/request classes.Do not block-refresh every request or forward credentials across origins.
OkHttp AuthenticatorRespond to an eligible 401 challenge, reuse an already-new token or join single-flight, then return a follow-up request or null.Do not treat every 401 as expiry, handle 403 as refresh, or create an unbounded loop.
Refresh clientCall the token endpoint with a bounded timeout and no resource Authenticator/access-token interceptor.Do not refresh recursively through the same authenticated client.

Check prior-response count, challenge/error contract, whether the failed request carried the expected old credential, and whether the replacement differs. Stop after one auth follow-up. A 401 does not always mean refresh. A 401 commonly means missing/invalid authentication or a challenge, while 403 commonly means authenticated but not permitted; backend contracts vary, so use status, WWW-Authenticate, and a documented error code.

Concurrent 401 single-flight refresh#

If N calls fail with access-token version 7, the first caller starts one refresh in an app scope and every caller, including it, awaits the same shared Deferred. Before starting and after waiting, compare versions: if the same generation already has version 8, reuse it. Run token-endpoint I/O outside the lock.

data class CredentialSnapshot(
    val generation: Long, val version: Long,
    val access: String, val refresh: String,
)


class RefreshCoordinator(
    private val store: SessionStore, // in-memory snapshot; no disk I/O under mutex
    private val refreshApi: RefreshApi, // dedicated client; no Authenticator
    private val appScope: CoroutineScope, // SupervisorJob; outlives every caller
) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private val inFlight = mutableMapOf<
        Pair<Long, Long>, Deferred<CredentialSnapshot?>
    >()

    suspend fun refreshAfter401(failed: CredentialSnapshot): CredentialSnapshot? {
        val flight = mutex.withLock {
            val current = store.current()
            if (current == null || current.generation != failed.generation) return null
            if (current.version != failed.version) return current
            val key = failed.generation to failed.version
            inFlight[key]?.takeIf { it.isActive }
                ?: appScope.async { rotate(failed, key) }.also { inFlight[key] = it }
        }
        // Cancelling a caller only stops its await; the shared refresh keeps running.
        return try {
            withTimeoutOrNull(REFRESH_BUDGET_MS) { flight.await() }
        } catch (e: CancellationException) {
            currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // this caller was cancelled: rethrow
            null // the refresh itself was cancelled (logout / app scope)
        }
    }

    private suspend fun rotate(
        failed: CredentialSnapshot, key: Pair<Long, Long>,
    ): CredentialSnapshot? {
        val self = currentCoroutineContext().job
        try {
            val fetched = try {
                refreshApi.rotate(failed.refresh)
            } catch (e: CancellationException) {
                throw e // never swallow cancellation
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                null // production: classify invalid_grant vs transient
            }
            return mutex.withLock {
                val current = store.current()
                val accepted = fetched?.takeIf {
                    current != null && current.generation == failed.generation &&
                        current.version == failed.version
                }?.also(store::replace)
                accepted ?: store.current()?.takeIf {
                    it.generation == failed.generation && it.version != failed.version
                }
            }
        } finally {
            withContext(NonCancellable) {
                mutex.withLock { if (inFlight[key] === self) inFlight.remove(key) }
            }
        }
    }

    private companion object { const val REFRESH_BUDGET_MS = 15_000L }
}

Authenticator.authenticate() is synchronous. A production bridge must be bounded and must not schedule refresh on the same saturated OkHttp Dispatcher; use a dedicated refresh client/executor or a coordinator designed for the blocking boundary. Do not hold a Mutex during token HTTP I/O, disk work, a biometric prompt, or unrelated I/O. Run the refresh in an app-scoped shared Deferred: cancelling one caller only ends its bounded await and never stops the refresh for others; CancellationException is rethrown, not swallowed, and a finally under NonCancellable removes the in-flight entry even when the refresh itself is cancelled (logout/app scope), in which case callers get null. Generation/version checks prevent a late response reviving logout or an older refresh overwriting a newer token.

Retry once, replayability, logout race, and 401/403#

  • The Authenticator rebuilds the original request with the new header at most once. A one-shot or streaming body may not be replayable; even a replayable POST may duplicate effects if the server processed a body before returning 401 or the response was lost.
  • An idempotency key plus server deduplication window reduces duplicate effects. Refresh serialization does not create exactly-once server effects.
  • Logout atomically advances/replaces the generation, clears usable credentials, cancels pending refresh where practical, starts best-effort revocation on a separate bounded path, and prevents late commit.
  • Logout cannot retract requests the server already processed. It also cannot guarantee immediate remote invalidation while offline; local UI/session state and server authorization must converge.

Storage threat model, Android Keystore, and biometrics#

  • Android Keystore protects cryptographic key material and can make it non-exportable; hardware backing or StrongBox depends on device, API, and algorithm. A token is arbitrary data: encrypt it with a key, but the app still obtains plaintext to send it.
  • Keystore does not make a token inaccessible after the app legitimately decrypts or uses it. A compromised process, instrumentation, screen scraping, or malicious accessibility can observe data in use.
  • Encrypted-at-rest choices are version-sensitive: library deprecations, backup, key invalidation, migration, and restore behavior must be verified for pinned AndroidX/platform versions. A deprecated convenience API is not an eternal best practice.
  • A biometric user-auth-bound key can require recent authentication for a crypto operation. Define timeout, enrollment invalidation, device-credential fallback, lockout, accessibility, and recovery/re-login. Biometric success does not authenticate a backend session by itself.
  • Exclude credentials and keys from backup or design restore so ciphertext without its original key is discarded. Consider blocking screenshots on sensitive screens, never copy tokens to clipboard, and redact logs, crash reports, and analytics.

TLS, Network Security Config, and certificate pinning#

  • Network Security Config defines cleartext policy, trust anchors, domain config, debug overrides, and declarative pins. Production API domains should reject cleartext; debug CA exceptions must not enter release configuration.
  • HTTPS authenticates the transport endpoint under its trust model, not business correctness. It does not prove authorization, safe payloads, absence of fraud, or a correct compromised endpoint.
  • Certificate pinning narrows accepted keys/chains but creates operational coupling: CA/key rotation, CDN migration, emergency replacement, and clock/config errors can brick clients that cannot be updated quickly.
  • If the threat model truly requires pinning, pin public keys, keep overlap and backup pins, stage rollout, define expiry/rotation and incident runbooks, collect telemetry, and maintain recovery. Android guidance does not treat pinning as a universal default.
  • Pinning does not protect a compromised app or process and can brick connectivity. A hook after TLS or plaintext inside the process remains visible.

Web, components, intents, deep links, and PendingIntent#

  • Prefer an external user-agent/Custom Tabs for authorization. An embedded WebView can hide or imitate origin, exposes more content to the app, and introduces phishing, cookie, and JS-bridge risks; allowlist navigation and avoid dangerous JS interfaces.
  • Every exported component is an IPC endpoint. Minimize android:exported, use permission/signature boundaries where needed, and validate caller, Intent action, MIME type, URI authority/path, flags, extra types/sizes, and nested intents.
  • Deep links remain untrusted even after App Link verification. Never perform a privileged action merely because a URI opened the Activity; require current server authentication and authorization.
  • A PendingIntent needs an explicit target, minimum mutability (FLAG_IMMUTABLE by default), deliberate identity, and safe extras. Mutable fill-in data, implicit targets, or reused identity can enable confused-deputy behavior.

Integrity signals, replay, device clock, and offline expiry#

  • Play Integrity and root/debug/hook detection are risk signals, not proof. They have false positives, false negatives, and bypasses; the backend validates verdicts, binds them to an action/request nonce, and applies proportional policy.
  • A replay-sensitive operation needs a server challenge/nonce, narrow validity, subject/device/session binding, and idempotency/deduplication. A timestamp derived only from the device clock is insufficient.
  • Clock skew affects JWT exp/nbf, certificates, and proactive refresh. Use bounded leeway and server-time hints, while keeping the server authoritative.
  • Offline behavior needs explicit policy: an expired access token does not become valid because the network is absent. Permit only locally authorized low-risk behavior; re-authorize and submit queued writes idempotently online.

Observability, incident response, and remote revocation#

Record an opaque/hashed session correlation, token version and generation—not token values—refresh leader/follower count, reason/status/error code, latency, retry-chain length, revocation outcome, pin/TLS category, integrity-verdict bucket, and app/API version. Redact Authorization, cookies, authorization code/verifier/state/nonce, raw deep links, PII, token-endpoint bodies, and account-revealing aliases.

An incident runbook covers server-side session/token-family revocation, signing/client/TLS configuration rotation, compromised-version blocking or step-up, remote controls with safe defaults, forced reauthentication, affected-version telemetry, user communication, and a postmortem. Recovery must not depend only on a release that cannot connect because of a bad pin.

Guarantees versus explicit non-guarantees#

MechanismProvidesDoes not guarantee
PKCEBinds code exchange to the verifier.PKCE mitigates authorization-code interception but not all phishing or device compromise.
HTTPSAuthenticated encrypted transport under a trust model.HTTPS authenticates the transport endpoint under its trust model, not business correctness.
PinningNarrows accepted certificate/public-key material.Pinning does not protect a compromised app or process and can brick connectivity.
Android KeystoreKey non-exportability/use restrictions where supported.Keystore does not make a token inaccessible after the app legitimately decrypts or uses it.
Single-flightOne refresh for concurrent stale credentials.Refresh serialization does not create exactly-once server effects.
LogoutStops future local commit/use of the old generation.Logout cannot retract requests the server already processed.
HTTP 401An authentication challenge/error under the server contract.A 401 does not always mean refresh.
Client secret / biometricBiometric policy can gate a local key operation.A mobile client cannot safely embed a universal secret. Biometric success does not authenticate a backend session by itself.

Version-sensitive behavior#

Check the pinned OkHttp Authenticator, prior-response API, and Dispatcher behavior; provider discovery, redirect, logout, and revocation contracts; App Links verification and exported/PendingIntent rules by API/target SDK; Keystore hardware, StrongBox, user-auth, and invalidation behavior; BiometricPrompt authenticator combinations; Network Security Config and cleartext defaults; AndroidX Security Crypto deprecations and migration; WebView/Custom Tabs updates; and Play Integrity verdict schema and quotas. Standards evolve: OAuth 2.0 Security BCP updates older patterns, so do not copy implicit or embedded-password flows from old tutorials.

Decision framework#

  1. Inventory assets, actors, origins, redirect/IPC entry points, token audiences, attacker capabilities, and compliance/recovery needs.
  2. Choose Authorization Code + PKCE in an external user-agent; register exact redirects and issuer/client/audience/scopes, with state/nonce transaction ownership.
  3. Define server lifecycle: access TTL, refresh rotation/family/reuse detection, revocation, account/device sessions, clock skew, and offline policy.
  4. Build an atomic session snapshot and single-flight coordinator with generation/version CAS, an independent refresh path, bounded waits, and one-retry/replayability rules.
  5. Minimize local storage: Keystore-backed key plus backup, biometric, recovery, and migration policy; eliminate logs, clipboard, screenshots, and embedded secrets.
  6. Harden transport and Android inputs; add pinning only for a documented threat model and an operational rotation/recovery plan.
  7. Test races and attacks, instrument redacted signals, and rehearse remote revocation and incident response.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A short TTL narrows exposure but amplifies refresh storms, offline friction, and clock edge cases; a long TTL improves availability but extends the theft window.
  • A hardware or user-auth-bound key gives stronger at-rest protection but adds unsupported hardware, biometric lockout, enrollment invalidation, background refresh, and recovery conflicts.
  • Single-flight blocking followers is better than N refreshes, but can starve the Dispatcher if refresh depends on the same saturated queue; an unbounded wait turns an outage into thread exhaustion.
  • Rotation detects reuse, but a crash between server rotation and durable local commit may lose the family; define server grace or idempotent rotation behavior explicitly.
  • Pinning narrows CA risk but increases outage risk. Integrity blocking can reduce abuse while excluding legitimate modified/unsupported devices and still proving nothing absolutely.

Production concurrent-401 scenario#

After resume, 24 API calls carry access v41 and receive the provider-defined 401 invalid_token. The first Authenticator sees session generation 9/version 41 and creates the in-flight operation; the others check version and join. A dedicated refresh client without an Authenticator rotates outside the Mutex. The server returns access/refresh v42; under the lock the shared refresh job verifies generation 9/version 41, commits v42, and completes the shared Deferred. Followers rebuild only replayable requests with v42, and each prior-response chain is capped at one follow-up.

The user may log out concurrently. Logout advances generation to 10 and clears credentials before the network response. Late v42 fails the generation CAS; followers become signed out and revocation proceeds best-effort. A non-replayable upload is not retried, and POST retry requires a server idempotency key. Metrics show one leader, 23 followers, latency, and generation discard without recording credentials.

Code-review / debugging / security trap#

override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? =
    synchronized(this) {
        val token = api.refresh(store.refreshToken).execute().body()!!
        store.accessToken = token.access
        response.request.newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${token.access}")
            .build()
    }

The trap holds a global lock across network I/O, uses the recursive authenticated client, blocks all 401 calls and can deadlock or starve the Dispatcher. It has no prior-response cap, challenge validation, failed-token version, rotating-token atomic commit, generation/logout guard, failure completion, body replayability rule, or redaction. Debug a timeline keyed by request, session generation, token version, leader/follower, and Dispatcher occupancy; reproduce concurrent 401 + delayed refresh + logout. Fix it with a dedicated client, I/O outside the lock, one in-flight result, CAS commit, and one eligible follow-up.

Security and concurrency testing#

  • MockWebServer: N simultaneous 401 responses cause exactly one refresh; followers use vNext; refresh 400/401/timeout; a second 401 stops; redirects do not leak Authorization; non-replayable bodies are not retried.
  • Deterministic races: logout/account switch during refresh, two generations, late or older response, one follower cancellation, leader failure, rotation crash window, and saturated resource Dispatcher with an independent refresh path.
  • OAuth/App Link: wrong state/nonce/issuer/audience/redirect, duplicate callback, expired transaction, malicious nested URI, custom-scheme collision, and browser/external user-agent integration.
  • Android security: exported components, intent fuzzing, PendingIntent mutability, backup/restore, screenshot/clipboard/log/crash/analytics scanning, Keystore invalidation, biometric lockout/recovery, cleartext, and debug trust.
  • Incident game day: remotely revoke a family/session, rotate signing/TLS/pins with backup pins, block a compromised version, force reauthentication, and prove observability contains no credentials.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. 1. Access, refresh, and ID token? Access authorizes a resource server; refresh obtains new access at the authorization server; ID token tells the OIDC client about authentication and is not an API credential.
  2. 2. Why Code + PKCE for native apps? A public client cannot keep a secret; the verifier binds an intercepted code to the initiating instance, while the external user-agent keeps passwords out of the app.
  3. 3. State versus nonce? State correlates the authorization response and CSRF boundary; nonce binds an ID token to the OIDC request and replay boundary.
  4. 4. Interceptor versus Authenticator? The Interceptor attaches the current credential to eligible requests; the Authenticator creates one bounded follow-up after an eligible 401 or returns null.
  5. 5. How do you prevent a refresh storm? Use a version check, one leader and in-flight Deferred, follower reuse, I/O outside the Mutex, and generation/version CAS commit.
  6. 6. Why a separate refresh client? It avoids recursively invoking the same Authenticator and avoids depending on a saturated resource Dispatcher or old access header.
  7. 7. 401 versus 403? Usually 401 means missing/invalid authentication or challenge and 403 means insufficient permission; only refresh for a documented backend error because contracts vary.
  8. 8. What does Keystore provide? Protection and possible non-exportability of key material plus use restrictions—not secrecy of a plaintext token in a legitimately running or compromised app process.
  9. 9. When should you pin? Only for an explicit threat model with backup pins, overlap, rotation/incident plan, and telemetry; it is not universal and can brick connectivity.
  10. 10. How does logout beat late refresh? Atomically advance generation and clear credentials; commit a refresh result only while generation and failed version still match, otherwise discard it.

4 senior follow-ups#

  1. How do you reconcile rotating refresh tokens, a crash between server success/local commit, and reuse detection?
  2. How does the bounded synchronous Authenticator bridge behave with 64 concurrent 401s and a saturated Dispatcher?
  3. What is the recovery policy for a biometric-bound key after enrollment change, restore, or lockout?
  4. How do you perform emergency TLS/key rotation if the old app has a broken pin set and cannot fetch a remote flag?

4 unanswered self-checks#

  1. Draw every trust boundary in your login redirect and prove exact issuer/state/nonce/URI validation.
  2. Trace 20 concurrent 401s plus logout; where exactly do version and generation prevent stale commit?
  3. Which credentials can reach backup, a memory dump, screenshot, clipboard, logs, crash reporting, or analytics?
  4. Which server revocation, deduplication, and incident controls still work when the device is offline or the app process is compromised?

English answer skeletons#

~30-second answer#

I treat a mobile app as a public client. I use Authorization Code with PKCE in an external user-agent, validate the exact redirect, state, issuer and OIDC nonce, and keep access, refresh and ID-token purposes separate. An interceptor attaches the current access token; an OkHttp Authenticator handles only eligible 401s through a versioned single-flight refresh and retries once. A generation check prevents late refresh from reviving logout. Keystore, biometrics, TLS, pinning and integrity are scoped defenses, not proof that a compromised process or backend action is safe.

~2-minute answer#

I start by separating OAuth roles and artifacts. The authorization server authenticates and issues grants; the resource server validates access tokens. An access token authorizes an API, a refresh token is only for the token endpoint, and an OIDC ID token is an identity assertion for the client. Because a native app is a public client, I use Authorization Code with S256 PKCE through the system browser or Custom Tabs. I validate the exact redirect URI, an outstanding single-use transaction, state, issuer, and ID-token signature, audience, expiry and nonce.

At runtime an application interceptor reads an immutable session snapshot and adds the current credential only to allowlisted requests. An OkHttp Authenticator handles a provider-defined invalid-token 401, not every 401 or 403. It checks the prior-response count and failed credential version. Concurrent failures join one in-flight refresh; network I/O runs outside the lock through a dedicated client without the resource authenticator. The result commits only if session generation and token version still match, so logout or account switch wins. Each replayable request gets at most one follow-up; one-shot bodies and non-idempotent effects require explicit policy and server idempotency.

For storage, Keystore protects cryptographic keys and may provide hardware-backed non-exportability, but the token is plaintext when the app uses it. Biometric success can gate a local key operation, not authenticate the backend session. I exclude credentials from backup, screenshots, clipboard, logs and analytics. HTTPS and Network Security Config are baseline; pinning is only for a justified threat model with backup pins and a rotation runbook because it can brick connectivity and does not protect a compromised process. Exported components, deep links, PendingIntent and WebView are untrusted input boundaries. Integrity verdicts are risk signals. I finish with race and attack tests, redacted metrics, server revocation and an incident-response drill.

  • RFC 6749: OAuth 2.0, RFC 6750: Bearer Tokens, RFC 7009: Token Revocation, OpenID Connect Core 1.0
  • OkHttp Authenticator API, OkHttp Interceptors, OkHttp HTTPS and Certificate Pinning

Local persistence: SQLite, Room, migrations, transactions, and DataStore boundariesexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage you should explain durability from SQLite pages to repository boundaries, design a constrained and indexed Room schema, place safe transaction boundaries, evolve every supported upgrade path, and choose Room versus Preferences or Proto DataStore. Pagination is only a boundary here; Paging and RemoteMediator are reserved for Stage 21.

Senior mental model#

Model: a database is a file of fixed-size pages; a connection executes SQL through the pager and B-trees; the journal protocol determines how committed state survives a crash. Room is a compile-time facade with generated adapters over SQLite, not another database; normalization is an explicit versioned design choice. DataStore is a separate transactional file-backed store for small typed/configuration state, not a relational engine.

  • ACID: atomicity, isolation, and durability apply to a DB transaction and its commit boundary. Process death before commit discards uncommitted work; after a successful durable commit, recovery follows the SQLite/device I/O contract.
  • Ownership: schema constraints defend invariants close to data; a repository defines the conceptual single source of truth, while offline-first orchestration is Stage 21.

Internals / topology#

Repository → RoomDatabase → generated DAO/adapters → SQLite connection(s)
                                            ↘ DB file + -wal/-shm or rollback journal
Settings repository → singleton DataStore → serializer/preferences → one file

SQLite caches pages per connection/process; transactions acquire locks and the journal keeps recoverable state. Room generates bind/read adapters, performs compile-time SQL/schema checks, and records a room_master_table identity hash. These layers do not combine network, DB, and DataStore into one atomic system.

SQLite: rollback journal, WAL, concurrency, checkpoints#

  • Rollback journal: before-images go to a journal; a writer normally excludes readers during the commit phase. Recovery restores old pages after an interrupted transaction.
  • WAL: a writer appends frames to -wal; readers retain an end mark and read a consistent DB+WAL snapshot. This improves reader/writer overlap, but WAL does not mean multiple simultaneous writers.
  • Checkpoint: copies committed frames into the main file. A long reader can retain an old end mark, prevent checkpoint progress, and grow the WAL. Observe size and latency; never “repair” by blindly deleting sidecar files.
  • Crash boundary: unfinished work is not partially visible. Process death around uncommitted work means rollback/recovery, not automatic retry of the business operation.

Room schema: entities, constraints, indexes, query plans#

@Entity defines a table; a DAO returns entities or projection POJOs. Generated adapters bind Kotlin values and materialize cursor columns. A type converter needs a deterministic reversible mapping; changing its encoding is a migration, not an ordinary refactor.

  • Choose a stable primary key. A unique constraint is an identity rule, not merely a performance hint. Foreign keys protect only declared valid constraints; specify parent/child columns, supporting indexes, and intentional cascade or restrict behavior.
  • Indexes cost write I/O and storage. For a composite index, column ordering should follow the equality prefix, range, and ordering needs. Test selectivity on realistic data with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
  • Normalization avoids update anomalies. A denormalized read model can avoid joins but needs an explicit consistency, rebuild, and versioning mechanism.
@Entity(indices = [Index(value = ["accountId", "updatedAt"])])
data class NoteEntity(@PrimaryKey val id: String, val accountId: String, val updatedAt: Long)

@Dao interface NoteDao {
  @Query("SELECT * FROM NoteEntity WHERE accountId=:id ORDER BY updatedAt DESC")
  fun observe(id: String): Flow<List<NoteEntity>>
}

Transactions, suspend context, conflicts, and upsert#

RoomDatabase.withTransaction or a generated @Transaction method groups DB work. Keep the transaction short, deterministic, and free of network I/O: locks and a connection remain held across suspension, while external timeout/cancellation creates unknown outcomes. A DB transaction is not an atomic network-plus-DB transaction. Use idempotency, an outbox, or a state machine where coordination is required.

  • Room runs supported suspend DAO work on configured executors. Do not block the main thread or assume arbitrary code is dispatched by magic.
  • Cancellation before commit should roll back, but cancellation after an external effect cannot retract it. Do not swallow CancellationException.
  • IGNORE, REPLACE, and ABORT differ in identity, FK, and trigger effects. @Upsert availability and generated semantics are version-sensitive; verify the Room version, SQLite behavior, and desired partial-update semantics.

Room observable Flow, invalidation, and threading#

An observable Room Flow registers tables with the invalidation tracker. A commit invalidates a table and an active collector gets a query rerun, not a row-level event. Room Flow does not identify the exact changed rows. The result may equal the prior value; use distinctUntilChanged only when its equality semantics and cost are acceptable.

The Flow is cold per collector, while DB/invalidation infrastructure is shared. Querying and mapping cost real work; cancellation should stop obsolete work as supported by the driver. Avoid heavy domain mapping inside a transaction and measure executor starvation.

Relations, junctions, N+1, batching, and limits#

@Relation and a junction model one-to-many and many-to-many projections; a consistent multi-query object graph needs @Transaction. Generated convenience does not promise one JOIN: @Relation issues one extra batched IN (…) query per relation level, not N+1; watch large IN lists and the mapping cost. True N+1 appears when app code calls a DAO per item. Explicit JOIN/projection queries are often better for hot paths.

Batch inserts reduce transaction overhead, but chunk large IN lists and bulk writes. The SQLite variable/query limits depend on the build/runtime, statement size, and bind count; “999” is not a universal constant. Mention keyset/cursor pagination only as a boundary—Paging and RemoteMediator belong to Stage 21.

Schema export and migrations#

  • Enable exportSchema = true, version-control JSON schemas, and provide the processor schema location. The history is input to auto migration and a reviewable contract.
  • AutoMigration fits an unambiguous structural delta. Rename/delete operations need a spec such as @RenameColumn/@DeleteColumn. Auto migration cannot infer a business transformation.
  • A manual Migration performs ordered SQL and data backfill. For a required column, consider expand/backfill/validate/rebuild rather than guessing a default; account for large-table lock time, disk, and restart behavior.
  • Test every supported path, not only latest-1→latest: each old→…→latest chain and every registered direct edge. MigrationTestHelper creates historical schemas, runs migrations, and validates the result.

On open, Room compares the schema to its expected model and identity hash. A prepackaged DB must match its declared version/schema and migration chain. fallbackToDestructiveMigration can recover by drop/recreate, but Destructive migration deletes data.

Multi-process, corruption, disk-full, backup, encryption#

  • Multiple processes have separate Room instances and caches. Enable multi-process invalidation only when required, configure journals/migrations consistently, and test races and process kill; invalidation is not a cross-process business transaction.
  • Disk-full/I/O: a write or commit can fail. Do not report domain success before commit. Free only controlled cache, surface a recoverable error, retain the cause, and avoid a tight retry loop.
  • Corruption: classify reconstructible cache versus irreplaceable user data. A policy may quarantine/export diagnostics, restore a validated backup, or rebuild only cache; silent destructive reset is data loss.
  • Backup/restore: classify DB, WAL/SHM, DataStore, keys, and server state as one policy. Restoring an old DB with a new account or key can be logically corrupt.
  • Encryption: persistence is not automatically encrypted or backup-safe. File encryption or a SQLCipher-like layer addresses a defined at-rest threat, not plaintext in a compromised process, logs, or authorized runtime access; key lifecycle matters.

DataStore: Preferences, Proto, ownership, and evolution#

Preferences DataStore provides schema-less typed keys. Proto DataStore provides an explicit serializer/schema/default and more controlled evolution. updateData serializes read-modify-write per store; the transform runs once under the store lock and the new value is written atomically (temp file + rename). If the transform or the write throws, the update is aborted. Return a new immutable value and never mutate the input. Keep the transform short, because it blocks every other update to that store. DataStore does not make cross-store operations atomic.

  • Create one singleton per file/process through a property delegate or DI. Multiple writers to one file violate ownership. Multi-process DataStore is a separate, version-sensitive API; all participants need compatible multi-process configuration.
  • Use a CorruptionHandler only for defined parse/corruption cases with a safe replacement; do not turn arbitrary I/O failure into defaults.
  • For Proto serializer evolution, never reuse field numbers and preserve compatible unknown-field semantics. Preferences keys also have versioned meaning.
  • SharedPreferencesMigration runs before normal reads; make it idempotent and define cleanup. Legacy apply() updates memory then flushes asynchronously; commit() synchronously returns success. Neither creates cross-store atomicity.

Repository / SSOT boundary#

A repository hides persistence APIs, maps storage entities to domain types, and owns placement: Room for relational/queryable durable state, DataStore for small configuration/preferences, memory for ephemeral state. A conceptual single source of truth means one authoritative read path, not one physical file. Network reconciliation, queues, and offline-first policy are Stage 21.

Guarantees / non-guarantees#

  • A committed DB transaction has SQLite atomicity; process death before commit does not leave half a transaction. It is not atomic with network or DataStore.
  • WAL permits reader/writer overlap, not multiple writers and not unbounded-WAL safety.
  • Room compile-time checks catch known SQL/schema mismatches, not data quality, query performance, or undeclared business invariants.
  • Foreign keys protect only declared valid constraints.
  • Room Flow is table invalidation plus query rerun, not exact changed-row delivery.
  • Auto migration cannot infer business meaning; destructive fallback deletes data.
  • DataStore updateData is atomic for one store, not DB+store or two stores.
  • Persistence is not automatically encrypted or backup-safe.

Version-sensitive behavior#

Verify pinned Room, DataStore, and Android SQLite versions before claiming behavior for @Upsert, auto-migration annotations/specs, KSP/KAPT output, WAL defaults, variable limits, cancellation, multi-instance invalidation, or MultiProcessDataStore. Framework SQLite varies with the OS; bundled SQLite changes capabilities and operational characteristics. State minimum/target SDK and library versions.

Decision framework#

  1. Need relationships, joins, constraints, partial queries, or many records? Use Room.
  2. Small configuration/preferences object read as a whole? Use Preferences or Proto DataStore; prefer Proto for explicit schema/evolution.
  3. Which invariants belong in constraints, a transaction, or the domain?
  4. Which process, backup, encryption, corruption, and migration paths are supported?
  5. What do measured plans, latency, storage cost, and rollback strategy show?

Trade-offs and failure modes#

ChoiceBenefitFailure mode
WALreader/writer overlaplong reader stalls checkpoint; WAL growth
Denormalized modelcheap readsstale duplicate data
Cascade deleteautomatic cleanuplarge or surprising deletion
AutoMigrationless boilerplatecannot express semantic backfill
Destructive fallbackdatabase opensuser data erased
Proto DataStoretyped schemaunsafe serializer/schema evolution

Production migration scenario#

v12→v15: replace ownerName with required ownerId and normalize owners. Export v12–v15 schemas. v12→13 creates owner table and nullable ownerId; a manual migration backfills deterministic IDs and quarantines ambiguous rows. v13→14 rebuilds the child table with FK/index and verifies zero orphans. v14→15 removes the legacy column with an explicit spec. Tests start at every supported version, insert edge data, open latest through production migrations, and assert schema, identity hash, rows, FKs, and index plan. Rollout monitors migration latency/failure/disk and forbids destructive fallback for irreplaceable data.

Code-review / debug trap#

@Transaction
suspend fun sync() {
  val remote = api.fetch() // network I/O while DB resources stay held
  dao.replaceAll(remote)
}

This is more than a “long transaction”: cancellation or timeout can leave a remote effect without DB state, readers/writer are delayed, and retry may duplicate an effect. Fetch first, then make a short DB commit with version/idempotency policy. For slow UI, investigate invalidation storms, N+1, a missing composite index, and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN rather than merely adding a dispatcher.

Testing and observability#

  • DAO integration tests for constraints, conflict/upsert behavior, cancellation, rollback, and concurrent readers/writer.
  • A migration matrix using historical exported schemas, real transformations, and every supported path.
  • Failure injection for process kill before/after commit, disk-full/I/O, corrupt bytes, long reader/checkpoint, and restore mismatch.
  • DataStore tests for concurrent updateData, serializer evolution, corruption handler, SharedPreferences migration, and singleton/multi-process configuration.
  • Measure DB open/migration/query/transaction latency, lock/busy events, WAL size/checkpoints, DB size, and corruption/destructive recovery counts without sensitive row values.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q1: Does WAL allow parallel writes? No. There is one writer; the gain is overlap with snapshot readers.
  2. Q2: What does a Room Flow emit? Table invalidation causes query rerun; it is not a row-event stream.
  3. Q3: When is @Transaction needed? When multiple DB operations must observe or create one consistent DB state.
  4. Q4: Why no network in a transaction? It holds DB resources and the external effect cannot roll back with the DB.
  5. Q5: Auto or manual migration? Auto for unambiguous shape changes; manual for semantic transformation/backfill.
  6. Q6: How should migrations be tested? Every supported start-to-latest path with historical schema, edge data, and Room validation.
  7. Q7: Preferences or Proto? Preferences for simple keys; Proto for an explicit typed schema and evolution.
  8. Q8: How do you choose a composite index? From actual predicates/order, equality prefix, range, selectivity, and query plan.
  9. Q9: Does encryption solve storage security? Only the at-rest slice of a threat model, not compromised runtime, logs, or key misuse.
  10. Q10: How do you handle corruption? Classify data, preserve diagnostics, restore a validated backup, or rebuild only reconstructible cache.

Follow-up prompts#

  1. How does a long-lived reader affect a WAL checkpoint?
  2. How would you run expand/backfill/contract on a large table?
  3. How does Room multi-process invalidation differ from MultiProcess DataStore?
  4. How would you detect N+1 and a poor index in a production trace?

Unanswered self-checks#

  1. Draw crash points for a network→DB flow and name each observable outcome.
  2. Design schema/indexes for many-to-many tags with an ordered recent query.
  3. Build a migration matrix when app versions 8, 10, and 11 can upgrade to 12.
  4. Define backup, encryption, and corruption policy for an irreplaceable draft and reconstructible cache.

English answer skeletons#

30-second answer

“I treat Room as a generated, compile-time checked layer over SQLite, not as a different database. I put relational invariants in keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, and tested indexes; keep transactions short and free of network I/O; and remember that WAL still has one writer and Room Flow reruns a query after table invalidation. I export schemas and test every supported migration path. I use singleton DataStore for small settings, with updateData atomic only per store, and define explicit corruption, backup, and encryption policies.”

2-minute answer

“At the bottom, SQLite persists pages and uses either a rollback journal or WAL. WAL lets readers keep snapshots while one writer appends frames; checkpoints copy frames back, so long readers can cause WAL growth. Room generates DAO implementations and adapters, validates known SQL/schema shapes at compile time, and checks the schema identity on open. I model stable keys, uniqueness, and foreign keys deliberately, order composite indexes from real predicates, and verify plans. Transactions protect only DB work, so I never hold one over a network request. Observable Flow is table invalidation followed by query rerun, not changed-row delivery. For evolution I export schemas, use auto migration only for unambiguous changes, write manual transformations for business meaning, and test every supported old-to-latest path with real data. Destructive fallback is data loss. DataStore is for small settings: Preferences is key-based, Proto has an explicit serializer/schema, and updateData serializes one store only. Both Room and DataStore need explicit single/multi-process ownership, corruption, disk-full, backup, restore, and encryption policies. Repository is the conceptual SSOT boundary; offline-first belongs to Stage 21.”

Offline-first architecture and Paging 3expand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to design and explain an offline-first repository where the local database is the canonical read source / single source of truth (SSOT), the network is a synchronization source, and Paging 3 provides bounded, generation-based access to a large dataset. The focus is sync and paging contracts and failure boundaries; SQLite/Room storage internals were covered in Stage 20, while broader reliability and testing depth belongs to later stages.

Senior mental model / topology#

UI ← Flow<PagingData<UiModel>> ← Pager ← Room PagingSource ← local DB (canonical reads)
                                      ↕ invalidation       ↑ transactional merge
UI command → local entity + outbox → sync worker → API/change feed → entities + remote keys
                    ↑ optimistic state       ↓ ack/conflict/reject

Online-only reads and writes the network and may keep an ephemeral cache. Offline-first guarantees useful local reads and explicitly defines which writes can be queued; it does not mean every action works offline. Local-first puts local ownership and peer/server convergence more centrally into the product model. SSOT is an architectural policy: observers read the canonical local model and synchronization changes it; SSOT does not create automatic consistency.

Read/write/synchronization internals#

  • Read path: UI continuously reads Room while the repository separately determines freshness. Persist fetchedAt, server version/change token, and provenance. TTL is product policy, not truth; stale-while-revalidate immediately shows cached data, marks stale/loading/error state, and refreshes in the background. Do not present old prices, permissions, or safety-critical state as fresh.
  • Pull refresh: fetch outside the DB transaction; then in one local transaction verify account/generation and merge entities, tombstones, ordering metadata, remote keys, and checkpoint. A transaction protects only the local DB, not network-plus-DB atomicity. On failure the old snapshot remains readable.
  • Invalidation: a push notification or WebSocket message is a hint, not payload truth: debounce/coalesce and pull by change token. Polling defines bounded staleness and cost. Socket disconnects, missed push, and foreground gaps require periodic or foreground reconciliation.
  • Write path: in one local transaction create a client-generated ID, optimistic entity, and outbox operation. State machine: PENDING → RUNNING → ACKED; transient failure returns to PENDING with attempt/nextAt; permanent rejection becomes FAILED/user action. Process death after any commit must allow resume.
  • Delivery: WorkManager with network/battery constraints and exponential backoff provides durable best-effort execution, not exact-time or exactly-once. A worker may run again; a lease/compare-and-set protects local concurrency. An idempotency key works only when the server atomically deduplicates key+scope+payload and retains the result long enough.

Optimism, conflicts, deletions, identity#

Optimistic UI exposes pending state and a fast result, but the server can reject it. On acknowledgement reconcile server-canonical fields/version; on rejection roll back only if the base version has not changed, otherwise perform a domain merge or show explicit conflict UI. A client-generated UUID/ULID supports references before upload; an idempotency key and entity ID serve different roles.

  • Conflict detection: compare server revision/ETag or base version. Server-wins is simple but loses local intent; client-wins risks overwrite; LWW requires an authoritative clock/HLC because device wall clocks are unreliable; version vectors detect concurrency but grow; field/domain merge preserves semantics; manual resolution is suitable for high-value ambiguity.
  • Deletes: a tombstone with server revision and deletion time propagates deletion and stops an old client from resurrecting a record. Purge only after retention/ack/checkpoint policy; hard delete without a protocol creates resurrection risk.
  • Isolation: every entity, outbox row, key, and checkpoint is scoped by account/tenant. Logout cancels tagged work, increments an auth/account generation, and transactionally purges or quarantines data; a late response must be rejected before merge.

Checkpoints, ordering, partial failure#

A change token/checkpoint means “all changes through a server-defined boundary are applied.” Advance it in the same local transaction as entities and tombstones. An expired/invalid token triggers a bounded full resync using a new sync generation and mark-and-sweep or a shadow set, not a dangerous blind clear. A partial page, parse failure, disk-full event, or process death must not advance the checkpoint.

Paging needs a backend total order with a tie-breaker, such as (updatedAt DESC, id DESC), and stable cursor semantics. Offset is simple, but inserts/deletes before the offset create duplicates or gaps. An opaque cursor can bind a boundary, but only the server contract defines snapshot and stability. Client deduplication by ID removes duplicate presentation; it cannot prove that no gap exists.

Paging 3 internals and generations#

  • Pager exposes a cold Flow<PagingData<T>>. One PagingSource serves one generation; invalidation makes it unusable and Pager emits a new PagingData. Invalidation discards a generation but cannot prove remote freshness.
  • load() receives LoadParams.Refresh, Append, or Prepend with key/loadSize/placeholders flag and returns LoadResult.Page, Error, or Invalid. Paging load order and completion can vary; each load must be race-safe, and business order cannot be inferred from completion time.
  • getRefreshKey(state) derives a restart key near anchorPosition, commonly using closestPageToPosition(). The anchor is a presentation hint, not a server checkpoint. Keys must belong to the same dataset/query/account identity.
  • UI CombinedLoadStates separates source from mediator, each with refresh/prepend/append. Render initial empty, cached plus mediator-loading, source error, mediator error, append retry, and end independently.
  • cachedIn(viewModelScope) shares transformed paging generations within that scope and should usually be applied after reusable transformations. It does not persist data or survive process death. Stable item identity/keys and pure map/filter/insertSeparators transformations avoid visual identity drift; separators need stable derived IDs and may be recomputed.

Config, Room, and RemoteMediator#

PagingConfig balances pageSize, initialLoadSize, prefetchDistance, placeholders, maxSize, and jumpThreshold. Placeholders require countable positions and source support. Page dropping under maxSize, jumping, and defaults are version-sensitive; inspect the pinned Paging release rather than promising an exact memory bound.

A Room DAO returns PagingSource<Int, Entity>: a generated LIMIT/OFFSET source that is invalidated on table change, creating a new generation. Cursor/keyset keys apply to the network side, stored as RemoteMediator remote keys, or to a hand-written PagingSource. With network plus DB, RemoteMediator.initialize() chooses SKIP_INITIAL_REFRESH or LAUNCH_INITIAL_REFRESH from freshness policy. load(REFRESH/APPEND/PREPEND) reads scoped remote keys, calls the API, and transactionally writes entities plus keys. On refresh it clears only the intended query partition and only under an explicit policy. endOfPaginationReached means that direction has no more remote data for that cursor/query, not that the cache is globally fresh. RemoteMediator coordinates loading; it does not solve conflicts itself.

Guarantees / non-guarantees#

  • Offline-first does not mean all actions work offline; publish each capability’s offline contract.
  • SSOT is a policy, not automatic consistency; a local transaction protects only the local DB.
  • WorkManager is durable best-effort, not exact-time or exactly-once; idempotency requires server cooperation.
  • Optimistic UI can be rejected. Exactly-once end-to-end effects are generally unavailable; design at-least-once delivery plus deduplication and reconciliation.
  • Paging invalidation replaces a generation; it does not prove remote freshness. cachedIn shares within a scope and does not make data durable.
  • Paging load order and completion can vary. RemoteMediator does not solve domain conflicts. Total order and stable cursor are backend contracts.

Version-sensitive behavior#

Pin and inspect AndroidX Paging, Room, and WorkManager release notes and API docs: PagingConfig defaults, maxSize/jump/placeholders behavior, Compose Paging helpers, RemoteMediator APIs, Room PagingSource invalidation, and WorkManager quota/expedited behavior evolve. State the app’s tested library and Android versions; do not universalize an observation from one release or OEM.

Decision framework#

  1. Classify each use case as online-only, cache-assisted, offline-first, or genuinely local-first; define unavailable offline actions.
  2. Choose the canonical read model, freshness SLA, visible stale semantics, and triggers: user pull, foreground, periodic poll, push/socket hint.
  3. Define identity, total order, cursor/change token, deletion retention, and account/tenant scope with backend owners.
  4. For each write choose pessimistic versus optimistic, outbox states, idempotency scope, retry budget, and conflict strategy.
  5. Choose PagingSource-only or Room plus RemoteMediator; model refresh/append/prepend and key lifecycle, then test races and crash points deterministically.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A short TTL improves freshness but spends radio/server/battery; stale-while-revalidate improves latency but needs honest stale UI.
  • Optimism improves responsiveness but adds pending/reject/conflict states. A blind rollback can erase a newer edit.
  • Offset pagination is inspectable but unstable under mutation; cursor pagination moves complexity into backend contract and remote-key lifecycle.
  • Clearing on refresh is simple but can flash empty data, destroy unsynced rows, or cross query/account boundaries. Merge by version and partition.
  • Push lowers latency but is lossy; sockets add lifecycle/reconnect cost; polling bounds drift but spends resources. All require pull reconciliation.

Production sync + paging scenario#

In a tenant-scoped field-work app, a technician edits task clientId=C1 offline. One transaction writes an optimistic task with syncState=PENDING and outbox key tenant:T/op:O1. Room invalidates the PagingSource immediately; a new PagingData generation shows the row under stable key C1. A connected WorkManager worker CAS-claims O1 and sends baseVersion plus idempotency key. A timeout leaves the outcome unknown, so retry uses the same key. The server returns canonical revision 43; one transaction reconciles fields, ACKs O1, and advances the change token. A push only schedules delta pull. Pull-to-refresh runs RemoteMediator REFRESH: fetch, then a tenant-scoped transaction merges entities, tombstones, and remote keys; disk-full leaves old data and checkpoint intact. If the token expired, a generation-scoped full resync preserves pending local edits. UI reports stale age, pending count, and per-direction load states.

Code-review / debugging trap#

// Trap: network inside transaction, global clear, offset key, new ID on retry
withTransaction { dao.clearAll(); dao.insert(api.page(offset)); keys.put(offset + 20) }
// Trap: Pager rebuilt on recomposition and cached in UI ownership
repository.pager(query).flow.cachedIn(rememberCoroutineScope())

Review asks whether fetch is outside the transaction; clear is scoped and preserves pending data; entity plus remote keys are atomic; Pager is built per query/account in the ViewModel; IDs and order are stable; getRefreshKey matches the key contract; retry preserves operation/idempotency key; and a late old-account response is rejected. Debug correlation ID → Paging generation/load type → API cursor → DB transaction/checkpoint → invalidation → presented item IDs. Observe stale age, sync lag, outbox depth/oldest age, retries/conflicts/rejections, full-resync rate, duplicate/gap detections, and source/mediator load latency/error with account-safe hashed correlation.

Deterministic sync and Paging testing#

Unit-test PagingSource Refresh/Append/Prepend, keys, getRefreshKey, invalidation, and errors against fixed data and order. Test RemoteMediator with a fake cursor API plus in-memory Room: initialize freshness, atomic entities/keys, empty page/end, retry, refresh partition, token expiry, and stale generation. Sync tests use a fake clock, deterministic backoff, injectable IDs, scripted duplicate/out-of-order responses, and crash hooks before and after every local commit. Assert model invariants and final convergence, not timing or one exact load sequence.

Likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: What is the SSOT? A: The local DB for reads; the network synchronizes it. This is policy, not automatic consistency.
  2. Q: Do all offline-first actions work offline? A: No. Reads and queueable writes need an explicit capability contract.
  3. Q: How does a write survive process death? A: Commit entity plus outbox atomically, keep durable states and the same operation/idempotency key, and use a resumable worker.
  4. Q: Why not exactly once? A: A timeout cannot distinguish a lost request from a lost response; use at-least-once retry, server deduplication, and reconciliation.
  5. Q: Which conflict policy is best? A: It is domain-dependent; detect by version, avoid device-clock LWW, and preserve intent or expose manual resolution.
  6. Q: What does PagingSource invalidation do? A: It ends the current generation and Pager creates another; it does not prove remote freshness.
  7. Q: What is getRefreshKey for? A: It provides a key near anchorPosition for a new generation; it is not a sync checkpoint.
  8. Q: Source versus mediator load states? A: Source describes DB loads and mediator the network-to-DB boundary, so cached data can coexist with a mediator error.
  9. Q: Should RemoteMediator refresh clear all? A: Not by default; merge or clear only the scoped partition with keys while preserving pending rows.
  10. Q: Does a cursor eliminate gaps? A: Only under a backend total-order/stability contract; client deduplication cannot prove completeness.

Follow-up prompts#

  1. Design an outbox state machine for an attachment upload with an unknown timeout outcome.
  2. Compare push, WebSocket, and polling for a “no more than two minutes stale” SLA.
  3. Explain RemoteMediator keys for two filters in one tenant.
  4. Resolve a concurrent offline rename and server deletion without resurrection.

Unanswered self-checks#

  1. Which exact fields form the total order and cursor in your backend?
  2. When is a tombstone safe to purge for the oldest supported client?
  3. What observable UI state should cached data have after failed refresh and expired TTL?
  4. Which crash points can leave an operation RUNNING, and how will lease recovery repair them?

English answer skeletons#

30-second answer

“I make the local database the canonical read source and treat the network as synchronization. Reads expose freshness and stale state; writes atomically persist optimistic data plus an outbox operation, then WorkManager retries with a stable idempotency key while the server resolves deduplication. Paging reads Room through generation-scoped PagingSources, and RemoteMediator transactionally merges entities with scoped remote keys. None of this guarantees exactly once, remote freshness, or conflict resolution without explicit backend contracts.”

2-minute answer

“First I classify the feature as online-only, offline-first, or genuinely local-first and publish which actions work offline. In offline-first, UI reads only the local canonical model. Freshness metadata drives stale-while-revalidate, and push or sockets are invalidation hints backed by delta pull and periodic reconciliation. A write transaction stores a client-generated ID, optimistic state, and outbox record. A constrained WorkManager worker retries durably, but not at an exact time or exactly once, so requests carry a stable idempotency key that the server must deduplicate. Revisions detect conflicts; resolution is domain-specific, and tombstones prevent resurrection. Checkpoints advance atomically with merged rows and expired tokens trigger a scoped full resync. For large lists, Pager emits PagingData generations backed by one-shot PagingSources. Refresh, Append, and Prepend use query-scoped keys; invalidation creates a new generation, while getRefreshKey uses anchor position only to preserve viewport. cachedIn shares work in a ViewModel scope but is not storage. Room plus RemoteMediator keeps entities and remote keys in one local transaction and exposes source versus mediator load states. I require a backend total order and stable cursor, test duplicate/gap/order-change races and crash boundaries with fake time/API/DB, and observe stale age, sync lag, outbox depth, conflicts, cursor errors, and load latency.”
