Senior Android testing strategyexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to build a risk-based Android test portfolio: choose the cheapest sufficiently faithful boundary for each risk, create deterministic seams for time, concurrency, storage, network, and platform behavior, and state what each test proves and does not prove. This is an engineering feedback strategy, not the future Stage 23 depth on production observability or reliability operations.

Senior mental model#

Start with risk—severity × likelihood × detectability × escape cost—not a pyramid percentage. The test pyramid suggests many fast isolated tests and few expensive E2E tests; the testing trophy emphasizes integration tests. Both are heuristics, not quotas. A portfolio needs a fast inner loop, enough boundary fidelity, and a small set of critical-path E2E journeys. E2E cannot cover all combinations.

risk/contract → smallest faithful boundary → deterministic control → observable outcome
pure policy → unit; adapters + collaborators → integration/component/contract
Android framework/UI → Robolectric or device; critical journey → narrow E2E

Test taxonomy and boundaries#

  • Unit: one policy/function/class with real value objects and no Android/runtime I/O.
  • Integration: multiple real collaborators at a boundary, such as repository + DAO + client mapping.
  • Component: a feature/deployable slice through its public API with controlled outside dependencies.
  • UI: one screen’s rendering, semantics, and interaction; E2E is a narrow user journey through real app layers and a controlled backend/device.
  • Contract/schema: producer/consumer payload compatibility and API invariants; it is not a substitute for behavioral integration.
  • Screenshot/golden: pixel/layout regression; performance checks latency/frame/startup budgets in a representative environment; accessibility covers semantics, labels, actions, focus, scanner, and manual checks. No category subsumes the others.

Deterministic architecture and test seams#

Separate pure decision policy from effects. Constructor-inject narrow interfaces for clock, ID/random source, dispatcher, scope ownership, filesystem, DAO, HTTP transport, and analytics sink; pass inputs explicitly. Control locale, time zone, ordering, and seed. A seam should match a production contract rather than exist only for mocking. Test doubles must preserve relevant contract: thread safety, ordering, cold/hot behavior, errors, cancellation, and persistence semantics that matter to the scenario.

Prefer assertions on observable state/output and invariants. Interaction verification fits a command boundary: one charge, an audit write, cancellation, or “do not call network.” Do not assert private call sequences unless sequence is the contract; refactor-safe tests describe behavior.

Fakes, stubs, mocks, and spies#

  • A Fake is a working simplified implementation, useful for stateful flows but prone to drift without contract tests against the real adapter.
  • A Stub returns scripted answers; it fails when the scenario needs state, ordering, or cancellation.
  • A Mock has programmed expectations; mocks verify configured interactions, not business correctness, and overmocking creates implementation-coupled tests.
  • A Spy records calls on a real/fake object; it can execute a dangerous real effect and mix state with interaction assertions.

Do not mock Android framework internals, Flow, NavController internals, Room generated code, or the Retrofit/OkHttp chain. Wrap an unstable external boundary in your contract, use real value objects and a fake domain port, use a Robolectric shadow only when its fidelity is enough, or run an instrumented integration test. Deep stubs and relaxed mocks often make impossible states green.

JVM, Robolectric, and instrumented/device tests#

  • Local JVM: fastest and hermetic for Kotlin policy; Android framework stubs do not provide device behavior.
  • Robolectric: a local simulated Android through shadows, faster than an emulator and useful for resources/lifecycle/UI; shadow/platform parity is incomplete.
  • Instrumented emulator/device: highest Android runtime, SQLite, and rendering fidelity, but slower, costlier, and more sensitive to API/OEM/device state. Emulators improve repeatability; representative physical devices expose hardware/OEM risks.

Move a test down only when the lower boundary preserves the risk. Duplicate a few high-risk contracts at different levels, not the whole suite.

ViewModel, use-case, and repository tests#

  • Use case: table-driven inputs, domain invariants, boundaries, and idempotency with pure tests, not a mock graph.
  • ViewModel: initial state, intent-to-state transitions, concurrent intents, loading/error/retry, SavedState input, and cancellation on clear; assert state rather than implementation calls.
  • Repository: real mapping/cache orchestration with a fake server/clock and Room where useful; test offline/cache freshness, duplicates, partial failure, cancellation, and source-of-truth ordering. Do not test Retrofit annotations using only mock interactions.

Coroutine test internals and virtual time#

runTest creates a TestScope and scheduler, waits for and propagates child failures, and has a timeout. A TestDispatcher delegates execution to TestCoroutineScheduler. StandardTestDispatcher queues new coroutines: use runCurrent() for the current-time queue, advanceTimeBy() plus runCurrent() at a boundary, or advanceUntilIdle(). UnconfinedTestDispatcher eagerly enters top-level launches but does not guarantee order after suspension; it is convenient when ordering is irrelevant but can hide production scheduling.

runTest virtualizes delays only on participating test dispatchers that share its scheduler, not arbitrary threads, Dispatchers.IO/Default, blocking code, or external systems. advanceUntilIdle() may hide scheduling assumptions; for causal assertions first assert the precondition, then use runCurrent() or advance the exact boundary. Launch intentional infinite collectors in backgroundScope, which is cancelled automatically; keep finite work as child work so leaks and failures remain visible.

Main replacement, scopes, cancellation, and failures#

In local tests replace Dispatchers.Main with Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) and always call Dispatchers.resetMain(); share one scheduler. Prefer injected dispatchers and owner CoroutineScope over hard-coded Dispatchers.IO or GlobalScope. Scope ownership must match the production lifetime.

Test that parents wait for/cancel children, cooperative cancellation, cleanup, timeout boundaries, exception propagation, and supervision policy. A leaked child makes runTest wait or fail; do not hide it in an unowned scope. Verify CancellationException is rethrown, inspect primary/suppressed failures only when contractual, and ensure cancellation is not converted into a domain error.

Flow testing#

Use first() for one value; use toList() and completion for a finite stream; start a collector in backgroundScope before triggering a hot/infinite stream. Turbine is useful for ordered awaitItem(), error/completion, and “no event,” but it is a third-party library, not an Android or Kotlin guarantee. Always terminate or cancel collection.

StateFlow conflates, so test state rather than every transient assignment. For SharedFlow/shareIn, subscription timing, replay, SharingStarted, and collector readiness are part of the scenario: subscribe, let the scheduler start the collector, then emit. first() cancels upstream after one value; toList() on an infinite flow hangs. Do not let an eager test dispatcher accidentally repair a race.

Room, network, contracts, and Paging#

  • Room DAO: instrumented tests exercise the real generated DAO, constraints, transactions, invalidation, and query results. In-memory Room is fast, but in-memory Room is not migration or disk fidelity, nor WAL/process-death fidelity. Migration tests open a file-backed old schema through MigrationTestHelper, apply every supported path, and verify schema plus preserved data.
  • Network: MockWebServer tests real HTTP-client serialization, headers, paths, errors, disconnects/timeouts, and the recorded request. It is scripted transport, not the production server. Contract/schema tests check consumer/provider compatibility and fixtures; versioned fixtures and unknown/missing/null fields matter.
  • PagingSource: deterministically test Refresh/Append/Prepend keys, loadSize, empty/end, error/retry, invalidation, and getRefreshKey. RemoteMediator: use a fake API plus test DB for initialize freshness, scoped remote keys, atomic writes, duplicate pages, refresh, end, error, and retry. Do not assert accidental load-completion order.

Compose UI testing#

Compose tests query the semantics tree, not the implementation tree. Merged nodes represent the user-facing accessibility surface; use useUnmergedTree=true only for intentional descendant detail. Prefer visible text, role, state description, content description, and actions. testTag is a stable fallback, but a tag-only suite does not prove accessibility.

The Compose rule synchronizes with Compose and registered idling resources; Compose idle does not mean arbitrary external async is done. Inject a controlled dispatcher/data source or register a legitimate idling boundary—do not sleep(). Disable mainClock.autoAdvance for exact animation/frame control and advance the clock explicitly. Test navigation through user actions and destination semantics, deep links/back, configuration recreation, and state restoration with StateRestorationTester separately; do not assert private NavController internals.

Hilt test graph boundaries#

@TestInstallIn replaces a production module for a test source set; @UninstallModules plus a nested test module gives a per-class override; @BindValue is convenient for an instance. HiltAndroidRule, the Hilt test runner/HiltTestApplication, and injection order are setup contracts. Use a custom application only when production base behavior is truly required; the test application cannot magically inherit an arbitrary @HiltAndroidApp application. Do not replace so much of the graph that the test stops checking production wiring; keep a separate real-graph smoke test.

Screenshot, performance, and accessibility#

Golden tests pin device/API, density, font scale/font files, locale, time zone, theme, dynamic color, animation, GPU/rendering pipeline, and seed; retain actual/expected/diff artifacts. A screenshot pass is environment-specific, and a pixel diff proves neither semantics nor interaction. Run performance tests as release/profileable with warmup, a representative device/baseline, statistical thresholds, and traces. Combine accessibility semantics assertions with scanner and manual TalkBack/switch/focus review.

Flakes, data, CI, coverage, and artifacts#

Taxonomy: uncontrolled time; concurrency/race; leaked global/static state; real network/service; device/emulator/resource pressure; animations/rendering; order/shared files/ports. Reproduce with seed, shard/order, device/API, scheduler timeline, and repeated targeted runs. Quarantine only with an owner, issue, expiry/SLA, and a blocked-release rule for critical paths; quarantine does not mean ignore. Retrying flaky tests does not make them deterministic: retry rate is a signal, not a cure.

Test-data builders provide valid defaults and named variants without hiding important fields. Parameterized/property-based tests check invariants across generated values and shrinking; fuzzing helps parser/state-machine robustness, but deterministic seeds and a reproduction corpus are mandatory. CI sharding lowers wall time but exposes global/order coupling. Record shard, seed, device, logs, screenshots, video, logcat, traces, DB/network fixtures, and coroutine diagnostics. Coverage reports executed lines/branches, not oracle quality: coverage is not confidence. Mutation testing asks whether assertions kill behavior changes, but has cost and equivalent mutants.

Guarantees / non-guarantees#

  • runTest virtualizes participating test dispatchers, not arbitrary threads or external systems.
  • advanceUntilIdle() may hide scheduling assumptions.
  • Mocks verify configured interactions, not business correctness.
  • In-memory Room is not migration or disk fidelity.
  • Compose idle does not mean arbitrary external async is done.
  • A screenshot pass is environment-specific; coverage is not confidence.
  • Retrying flaky tests does not make them deterministic.
  • E2E cannot cover all combinations; test doubles must preserve relevant contract.

Version-sensitive guidance#

Pin and verify Android Gradle Plugin/managed devices, AndroidX Test/Espresso, Compose UI test, Room, Paging, Hilt/Dagger, Robolectric, Kotlin, kotlinx-coroutines-test, Turbine, OkHttp/MockWebServer, and the screenshot plugin. APIs, default timeouts, idling, semantics, runners, generated schemas, and artifact coordinates evolve. Turbine, Robolectric, MockWebServer, and screenshot frameworks have their own support/version policies; do not call third-party behavior a platform guarantee. Check pinned release notes and APIs instead of copying a snippet from another major version.

Decision framework#

  1. Name the risk, impact, and observable contract/oracle.
  2. Choose the lowest boundary that faithfully contains the risk; state what remains outside.
  3. Control clock, scheduler, IDs, network, storage, locale/device, and make failures scriptable.
  4. Choose a real collaborator or contract-preserving double; add a higher-fidelity test for adapter assumptions.
  5. Design success, boundary, cancellation, concurrency, malformed/partial failure, and recovery cases.
  6. Define CI lane, artifact package, runtime/flakiness budget, owner, and a condition for deleting duplicate tests.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • More isolation speeds feedback but increases fake-real drift; more fidelity catches integration risk but costs time and determinism.
  • State assertions survive refactors; interaction assertions are useful for effect cardinality but become brittle when overused.
  • Virtual time is fast but does not reproduce thread races or blocking; add stress/device tests when risk warrants them.
  • Golden diffs catch pixels, but environmental churn can normalize blind approval.
  • A large E2E smoke gives broad wiring confidence but poor failure localization and combinatorial coverage.

Production flaky-test / CI scenario#

A checkout Compose test fails 3% only on shard 4: after tapping it expects “Paid,” and retry makes the pipeline green. Artifacts show advanceUntilIdle() on the test scheduler, while the repository hard-codes Dispatchers.IO; the MockWebServer response, DB invalidation, and animation live outside the controlled clock. A previous test also leaves a singleton session and reuses the DB file. The team quarantines with owner/expiry, captures seed/order/logcat/video/network requests, injects shared dispatchers and a per-test file, resets the graph, starts the hot Flow collector before the trigger, waits for domain state, and controls animation with the manual Compose clock. Repeated randomized-order runs pass without retries; a narrow device smoke confirms real Room/Compose wiring.

Code-review / debugging trap#

@Test fun paid() = runTest {
  every { repo.pay() } returns flowOf(Paid)
  vm.pay(); advanceUntilIdle()
  verify(exactly = 1) { repo.pay() }
}

The test proves only a configured mock interaction: it does not collect state, check cancellation/error, necessarily control the ViewModel Main dispatcher, or test serialization/DB/UI. The review trap is to add relaxed mocks and global advanceUntilIdle(). First state the user-visible contract, inject a shared scheduler, use a contract-preserving fake, and assert pre/post state with runCurrent(); separately test MockWebServer + Room integration and a small Compose surface. Debug in order: reproduce seed/order → identify uncontrolled boundary → inspect owner/scheduler/subscription → collect artifacts → fix the cause rather than increasing sleep/retry.

Likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: Pyramid or trophy? A: They are heuristics; risk, feedback speed, and fidelity determine the portfolio, not a percentage quota.
  2. Q: Fake or mock? A: Use a fake for stateful behavior and a mock for a narrow interaction contract; both must preserve relevant behavior.
  3. Q: What does runTest virtualize? A: Delays on participating TestDispatchers with a shared scheduler, not real threads or I/O.
  4. Q: Standard versus Unconfined? A: Standard queues work for explicit scheduling; Unconfined enters eagerly and gives no post-suspension order guarantee.
  5. Q: How do you test a hot Flow? A: Start a background collector before emit, synchronize readiness, account for replay/conflation, and terminate collection.
  6. Q: Is in-memory Room enough? A: Often for DAO logic; not for migration, disk, WAL, or process fidelity, which need a file-backed DB.
  7. Q: What does MockWebServer prove? A: Real HTTP-client behavior against scripted transport, not production backend correctness.
  8. Q: Why is Compose waitForIdle insufficient? A: It does not wait for arbitrary external async without an idling integration or controlled source.
  9. Q: What do you do with a flaky test? A: Preserve artifacts, classify, quarantine with owner/expiry, and fix determinism; retries only expose a signal.
  10. Q: Does 90% coverage imply confidence? A: No; meaningful oracles, risk coverage, boundary fidelity, and sometimes mutation testing matter.

Follow-up prompts#

  1. Build a test portfolio for offline checkout using Room, Paging, and a payment API.
  2. Find the race in a StateFlow test that passes only with UnconfinedTestDispatcher.
  3. Design migration, DAO, and contract tests for a breaking server-field change.
  4. Propose a quarantine SLA and artifact bundle for a 2% Compose flake.

Unanswered self-checks#

  1. What are your feature’s three costliest escaped risks, and the smallest faithful boundary for each?
  2. Which fake in your suite might violate ordering, cancellation, or persistence contracts?
  3. Which tests depend on wall clock, global state, order, port, device locale, or a hidden dispatcher?
  4. Which failure artifact would let you reproduce your most common CI flake locally?

English answer skeletons#

30-second answer

“I build a risk-based portfolio, not a fixed pyramid quota. Pure policies get fast JVM tests; adapters get integration and contract tests; Android and critical journeys get a small number of Robolectric, device, UI, screenshot, accessibility, and performance tests. I inject clocks, dispatchers, scopes, IDs, storage, and network boundaries, assert observable state, and use interaction checks only for real command contracts. Virtual time, mocks, coverage, screenshots, retries, and E2E each have explicit non-guarantees.”

2-minute answer

“I start with failure impact and choose the cheapest boundary that preserves the risk. Use cases and ViewModels mostly run on the JVM; repositories combine contract-preserving fakes with Room and MockWebServer integration tests. File-backed migration tests cover schema and data preservation, while PagingSource and RemoteMediator tests script refresh, append, errors, retries, and keys. For coroutines I use runTest with one shared TestCoroutineScheduler, StandardTestDispatcher for explicit causality, backgroundScope for intentional infinite collectors, and injected Main/IO dispatchers. I subscribe to hot Flows before emitting and use first, finite toList, or Turbine deliberately. Compose tests target user-facing semantics, control clocks, and do not confuse Compose idleness with external completion. Hilt replaces only the required boundary. CI records seeds, order, device and failure artifacts; quarantine has an owner and expiry, and retries remain a flake signal. Coverage is not confidence, screenshots are environment-specific, and a few E2E tests cannot cover combinations.”

Senior Android reliability and observabilityexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should define reliability through successful user journeys, design mobile SLI/SLO and error-budget policies, distinguish client, backend, and network failure, build bounded recovery and degradation, and lead an incident from signal to evidence-backed learning. The goal is actionable production ownership; Stage 24 keeps deep memory/thread diagnostics, while Stage 25 keeps detailed performance optimization.

Senior reliability mental model#

Reliability is a property of a user journey, not just an app process. “Open item → pay → see confirmation” crosses a UI state machine, local storage, OS/runtime, radio/DNS/TLS, API, dependencies, and asynchronous processing. For each journey, define the expected outcome, deadline, permitted freshness, and durable checkpoint; then instrument boundaries so a symptom can be separated from a component cause.

intent → client validation/state → cache/queue → network edge → backend/dependency
       ↘ release/build/device/OS/network cohorts ↗
SLI/SLO + traces/events/crash reports → alert → runbook → owner

Reliability topology and attribution#

  • Availability: whether a journey can complete by its deadline; a live app process is insufficient.
  • Correctness: the right result and state transition; a no-crash session is not a correct session.
  • Durability: an acknowledged write survives process, device, and server failures.
  • Freshness: how far data trails authoritative state; an available stale cache may violate the product contract.

Attribution needs phase timings and typed outcomes: client policy/validation, local DB/disk, queue delay, DNS/connect/TLS, request/upload, server time, HTTP/domain response, parse/apply. “Network error” is not a root cause. For a multi-hop journey, retain a stable operation ID/idempotency key and accepted server correlation/trace ID, but do not infer causality from a matching ID.

SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets for mobile#

An SLI is a measured fraction of good events or a latency distribution; an SLO is an internal target over a window; an SLA is an external agreement with consequences. Example: “99.5% of eligible checkout attempts become confirmed or safely pending within 10 seconds over 28 days,” separate from crash-free sessions. Define denominator, eligibility, duplicate attempts, offline semantics, clock source, and late upload.

Error budget = 1 − SLO. A budget policy connects burn to action: freeze a risky rollout, allocate reliability capacity, or permit experiments. Use short- and long-window burn-rate awareness for fast and slow incidents, while remembering mobile telemetry can be delayed, sampled, or lost. An SLO does not guarantee every session and does not replace a correctness invariant.

Structured error taxonomy and domain errors#

Do not expose raw exceptions or strings to UI. Map evidence into stable domain outcomes such as InvalidInput, Unauthenticated, Forbidden, Conflict, RateLimited(retryAfter), Unavailable(retryable), Timeout(phase), Offline, Stale, CorruptLocalData, and Unknown. Preserve the cause chain for diagnostics, but let UI policy choose retry, fallback, and message from domain semantics. Distinguish an expected handled failure, a handled exception, a recorded non-fatal, and an uncaught crash: telemetry classification does not change the business outcome.

Retries, isolation and overload controls#

  • Retry: only a transient, replayable operation, with bounded attempts/deadline, exponential backoff, full/decorrelated jitter, server Retry-After, and cancellation. Retries can amplify incidents and duplicate effects; mutations require server-side idempotency/deduplication because a timeout does not prove non-commit.
  • Circuit breaker: locally fast-fails an unhealthy dependency and probes half-open. A client-side circuit breaker does not protect all clients globally; process restart clears in-memory state and stale cohorts may keep loading the service.
  • Bulkhead: separate dispatcher/semaphore/queue budgets for critical and optional work; an unbounded queue merely postpones failure.
  • Rate limit: client debounce or token bucket improves UX, but authoritative global enforcement belongs on the server; respect retry-after, background constraints, and synchronized reconnect storms.

Graceful degradation, offline and fallbacks#

Expose capability, freshness, and pending state. A read may show a timestamped cache and refresh action; a write may use a durable outbox with an idempotency key or be honestly blocked; optional recommendations can disappear, but a checkout invariant cannot. A fallback must be semantically safe, bounded, and observable. Do not relabel stale or partial data as success; reconciliation after reconnect resolves duplicates and conflicts.

Mobile health signals and Android vitals#

  • Startup: cold/warm/hot and time to initial/full display; segment process state and entry path.
  • Stability: user-perceived crash/ANR rates, crash-free users/sessions, and handled/non-fatal outcomes.
  • Rendering: slow/janky frames and frozen frames; an aggregate may conceal one screen or cohort. Detailed tuning belongs in Stage 25.
  • Efficiency/network: battery/background wakeups, excessive partial wake locks, bytes/latency/failure by phase, cache hits, and offline queue age—in journey context, not as vanity totals.

Android vitals in Play Console has its own definitions, thresholds, eligible populations, reporting delays, and dimensions; they change with Android and Play Console versions. Compare release, app version/build, device model/class, OS/API, country/region, and network type only in sufficiently large cohorts. ANR rate aggregates can hide cohorts.

Crashes, ANRs, native failures and OOM#

A crash is an uncaught Java/Kotlin exception or native signal that terminates the process; a handled exception is not a crash, and a recorded non-fatal is a best-effort diagnostic event. Crashlytics/nonfatal capture is best effort: SDK initialization, consent, local persistence, a later launch/network, quotas/sampling/grouping affect delivery. A stack trace alone is not root cause: attach state transition, breadcrumbs, release, device, recent config, correlation, and reproduction evidence.

An ANR means the app failed a platform-defined responsiveness condition: input dispatch timeout, timed broadcast receiver, executing service, or content-provider interaction; exact categories, timeouts, and reporting can depend on Android version and foreground/background context. Frequent mechanisms include blocking I/O, lock, or binder work on main; lock inversion; expensive startup; and main-queue starvation. One captured stack may be a late symptom; correlate traces, locks, binder, lifecycle, and cohort.

A tombstone contains native crash signal, registers, and backtraces, but symbolication needs the exact native symbols/build. Java OutOfMemoryError, low-memory-killer/process reclaim, and native allocator failure are different; process death may have no catchable exception or crash report. Android vitals and Crashlytics are not a complete census of every OOM or kill. Deep heap/thread/native diagnostics belong in Stage 24.

Logs, metrics, traces, events and crash reports#

  • Logs/events: discrete facts with timestamp, schema, and context; logs are events, not metrics.
  • Metrics: counters, gauges, and histograms for rates/distributions with bounded dimensions; never use a user or request ID as a label.
  • Traces: causal execution spans and propagation context; sampling leaves gaps.
  • Crash reports: exception/signal, stack, threads, and attached context; grouping may split or merge issues.
  • Breadcrumbs: a bounded, redacted trail of meaningful transitions, not a verbose input dump.

A correlation ID helps join evidence but not causality. Trace context should propagate through HTTP and queues, but client-generated fields must not be trusted blindly. Standardize event schemas, monotonic duration for local intervals, server timestamps/checkpoints for distributed ordering, sampling metadata, and telemetry-health counters.

Privacy, cardinality and cohort design#

Before collection, create a data inventory: purpose, legal/consent basis, minimization, access, retention/deletion, and vendor transfer. Never log auth tokens, secrets, raw headers, passwords, full URLs with queries, user text, or stable identifiers without a justified need; redaction should be allowlist/schema based and cover messages, exceptions, breadcrumbs, and network metadata. Consent may require collection/upload disablement and a deletion workflow.

Segment release/build/version/device/OS/network with curated buckets and top-N/other. High-cardinality labels such as user ID, request ID, stack text, and URL belong in searchable events/traces, not metric dimensions. Sampling controls cost but creates bias; rare severe events may use tail/head rules, yet telemetry absence is not evidence of health.

Alerting, dashboards and runbooks#

Page on a user symptom or SLO burn with sufficient volume. Cause signals such as CPU, 5xx, and SDK failures aid diagnosis but should not create an alert storm. Combine threshold, rate of change, and multi-window burn; deduplicate by incident/release/cohort and define cooldown and escalation. A dashboard starts with journey success, latency, and freshness, then release/cohort, client phases, backend dependencies, and telemetry health.

A runbook needs an owner/on-call, impact query, known-good baseline, cohort cuts, recent release/config/backend changes, safe mitigations, flag/rollback caveats, verification queries, escalation/communication, and evidence retention. An alert without a concrete owner and permitted action is a backlog signal, not an actionable page.

Feature flags, remote config and release safety#

Every flag needs a typed local default, last-known-good cached value, safe parse/validation, owner, purpose, creation/expiry, and removal issue. Define behavior before fetch, on timeout/invalid payload, offline, process restart, SDK outage, and old app version. Targeting is not authorization. A kill path must disable the effect at a safe boundary and have a test and monitoring.

A feature flag is not an instant guaranteed kill switch due to cache, offline state, process lifetime, fetch interval, propagation, and app version. Real-time Remote Config reduces latency for supported clients but does not remove fallback behavior. A staged rollout/canary limits exposure but does not prove safety: its sample can be small or unrepresentative and telemetry delayed. App rollback is not instant and does not reverse server schema/data effects; backend APIs must remain backward/forward compatible with active old clients.

Incident lifecycle and evidence#

  1. Detect: validate the signal, telemetry-pipeline health, and user impact.
  2. Triage: build a timestamped timeline, first-bad release/config/backend change, cohorts, and reproduction attempts; do not confuse correlation with cause.
  3. Mitigate: stop rollout, use a safe flag, server throttling/fallback, or rollback; minimize harm rather than seeking a perfect root cause during the outage.
  4. Recover: verify the journey SLI plus backlog and reconciliation, not merely alert disappearance.
  5. Learn: run blameless causal analysis with contributing conditions, detection gaps, and owned actions with deadlines and verification.

Retain exact build, config snapshot, account/data preconditions, device/API/network, timestamps/time zones, request/operation IDs, and permitted screen recording, logcat, and system traces. Reproduction is strong evidence, but inability to reproduce does not disprove a field failure.

Initialization, clocks and telemetry loss#

Observability initialization should be early, bounded, and unable to break startup, but a crash before initialization creates a blind spot. An SDK may buffer locally and upload on a later launch; uninstall, storage pressure, process death, offline state, or consent still causes loss. Measure “SDK ready,” queue/drop count, and upload lag without making the SDK a single point of failure.

Client wall clocks can be wrong; offline upload separates occurrence time from ingestion time. Use a monotonic clock for durations, retain both timestamps and uncertainty, and use server receipt/version/checkpoint for distributed ordering. Sampling and delivery are non-guarantees, not a census.

Fault testing and actionable ownership#

In tests/staging and bounded production experiments, inject timeout, disconnect, 429/5xx, malformed/partial payload, slow disk, full queue, process death, stale config, and dependency latency. Verify bounded retry plus jitter, idempotency, fallback semantics, recovery/reconciliation, alert, and runbook. Chaos awareness does not mean uncontrolled blast radius: require a hypothesis, guardrails, abort, owner, and evidence.

For every SLI, alert, flag, and runbook, name one accountable team, responding role, dependency escalation, and action deadline. “Shared mobile/backend” without decision rights is not ownership.

Guarantees and non-guarantees#

  • A no-crash session is not a correct session; an SLO does not guarantee every session.
  • Telemetry absence is not evidence of health; Crashlytics/nonfatal capture is best effort.
  • A stack trace alone is not root cause; a correlation ID joins evidence, not causality.
  • A client-side circuit breaker does not protect all clients globally.
  • Retries can amplify incidents and duplicate effects.
  • A feature flag is not an instant guaranteed kill switch; staged rollout limits exposure but does not prove safety.
  • ANR rate aggregates can hide cohorts; logs are events, not metrics.

Version- and vendor-sensitive guidance#

Re-check at release time: Android ANR definitions, timeouts, and background rules; Play Android vitals metrics, thresholds, eligible population, and dimensions; OS/OEM process and battery behavior; Firebase SDK initialization, consent, persistence, grouping, and non-fatal limits; Remote Config fetch, real-time, and version behavior; OpenTelemetry Android instrumentation maturity, semantic conventions, and exporter support; and Play staged-rollout controls. Record SDK/plugin/app versions in the runbook. A vendor-dashboard definition is not a universal platform contract.

Decision framework#

  1. Choose a critical journey and its correctness, durability, and freshness contract.
  2. Write the SLI event, denominator, deadline, cohorts, window, and SLO/error-budget action.
  3. Draw failure boundaries and a stable domain taxonomy.
  4. Add minimal metrics plus sampled traces/events plus crash/ANR evidence, a privacy policy, and telemetry-health signal.
  5. For each failure class, choose fail, bounded retry, fallback/cache/offline queue, circuit, bulkhead, or rate limit.
  6. Connect alert → dashboard → runbook → owner → tested mitigation/rollback, and revise after incidents.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • More telemetry aids diagnosis but raises privacy, battery, network, storage, and cost risk.
  • Aggressive retry improves local success during a short glitch but can cause retry storms and duplicate side effects.
  • Cache and offline support improve availability but complicate freshness, conflicts, and truthful UX.
  • Fine cohorts find regressions, but small denominators are noisy, cardinality is expensive, and deanonymization risk rises.
  • Flags accelerate mitigation but add combinatorial states, stale config, and cleanup debt.
  • Crash/ANR rate can improve because usage or telemetry fell; inspect journey denominator and pipeline health.

Production incident scenario#

After a 10% rollout, checkout burns its SLO quickly only on Android 14 and one device cohort. Crash rate is normal, non-fatal timeout events rise, and global backend 5xx is normal. On-call halts rollout, checks telemetry ingestion, and splits phase metrics: TLS and server latency are normal, but local request-queue age grows after a Remote Config experiment. Correlation IDs join client spans to server requests but do not prove cause. Reproduction with the exact build/config reveals a semaphore permit leak on cancellation. Cached flags mean disablement is not instant; the server temporarily reduces optional fan-out, the app release rolls back, and active old clients remain compatible. Recovery verifies the checkout journey, queue drain, and affected cohort. The postmortem adds an invariant test, flag expiry, queue-saturation alert, and owner.

Code-review/debug trap#

suspend fun submit(order: Order): Result<Receipt> = runCatching {
    retry(5) { api.charge(order) } // fixed delay, no idempotency/deadline
}.onFailure { crashlytics.recordException(it) }
 // “No Crashlytics issue” => healthy

The trap catches cancellation, retries an unsafe mutation, may produce six charges, lacks jitter/deadline/Retry-After, conflates domain failure with exception, may send PII through Order.toString(), and treats best-effort non-fatal reporting as a census. Review should require a stable idempotency key, retry classification/budget, cancellation propagation, a redacted structured event, journey outcome metric, offline/unknown-commit UX, and fault-injection tests.

Likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: How do you define a mobile SLO? A: Start with a user journey: eligible attempts, good outcome, deadline/freshness, rolling window, cohorts, and error-budget action; crash-free rate is only one signal.
  2. Q: How does availability differ from correctness? A: A journey can finish without a crash yet produce a wrong, duplicate, or stale result; measure both contracts.
  3. Q: When is a retry safe? A: For a classified transient replayable operation with budget, backoff, and jitter; mutations need server idempotency and unknown-commit reconciliation.
  4. Q: What does a correlation ID provide? A: It joins client and server evidence for one operation; it proves neither causality nor correctness.
  5. Q: Crash, non-fatal, and handled failure? A: An uncaught crash terminates the process; a non-fatal is an explicit best-effort report; a handled domain failure may not be an exception.
  6. Q: How do you triage an ANR? A: Identify type, cohort, and version; inspect main-thread, locks, binder, and timeline; one stack and aggregate rate are insufficient.
  7. Q: How do you prevent metric-cardinality explosion? A: Use bounded release/device/OS/network buckets as labels; keep request/user/URL IDs in retained, sampled events or traces.
  8. Q: Why is a flag not a guaranteed kill switch? A: Offline/cache/fetch interval/process/version/targeting can delay or prevent activation; require safe defaults and server mitigation.
  9. Q: What belongs in a reliability runbook? A: Owner, impact/cohort queries, recent changes, safe mitigations, verification, escalation, communication, and evidence.
  10. Q: How do you test resilience? A: Controlled fault injection for timeout/429/5xx/offline/process death/stale config, asserting bounded load, semantics, recovery, alerts, and privacy.

Follow-up prompts#

  1. Design a checkout SLI, SLO, and burn-rate alert with delayed mobile telemetry.
  2. Compare retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, and server rate limit for a reconnect storm.
  3. Describe a safe Remote Config rollout with old app versions and offline clients.
  4. Build an incident timeline for a cohort-only ANR regression.

Unanswered self-checks#

  1. Which denominator and eligibility rules would you choose for an offline-first sync SLI?
  2. How would you distinguish real recovery from telemetry upload failure?
  3. What safe state should an unknown-commit payment have after process death?
  4. Who may halt rollout, and how is the mitigation verified?

English answer skeletons#

30-second answer

“I define reliability around a user journey, not process uptime. I specify correctness, durability and freshness, then a measurable SLI/SLO with an error-budget action. I instrument bounded client phases and domain outcomes, segment by release and coarse device/OS/network cohorts, and correlate them with backend evidence. Recovery is policy-driven: safe retries require jitter, budgets and idempotency; otherwise degrade honestly. Alerts lead to an owned runbook, while telemetry, flags and staged rollout are all explicitly best effort.”

2-minute answer

“First I choose a critical journey and define a good event, eligible denominator, deadline, freshness and durable checkpoint. Availability is separate from correctness: a crash-free checkout can still duplicate a charge or show stale confirmation. I map each boundary—client state, storage, network phases, backend and dependencies—to structured domain outcomes. Metrics show rates and distributions; sampled traces and redacted events provide context; crash and ANR reports add stacks and threads. Correlation IDs join evidence but do not prove cause, and telemetry loss, clock skew and crash-before-init are measured blind spots. For transient replayable work I use bounded exponential backoff with jitter; mutations need server idempotency. Circuit breakers and bulkheads isolate locally but cannot protect the whole fleet. Cache and offline queues expose freshness and pending state. Alerts use journey symptoms and burn-rate awareness, then an owned dashboard and runbook. Flags have typed defaults, cached-value behavior, owners and expiry; they are not instant kill switches. Staged rollout limits exposure but delayed, biased telemetry cannot prove safety. During an incident I detect, triage by release/cohort, mitigate, verify journey recovery and reconciliation, then produce evidence-backed actions.”

Android memory and threadingexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should explain Android memory from the Linux process to the ART object graph, find a retention path instead of guessing from an OOM stack, design lifecycle-safe resource and cache ownership, and prove concurrent-state correctness with the Java Memory Model (JMM), structured concurrency, and confinement. The goal is to separate symptom from root cause and state guarantees precisely; detailed startup and rendering optimization remains in Stage 25.

Senior mental model and topology#

Linux process address space / RSS / PSS
├─ managed ART heap: objects → references → GC roots
├─ native heap/JNI allocations and explicitly owned resources
├─ code/JIT/AOT, stacks, mmap/shared pages, ashmem/shared memory
└─ graphics: decoded pixels, GPU/driver buffers, hardware bitmaps

producer/callback → execution context → owned mutable state → resource/lifecycle
main Looper → MessageQueue → Handler; Binder pool → callback; coroutines → dispatcher/context

Do not reduce memory to the Java heap: process footprint includes managed and native heaps, thread stacks, code, graphics, and mapped/shared pages; RSS double-counts shared pages across processes while PSS apportions them. Do not reduce threading to “use a background thread”: identify state owner, permitted execution contexts, ordering, cancellation, and resource boundary.

Android/Linux process memory model#

  • Managed heap: Kotlin/Java objects traced by ART from GC roots.
  • Native heap: C/C++/JNI and native library parts; GC does not understand arbitrary native ownership.
  • Code, stacks, mappings: DEX/OAT/JIT code, libraries, per-thread stacks, and file-backed mmap. Shared or clean pages can be reclaimed and are not automatically a private leak.
  • Graphics/shared memory: decoded pixels, hardware buffers, GPU/driver allocations, and ashmem/shared-memory regions; placement and accounting changed across Android versions.

Inspect trends and categories with Memory Profiler and dumpsys meminfo, interpreting RSS, PSS, and private dirty against process state, workload, and device. Memory pressure is system-wide scarcity and reclaim; managed/native OOM is an allocation failure in a particular budget/address space; LMK can terminate a less important process with no catchable OOM.

ART allocation, generations, roots and reachability#

Allocation is often a cheap bump-pointer or thread-local path; cost appears through zeroing, large objects, promotion, collection, and pause/concurrent work. Modern ART applies generational assumptions and multiple collectors/spaces, but collector implementation, thresholds, compaction, and accounting vary by runtime, OS, and device. Never build application policy around one collector.

GC starts at roots—thread stacks/registers, static fields, JNI globals, and runtime references—and traces the strong-reachable graph. Unreachable managed objects become eligible for reclamation, with no prompt-timing guarantee. An Activity reachable through static registry → callback is a logical retention leak while GC behaves correctly. A native allocation whose required close/free is lost is a true native/resource leak; its managed wrapper may remain reachable or already be reclaimed.

Strong, weak, soft and phantom references#

  • Strong: an ordinary reference maintains reachability.
  • WeakReference: the referent may disappear after GC; get() can become null once strong reachability is lost. A weak reference does not guarantee availability and is not lifecycle design.
  • SoftReference: a pressure-sensitive heuristic, not deterministic cache policy; Android caches need explicit size and eviction.
  • PhantomReference + ReferenceQueue: post-mortem notification/cleanup coordination without access to the referent; not a substitute for deterministic close().

A weak listener can sometimes limit retention, but it may silently disappear, obscures ownership, and does not guarantee unregister. The lifecycle owner should explicitly subscribe/unsubscribe or collect in a lifecycle-bound scope.

Common Android retention paths#

  • A static, singleton, or cache holds an Activity, Fragment, View, or short-lived Context instead of application Context or a value.
  • A listener, callback, observer, BroadcastReceiver, adapter, or registry is not unregistered.
  • A non-static inner Handler, Runnable, or queued Message captures a screen; delayed work outlives destruction.
  • A Fragment outlives its View while binding, adapter, listener, or animator keeps the old tree.
  • A coroutine/Flow collector has a longer scope than UI; a hot upstream, callbackFlow cleanup bug, or hidden repository scope keeps working.
  • Compose remember retains an object while the composition lives; a wrong key, missing onDispose, stale Activity/View capture, or app-wide holder extends ownership.

remember is neither process persistence nor a lifecycle cleanup API. Use a correctly keyed DisposableEffect for registration, rememberUpdatedState for a current callback without restart, and lifecycle-aware collection when visibility is the contract.

Lifecycle cleanup and resource ownership#

private var _binding: FragmentOrdersBinding? = null
private val binding get() = checkNotNull(_binding)

override fun onCreateView(...): View =
    FragmentOrdersBinding.inflate(inflater, container, false).also { _binding = it }.root

override fun onDestroyView() {
    binding.recycler.adapter = null
    _binding = null
    super.onDestroyView()
}

A Fragment lifecycle is longer than its view lifecycle, so create ViewBinding in onCreateView, clear it in onDestroyView, and never access it afterward. Symmetrically own registration tokens, Cursor, streams, ParcelFileDescriptor, OkHttp Response/body, and JNI handles via use, try-finally, or Closeable. Finalization is deprecated/unreliable; Cleaner or phantom cleanup is a nondeterministically timed safety net, not a resource protocol.

Caches, LruCache and bitmap memory#

A cache needs a contract: source of truth, key/value cost, maximum budget, hit target, staleness, eviction, invalidation, concurrency, and pressure response. Size LruCache with sizeOf() in bytes, not item count; choose the cap from a measured device/process budget rather than one fixed heap percentage. Eviction must not break correctness, and other strong owners can keep an evicted value alive.

Bitmap cost is approximately width × height × bytes per pixel after decode, not compressed file size. Decode near target dimensions, choose config with an explicit quality trade-off, and avoid duplicate transformations. Pixel placement changed across releases; hardware bitmaps keep pixels in graphics memory, are immutable, and have API/Canvas/readback restrictions. Manual recycle() is mainly legacy/old-API ownership and dangerous under sharing; modern code releases references/resources rather than recycling blindly. Re-check current Android and image-library semantics.

Large objects, churn, boxing and collections#

One large allocation can fail despite an acceptable average; a large bitmap or array raises fragmentation and GC pressure. Churn in a frame/data loop creates frequent collections through temporary lambdas/iterators, string concatenation, parsing, and copies. Nullable/generic primitives, collections, and interfaces can box values; object-heavy maps/lists add headers and references. Profile allocation rate and retained graph first. Primitive arrays, reuse, or pooling belong only in a measured hotspot because pools retain worst-case memory and complicate ownership.

Low-memory signals, process death and OOM#

onTrimMemory(level) is a hint to release reducible caches/resources, not a promise or pre-kill callback. On devices running Android 14 (API 34)+, the system delivers only TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN and TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND; the RUNNING_*, MODERATE, and COMPLETE levels are no longer sent (deprecated in API 35), and onLowMemory() is never called. Treat trim callbacks as hints. onTrimMemory may not arrive before kill, and the low-memory killer can reclaim the process, so state restoration and durable work must tolerate process death without any callback.

An OOM allocation stack is where the next allocation failed, not necessarily the root cause; accumulation may have happened earlier in another feature, native buffer, or cache. Triage LMK/process death, managed OOM, native allocator failure, and address-space exhaustion separately.

Evidence-driven memory profiling#

  1. Record a reproducible journey, build/device/API, and a settled baseline; forced GC is only an experimental control.
  2. Compare category trends, allocation rate, and retained instances after navigation. Allocation tracking explains churn, not automatically a leak.
  3. A heap dump is a snapshot: find classes/instances, shallow versus retained size, dominator tree, and shortest strong path to a GC root. Retained size needs context because shared dominators and snapshot timing can mislead.
  4. Repeat create/destroy cycles; inspect native/graphics counters/tools when Java heap is stable.
  5. LeakCanary watches objects expected to die and heuristically analyzes heap paths. LeakCanary detects retained objects heuristically, not all leaks; confirm ownership and impact.

Looper, Binder and callback execution contexts#

The main thread has a Looper that sequentially dequeues work from a MessageQueue; a Handler posts to a specific Looper. Queue order does not make background data safe, and a delayed message can retain captures. Choreographer conceptually coordinates frame callbacks with display deadlines; Stage 25 covers rendering depth. Never block main on I/O, locks, Binder, or CPU work.

A Binder entry may execute on a Binder thread-pool thread; a library callback can use main, an executor, Binder, or an arbitrary thread according to its contract. Never assume affinity—normalize onto an owned executor/dispatcher before touching mutable or UI state. A service callback into an Activity needs a lifecycle check and main dispatch for UI.

JMM: visibility, atomicity, order and happens-before#

  • A data race permits stale or inconsistent observation even when it “usually works.”
  • A volatile read/write provides visibility and ordering for that variable, but count++ and check-then-act are not atomic.
  • A synchronized unlock happens-before a later lock of the same monitor; every field in the invariant needs the same protocol.
  • Atomic* provides atomic operations/CAS for its own state; atomics do not make a multi-variable invariant atomic.
  • An immutable snapshot safely published via lock, volatile, atomic, or channel reduces shared mutation; val is not deep immutability.

A thread-safe collection makes individual operations safe, but if (!map.containsKey(k)) map[k] = v races. Use an atomic compound API such as computeIfAbsent, a lock, or one state owner.

Races, deadlock, liveness and confinement#

A race depends on interleaving; check-then-act can duplicate a payment or request. Deadlock is cyclic waiting—use global lock ordering and avoid unknown code under a lock. Livelock retries actively without progress—bound and randomize backoff. Starvation denies a task resources; fairness and queue bounds matter. Priority inversion makes high-priority work wait for a low-priority lock owner. Prefer thread/state confinement: one owner serially applies messages and publishes immutable snapshots.

Coroutines, dispatchers and structured ownership#

suspend means a coroutine may suspend, not that implementation is off-main or non-blocking. A dispatcher is scheduling policy/context, not guaranteed permanent physical thread identity; the thread may change across suspension. withContext creates a structured context boundary. Switching off Main prevents UI blocking only if downstream does not block shared resources, locks, or pools needed by Main.

limitedParallelism(n) is a version-sensitive dispatcher view limiting tasks executing in parallel, not the number of suspended coroutines and not necessarily a separate pool/thread. A thread-affine native API needs explicit single-thread owner/executor semantics, not an accidental identity assumption.

Prefer caller-owned scope: a repository exposes suspend/Flow, and its caller decides lifecycle. UI work belongs to viewModelScope or view lifecycle scope. App-long work requires an explicit application owner or durable WorkManager contract, not a hidden scope or fire-and-forget.

Cancellation, Mutex, channels and blocking boundaries#

Cancellation is cooperative: cancellable suspension/checks respond, while a non-cooperative blocking or JNI call can continue, and cancellation does not undo committed effects. Preserve CancellationException: catch specific failures or rethrow cancellation; put cleanup in finally, with bounded NonCancellable only when cleanup must suspend.

synchronized/ReentrantLock blocks an OS thread, and its critical section must not suspend. Coroutine Mutex suspends a waiter but gives no thread affinity; do not hold it across slow I/O/callbacks or assume reentrancy. Channels/actors serialize commands and centralize ownership; define capacity, overflow, shutdown, and failure policy. runBlocking blocks its caller: reserve it for genuine blocking boundaries or tests; on main or a pool worker it risks ANR, starvation, and deadlock.

StrictMode and diagnostic limits#

StrictMode can flag accidental disk/network/main-thread work and selected resource/lifecycle violations under configured policies, but StrictMode is detection, not proof: it is best effort, not a security boundary, misses some JNI/library work, and a quiet run proves neither responsiveness nor thread safety. Combine traces, thread dumps, lock ownership, queue/pool saturation, reproducible schedules/tests, and production evidence.

Guarantees and non-guarantees#

  • GC eventually reclaims unreachable managed objects; it does not reclaim reachable leaks or arbitrary native resources promptly.
  • A weak reference guarantees neither availability nor lifecycle cleanup; soft/phantom references do not replace a bounded cache or close.
  • onTrimMemory may not arrive before kill; process death is a normal boundary.
  • volatile gives visibility/order for a variable, not compound atomicity; atomics do not make a multi-variable invariant atomic.
  • synchronized establishes happens-before for the same monitor.
  • Coroutine confinement depends on dispatcher/context design; a dispatcher does not promise one physical thread.
  • Cancellation does not stop non-cooperative blocking code or undo effects.
  • StrictMode is a detector, not proof; a heap dump is a snapshot; LeakCanary is a heuristic retained-object detector.
  • The OOM allocation site may not be the root cause.

Version-sensitive guidance#

At release time, re-check ART collector/heap behavior on the Android/API/OEM cohort; bitmap pixel accounting, hardware bitmap restrictions, and image-library version; ComponentCallbacks2/onTrimMemory delivery, especially on devices running API 34+; Memory Profiler/heap-dump format; lifecycle/Compose APIs; kotlinx.coroutines version for limitedParallelism, cancellation, and dispatchers; and Cleaner/finalization availability. Follow current runtime contracts, not Dalvik folklore or old recycle() rules.

Decision framework#

  1. Classify the symptom: retained managed graph, native/graphics growth, allocation churn, pressure/LMK, main stall, or data race.
  2. Name owner, lifetime, release point, execution context, and invariant for every object/resource/state.
  3. Choose a deterministic lifecycle/resource protocol; give caches byte budgets/eviction; choose confinement, immutable snapshot, lock/atomic, or actor for concurrency.
  4. Write the required happens-before and cancellation/effect semantics; never assume callback thread.
  5. Collect evidence: repeatable scenario, category trend, heap/root path, or thread/lock timeline; compare cohorts and versions.
  6. Fix the earliest wrong ownership edge, add regression test/monitoring, and verify both symptom and contract improve.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A larger cache raises hit rate but adds pressure/retention; aggressive eviction adds decode/network churn.
  • Pooling reduces allocation only in a measured hotspot but retains worst-case capacity and creates stale-state bugs.
  • A coarse lock is simple and correct but increases contention/priority inversion; fine locks scale but add deadlock/invariant risk.
  • Atomics suit independent state; a complex CAS invariant becomes unreadable, where a lock or actor may be safer.
  • Unbounded channels/executors disguise backpressure as memory growth; tiny bounds can drop critical work.
  • Moving work off Main can move blockage into a shared DB/connection pool and stall Main through dependencies.

Production leak/race scenario#

After several checkout rotations, memory rises and submit occasionally runs twice. A heap dump shows a destroyed Fragment View dominating a RecyclerView with path singleton analytics registry → listener lambda → Fragment binding. Meanwhile a Binder callback and main click perform if (!submitted) { submitted = true; charge() }; submitted is volatile, but the compound action is not atomic. The OOM stack in bitmap decode is a symptom because retained old screens keep their images. Fix: unregister the token in onDestroyView, clear binding/adapter, pass an application-safe analytics value, and collect in the caller-owned view lifecycle; serialize submit commands under one ViewModel owner/Mutex around the state transition, while server idempotency protects the effect. Repeated-rotation heap comparison and a concurrent-submit test verify the contracts; LeakCanary is evidence, not complete proof.

Code-review/debug trap#

object Repo {
    private var loaded = false
    fun attach(activity: Activity) {
        GlobalScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            if (!loaded) { loaded = true; client.execute().body!!.string() }
            Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).postDelayed({ activity.render() }, 30_000)
        }
    }
}

The singleton and delayed Runnable retain the Activity; hidden GlobalScope has no owner; blocking response is not closed; loaded races (volatile would not repair check-then-act); cancellation does not control the HTTP effect; render may run after destruction. Review should require caller-owned scope, a suspend/cancellable adapter, use for the response, one atomic state owner or Mutex, a lifecycle-safe value/callback, injected dispatchers, and an idempotent downstream operation.

Likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: Why does GC not collect a reachable Activity? A: GC correctly preserves every strongly reachable object; find its path from a GC root and repair owner/registration.
  2. Q: Managed retention versus native leak? A: The first is a reachable graph past its intended lifetime; the second loses timely free/close ownership and may be absent from the heap dump.
  3. Q: Why is WeakReference not lifecycle design? A: The referent can disappear nondeterministically, availability is not guaranteed, and unregister/close ownership stays implicit.
  4. Q: How do you size LruCache? A: Count bytes with sizeOf, measure working set and device budget, cap it, define eviction/invalidation, and respond to pressure.
  5. Q: How do you triage an OOM? A: Separate managed, native, graphics, and LMK; reproduce trends and inspect dominators/root paths because the allocation stack may be the victim.
  6. Q: What does volatile guarantee? A: Visibility/order for reads and writes of one variable, not atomic check-then-act or a multi-field invariant.
  7. Q: Atomics or a lock? A: Atomics for one simple state/CAS; a lock or actor for compound invariants, with documented happens-before and contention.
  8. Q: Does suspend mean off-main? A: No; implementation can block the current thread. A dispatcher is policy, and downstream shared resources can still block Main.
  9. Q: Mutex versus synchronized? A: Mutex suspends coroutine waiters with no affinity; synchronized blocks a thread and gives monitor happens-before. Never suspend inside a thread lock.
  10. Q: How do you find callback races? A: Record thread contracts, invariant, and happens-before; reproduce interleavings, centralize state ownership, and test duplicate/lost transitions.

Follow-up prompts#

  1. Compare heap dump, allocation tracking, and native/graphics counters for an image-screen OOM.
  2. Design a cache budget and trim policy without relying on a pre-kill callback.
  3. Prove happens-before for a UI snapshot flowing from a Binder callback to main.
  4. Redesign a multi-resource update with a lock, actor/channel, or immutable CAS state.

Unanswered self-checks#

  1. Which longest-lived owner can retain each screen callback in your architecture?
  2. Which native or Closeable resources have deterministic release on exception and cancellation?
  3. What exact happens-before edge protects your most important multi-thread invariant?
  4. Which signal distinguishes cache growth from a true leak and LMK pressure?

English answer skeletons#

30-second answer

“I split memory into managed, native, code, stack, graphics, and shared mappings, then distinguish reachable retention, native resource leaks, allocation churn, and system pressure. I use heap paths from GC roots and lifecycle ownership rather than blaming the OOM allocation site. For concurrency I name the state owner and required happens-before edge: confinement or immutable snapshots first, then a lock, atomic, or actor. Coroutines are structured and caller-owned; suspension is not automatically off-main, and cancellation is cooperative.”

2-minute answer

“I begin with process topology and evidence. ART reclaims unreachable managed objects, so a destroyed Activity retained from a static listener is an ownership leak, not a GC failure; arbitrary native resources still require deterministic close. I compare managed, native and graphics trends, then use allocation tracking for churn and a heap dump for dominators, retained size and paths to GC roots. A dump is only a snapshot and LeakCanary is heuristic. Caches have byte budgets, eviction and correctness rules; images decode near pixel size, while hardware and recycling behavior are version-sensitive. onTrimMemory is a hint and may never precede process death. For threading, I do not assume Binder or library callback threads. Under the JMM, volatile provides visibility for one variable, synchronized publishes through the same monitor, and atomics do not protect multi-field invariants. I prefer one state owner and immutable snapshots; otherwise I choose locks, Mutex or actors by whether blocking, suspension and compound invariants are involved. Suspend does not mean off-main, dispatchers do not promise permanent thread identity, cancellation cannot stop non-cooperative blocking code or undo effects, and repositories expose suspend/Flow to a caller-owned scope. Finally I reproduce the lifecycle or interleaving, fix the earliest wrong ownership edge, and verify both the contract and symptom.”
