Duplicates are upserted, gaps trigger HTTP backfill, late edits/deletes use versions and tombstones, and cursor expiry triggers full resync. Foreground may keep a justified socket; background relies on OS-compliant push and persistent catch-up, because FCM, WorkManager, connectivity callbacks and process survival have limited guarantees. Durable events are never conflated; presence and typing may be TTL/lossy. I define server-side authorization, token and account isolation, media and notification privacy, and conceptual E2EE key lifecycle without inventing crypto. Finally I instrument reconnects, outbox age, ACK latency, gaps, dedupe, sync lag and battery cost, and test deterministic duplicates, reorder, disconnect, token expiry, process death, network switch, migrations, contracts, load and chaos.”

Official references

  • Android Developers — Offline-first data layer; Data layer; Room
  • Android Developers — Background work; WorkManager; Doze and App Standby
  • Android Developers — Receive messages reliably; Firebase — Receive FCM messages; FCM delivery reporting; FCM token management
  • Android Developers — Security best practices; Notification permission
  • Kotlin — Flow; StateFlow API (official Kotlin library docs)
  • IETF RFC 6455 — WebSocket; WHATWG — Server-sent events (protocol/specification docs, not Android guarantees)
System design: payments and ordersexpand / collapse

Objective

Lead a payments/orders system-design interview from business requirements, invariants, and failure cost to state machines, recovery, and evidence—not provider SDK trivia. Stage 29 covers checkout, order, payment, fulfillment, and refund; deep Stage 30 auth, analytics, and feature-flag architecture is out of scope.

Senior mental model

A payment is not one API call but an external workflow with several authorities and irreversible effects. Separate transport receipt, provider acceptance, authorization, capture, settlement, fulfillment, and business success. Payment UI success is not durable order confirmation; webhook receipt is not necessarily settlement. Exactly-once end-to-end cannot be assumed. Start with boundaries, money invariants, legal transitions, and ambiguous recovery before selecting UI/provider mechanisms.

Requirements variables and constraints

  • Journeys: cart, quote, checkout, pay/challenge/redirect, order tracking, cancel, fulfillment, void, full/partial refund, dispute/chargeback.
  • Product: digital good/subscription, physical good, or service; guest/account; split shipment; delayed/partial capture only where provider/rail supports it; inventory and refund policy.
  • Variables: users U, checkouts/sec C, payment attempts/order A, amount/currency set M, inventory contention I, challenge/redirect share R, webhook delay/loss W, fulfillment duration F, refund/dispute window D, latency/availability targets L/S. Ask for distributions and legal/business constraints; do not invent fixed scale.
  • Semantics: when reservation, order, and entitlement become durable; who may retry/cancel/refund; meanings of authorization/capture/settlement; support and audit retention.

Domain and policy boundaries

Cart is mutable user intent; checkout is a server-revalidated quote/session; order is an immutable commercial snapshot plus lifecycle; payment is one or more money-movement attempts; fulfillment is shipment/service/entitlement; refund is a compensating financial workflow. One order may have several payment attempts, captures, fulfillments, and refunds. A refund does not instantly erase settlement or fulfillment effects; a shipped item or consumed entitlement needs separate business compensation.

For Play-distributed apps, the digital goods/services versus physical goods/services boundary is policy-, region-, program-, and version-sensitive. Do not hardcode an old rule: check the current Google Play Payments policy and current Play Billing guidance for the target distribution/region. Play Billing purchases require backend verification/acknowledgement handling and current official guidance. Physical goods/services usually follow a different payment flow, but policies and exceptions evolve.

Text architecture and data-flow diagram

Android UI → Checkout ViewModel → repository → Room projection (provisional)
                    │                  │
                    └── authenticated backend API ──┐
                                                   ↓
 cart/price/inventory → checkout/order service → payment orchestrator → provider/rail
            │                  │        │                    │
 reservation/expiry      order DB + transition ledger       challenge/3DS/browser
            │                  │        │                    │
 fulfillment ← durable outbox ┘        inbox ← verified webhooks
            ↑                           │
            └──── reconciliation/polling/status repair ─────┘

The client is never authority for amount, currency, price, tax, promotion, shipping, inventory, or order confirmation. The backend revalidates, authorizes principal/account, owns invariants, and holds provider credentials. Room is a recoverable UI projection; local optimistic order state is provisional.

Data model and immutable snapshots

Use Money(minorUnits:Int64,currency) or exact decimal semantics with explicit scale/rounding per currency/business rule; never binary floating point. Do not assume two decimal places for every currency. Store currency with value, rounding provenance, and component totals; backend checks sum(lines)+tax+shipping-discounts=orderTotal.

Core records: Cart; CheckoutQuote(id,version,expiresAt,totals); Order(id,accountId,state,stateVersion,snapshot,createdAt); immutable OrderLineSnapshot with product/price/tax/promo/shipping facts; InventoryReservation(id,sku,qty,expiresAt,state); PaymentAttempt(id,orderId,providerRef,state,stateVersion,amount,currency,reasonCode); Capture, Refund, Dispute; IdempotencyRecord(scope,key,payloadFingerprint,response,status,expiresAt,apiVersion); WebhookInbox(provider,eventId,receivedAt,payloadDigest,processedState); append-only TransitionLedger and durable Outbox. Server timestamps and versions are authoritative; clock/client timestamps are not authoritative.

Order state machine

DRAFT → QUOTED → PENDING_PAYMENT → CONFIRMED → FULFILLING → FULFILLED
  └──────────────→ CANCELLED        ↘ CANCEL_REQUESTED ↘ PARTIALLY_FULFILLED
CONFIRMED/FULFILLING/FULFILLED → RETURN_OR_REFUND_PENDING → PARTIALLY_REFUNDED/REFUNDED
                                       ↘ DISPUTED (separate case lifecycle)

Names are domain-specific, but a legal transition table needs source, event, target, guard, reason code, actor, state-machine version, and side effects. Mark terminal/nonterminal explicitly: CANCELLED may terminate fulfillment while a refund/dispute record remains active; PENDING_PAYMENT is nonterminal. Fulfillment is not inferred from payment alone: policy may require capture, fraud review, or inventory. Server CAS/version/transaction enforce transitions and invariants; a client reducer only projects.

Payment state machine

CREATED → REQUIRES_METHOD → REQUIRES_ACTION → PROCESSING
   ├→ DECLINED / CANCELLED / EXPIRED
   └→ AUTHORIZED → CAPTURE_PENDING → PARTIALLY_CAPTURED → CAPTURED → SETTLED
                     └→ VOIDED              └→ REFUND_PENDING → PARTIALLY_REFUNDED → REFUNDED
CAPTURED/SETTLED → DISPUTED → WON/LOST (conceptual provider/rail case)

Provider capabilities differ: authorization/capture may be immediate, delayed, partial, or unsupported; void generally addresses an uncaptured authorization while refund addresses a captured payment. Decline, cancellation, expiry, void, refund, and dispute use stable internal reason categories plus a redacted provider code. Do not invent universal provider transitions. HTTP 2xx is request-level success only; provider acceptance is not authorization, authorization is not capture, capture is not settlement, and none alone proves fulfillment/business success. Every server transition validates amount/currency, cumulative capture ≤ authorized, cumulative refund ≤ captured under agreed fee/rail semantics, version, and legal predecessor.

Checkout sequence

  1. Client requests checkout with cart version; backend authenticates account, reloads catalog facts, revalidates price/tax/promotion/shipping/inventory, reserves stock with expiry, and returns a versioned quote.
  2. On explicit user confirmation, client submits a stable business operation key plus quote/version. A backend transaction creates order snapshot, PENDING_PAYMENT, idempotency record, and durable outbox intent.
  3. Backend creates provider payment intent/session with server-held credentials and documented provider idempotency; hosted/provider UI or tokenization keeps raw card entry away from app/backend where feasible.
  4. Client presents provider UI. Browser/3DS/external app may kill/recreate process. Persist only a safe order/session reference; restore through backend status, never trust a UI callback.
  5. Backend verifies provider status/webhook, applies payment transition, commits order transition and outbox. Fulfillment consumes a durable confirmed-policy event, not a return URL.
  6. Client observes/polls backend order. Only durable backend state may show confirmed; receipt/support path exposes order ID, not secrets.

Redirect, process-death, and ambiguous recovery

A deep link/app link carries opaque correlation/state, not amount or authorization. Validate scheme/host/path, one-time nonce/state binding, account/session, expiry, and expected order; reject replay/tampering. A return URL is a hint only. After timeout, app death, browser/3DS/external-app redirect, or provider success with lost response, mark UNKNOWN/PENDING_RECONCILIATION, query backend by operation/order ID, and have backend verify provider state. Never blindly start a fresh payment. Local optimistic order state is provisional. Client clock cannot decide expiry; use backend/provider state and authoritative timestamps.

Idempotency contract

A stable operation key identifies one business operation such as “submit quote v7 for account X” and is reused for the same retry/recovery. Server atomically stores scope/principal + key + payload fingerprint + API/semantic version + status/result and replays the same response. Same key with a different fingerprint is a conflict, not a new charge. Define endpoint/provider scope, concurrent behavior, TTL/retention, and behavior after expiry/version change. A client UUID alone and retries alone do not guarantee dedupe. Idempotency narrows duplicates only when server/provider semantics implement it; exactly-once end-to-end cannot be assumed.

Webhooks, inbox, and reconciliation

Authenticate webhooks using the provider's current documented scheme: verify signature/key/secret, raw-body/canonicalization, and timestamp/replay window exactly as specified—do not invent crypto rules. Rotate keys by provider guidance. Persist an inbox/event ledger before processing and dedupe by provider+event ID. Expect duplicate, out-of-order, and missing events. Event creation time alone cannot authorize state regression; fetch current provider object/version when needed, apply legal monotonic transitions, and record ignored/conflicting reason.

Fast receipt/ACK is transport handling, not settlement. A durable worker processes inbox; polling/status lookup and scheduled reconciliation repair missing webhooks and aged ambiguous states. Measure webhook lag, signature failures, duplicates, oldest inbox item, unknown-state age, and reconciliation mismatches.

Atomicity, saga, inventory, and compensation

A Room transaction, backend DB transaction, and provider operation are not one distributed transaction. Use a saga: durable local/server state, outbox before external call, idempotent step, inbox/result, next transition. Compensation such as releasing reservation, voiding authorization, or initiating refund is itself fallible and tracked—not rollback magic. An inventory reservation has owner, quantity, authoritative expiry, and release; late capture after expiry needs explicit policy. Strong reservation reduces oversell but lowers availability/utilization; optimistic stock improves conversion but risks backorder. Server revalidates price, tax, promotion, shipping, and inventory at commitment boundaries; client cart is not authority.

Offline, PCI, and mobile security boundaries

Browsing/cart may work offline; payment confirmation needs backend/provider. Never queue a payment invisibly as ordinary background retry. WorkManager is not an exact scheduler and should not own silent payment retries; it may refresh visible pending status/reconciliation with safe idempotent reads under policy. Require fresh explicit user action when a new charge operation is needed.

Minimize PCI scope: prefer provider-hosted UI/components or platform billing and provider tokenization; custom PAN entry expands scope and operational burden. Never store/log raw PAN or CVV; CVV must not be retained after authorization even encrypted, and safer mobile design avoids receiving it outside approved provider UI. Tokens are scoped references, not universally harmless data. TLS protects transport, not compromised endpoints or business correctness. Android Keystore can protect non-exportable key material/use but does not make plaintext safe while legitimately used and does not authorize backend actions. Obfuscation/encryption do not turn shipped secrets into secrets; provider secret keys stay backend-side.

Observability, audit, and support

Propagate correlation ID, client operation ID, order ID, payment-attempt ID, and provider reference. Transition ledger records from/to/version/reason/actor/source/event, amount/currency, and redacted evidence. Logs exclude PAN/CVV/token/secret/full webhook body/PII; balance auditability against minimization, access control, and retention/deletion law. Dashboards cover payment-state funnel by approved dimensions, ambiguous count/age, authorization→capture age, reservation expiry/release, webhook/inbox lag, dedupe conflicts, reconciliation mismatch, refund age, fulfillment-after-cancel, and support cases. Support tools expose a safe timeline and authorized, audited reconcile/refund actions.

Reliability, security, and testing

Backend enforces authenticated account partition/ownership, amount/currency/quote version, rate limits, and conceptual replay/fraud controls; never trust client or redirect fields. Use a fake provider with deterministic clock plus provider contract/sandbox tests. Test duplicate/reordered/dropped webhooks; timeout after provider success; app/process death during challenge; redirect replay/tamper; concurrent same/different idempotency payload; authorization/capture/void; partial capture/refund; dispute; reconciliation; inventory expiry/oversell; Room/backend migrations; old/new state-machine versions; and property/model tests proving every generated transition preserves money/order invariants. Sandbox proves integration shape, not production rail behavior.

Failure matrix

FailureState/responseRepair
Offline before confirmationCart retained; no success/charge queuedUser resumes explicit checkout online
Timeout after provider successUNKNOWN, no new attemptSame key + backend/provider lookup/reconcile
Process death in 3DS/browserSafe order reference onlyReturn hint then backend verification
Duplicate/out-of-order webhookInbox dedupe/legal transition guardFetch provider current state
Missing webhookState age alarmPolling/reconciliation
Reservation expiresNo silent fulfillmentReprice/re-reserve/cancel or explicit policy
Capture succeeds, DB write failsAmbiguous durable provider effectProvider query + inbox/reconcile, then order transition
Refund succeeds, response lostREFUND_PENDING/UNKNOWNReuse refund operation key/status lookup
Account switch/replayReject partition mismatchFence local work; server ownership check
Currency/amount mismatchFail closedRecreate from authoritative quote

Guarantees and non-guarantees

  • Exactly-once end-to-end cannot be assumed; idempotency narrows duplicates only with implemented server/provider semantics.
  • Payment UI success is not durable order confirmation; local optimistic order state is provisional.
  • Webhook receipt is not necessarily settlement; HTTP 2xx/provider acceptance/authorization/capture/settlement/fulfillment/business success differ.
  • Room, backend DB, and provider are separate atomicity boundaries; saga compensation can also fail.
  • WorkManager is not an exact scheduler and must not own silent payment retries.
  • Return URL/deep link is a hint; backend/provider verification is authority.
  • Clock/client timestamps are not authoritative.
  • Refunds do not instantly erase settlement/fulfillment effects.
  • TLS/Keystore/obfuscation do not make shipped secrets or a compromised endpoint safe.
  • Play Billing and payments policy are version/region/distribution sensitive; verify current official guidance.

Decision framework

  1. Classify product/rail and current policy: digital versus physical/service, region/distribution, authorization/capture/refund needs.
  2. Define journeys, money/inventory/fulfillment invariants, terminal states, and cost of false success.
  3. Draw cart→quote→order and separate payment state machines; name every authority and atomic boundary.
  4. Select hosted/provider UI versus custom entry by UX, capability, and PCI/security scope—not styling alone.
  5. Specify idempotency, ambiguous recovery, webhook inbox/reconciliation, and reservation/compensation.
  6. Finish with account authorization, audit/privacy, support, metrics, failure matrix, tests, and versioned evolution.

Trade-offs and evolution

Hosted UI/tokenization minimizes card-data exposure but limits styling/control; custom entry raises PCI/security/testing burden. Immediate capture simplifies flow but reduces cancel-before-fulfillment flexibility; delayed capture risks authorization expiry and needs reconciliation. Strong inventory reservation reduces oversell but ties stock; optimistic inventory improves availability but increases backorder/compensation. Longer idempotency/event retention improves replay repair but costs privacy/storage. Polling repairs missing webhooks but costs provider quota. Evolve through versioned state/event schemas, additive fields, tolerant readers, expand-contract DB migration, dual-read/shadow reconciliation, and measured cutover; never silently reinterpret old terminal states.

Production incident

After 3DS, the provider authorizes payment but the mobile return is lost. App timeout marks the attempt failed; WorkManager silently creates a new UUID and retries the charge. The second webhook arrives before the first: two captures, one order. Containment: stop silent retries, mark affected orders unknown, query provider by merchant/order references, and void/refund duplicates with support audit. Root cause: UI callback was authority, keys were per attempt, inbox lacked legal transition guards. Fix: stable business key+fingerprint and response replay, backend status authority, event inbox/reconciliation, separate states, and ambiguity-age alerts.

Code-review/design trap

Trap: Double total, client sends amount, app stores card data encrypted in Room, marks PAID on provider UI callback, and a OneTimeWorkRequest retries charge with a fresh UUID. This enables rounding drift, tampering, PCI expansion, false confirmation, and duplicate charges. Replace it with Money currency+minor units/exact decimal, server quote/order snapshot, provider-hosted tokenization, stable operation key+fingerprint, backend verification, and explicit unknown/reconcile path.

Likely practice Q&A

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: Where do you start a payment design? A: Product/rail/policy, journeys, money/inventory invariants, failure cost, and authorities.
  2. Q: Are cart, order, and payment one object? A: No: mutable intent, commercial snapshot/lifecycle, and money workflow need separate identities/states.
  3. Q: How do you model money? A: Integer minor units or exact decimal + currency + explicit scale/rounding, never binary float.
  4. Q: When show confirmed? A: Only after durable backend order state; UI/provider callback is a hint.
  5. Q: How prevent duplicate charge? A: Stable business key, server record/fingerprint/replay, provider semantics, and reconciliation.
  6. Q: What after timeout? A: UNKNOWN; look up the same operation/order, verify provider, never blind new charge.
  7. Q: Is a webhook truth? A: Authenticated input; dedupe/inbox/legal transition, current-state fetch, and reconciliation.
  8. Q: Where is atomic transaction? A: Room, backend DB, and provider are separate; saga/outbox/inbox bridge them and compensation is tracked.
  9. Q: Offline payment? A: Browse/cart can work; confirmation needs backend/provider and no invisible queued charge.
  10. Q: How do you test? A: Fake provider, sandbox/contracts, failures/reorder/duplicates/process death, model/invariant/migration tests.

Senior follow-ups

  1. Design split shipment with delayed/partial capture, authorization expiry, and partial cancellation.
  2. Define idempotency scope/TTL/version migration when a mobile client outlives a server release.
  3. Build reconciliation for missing/out-of-order webhooks without unsafe state regression.
  4. Compare reserve-before-pay and pay-before-reserve for oversell, abandonment, and compensation.

Unanswered self-checks

  1. Which exact durable fact permits fulfillment, and what prevents it twice?
  2. How do you prove outcome if a process dies between provider success and backend commit?
  3. What are idempotency scope, fingerprint, retention, and expired-key semantics?
  4. Which payment/audit data is truly needed, who can access it, and when is it deleted?

English answer skeletons

30-second answer

“I start by classifying digital versus physical goods and current store/payment policy, then define money, inventory, order, fulfillment and refund invariants. Cart, order and payment are separate models and order/payment have separate server-enforced state machines. The backend owns amount, currency, authorization and durable confirmation; hosted provider UI minimizes PCI scope. A stable business idempotency key, inbox/outbox and reconciliation handle duplicate and ambiguous outcomes. A UI success or webhook receipt is not final business success.”

2-minute answer

“I ask about product type, region/distribution policy, authorization versus capture, partial shipment/refund, scale, inventory contention, offline UX and audit retention. Money uses minor units or exact decimal with currency and explicit rounding, never binary floating point. The server revalidates cart prices, tax, promotions, shipping and stock and creates an immutable order snapshot plus reservation. Order and payment have independent versioned state machines with legal transitions, reason codes and server-side invariants. A stable operation key is bound to principal, payload fingerprint and semantic version; the server stores and replays the result, while provider idempotency is used where documented. Hosted/provider UI tokenizes data and keeps raw PAN/CVV away; TLS, Keystore and obfuscation are not backend authorization or secret storage. Redirects are hints: after 3DS, timeout or process death, the app queries backend and the backend verifies provider state. Signed webhooks enter a deduplicating inbox; duplicates, reordering and loss are repaired by monotonic transition guards, polling and reconciliation. Room, backend DB and provider cannot share one transaction, so durable outbox/inbox and a saga track compensation, inventory release, void or refund. I expose provisional local states honestly, never silently retry a charge with WorkManager, and test fake-provider contracts, timeout-after-success, duplicate/reordered/missing webhooks, process death, refunds, migrations and state-machine properties.”

Official references

  • Google Play — Payments policy; Android Developers — Play Billing; Integrate Play Billing; Backend integration
  • PCI SSC — Tokenization Guidelines; PCI SSC — Data storage do’s and don’ts; PCI SSC — Card verification code FAQ
  • Android Developers — Android Keystore; Security best practices; WorkManager task scheduling
  • EMVCo — EMV 3-D Secure; IETF RFC 9110 — HTTP semantics
System design: auth, analytics and feature flagsexpand / collapse

Objective and senior mental model

Design three separate but integrated platform subsystems: auth establishes session context, analytics asynchronously measures permitted facts, and feature flags provide a versioned policy snapshot. This is a cross-cutting design, not one “SDK manager”: each has a separate owner, storage, failure domain, privacy/security contract, and data/control plane. Stage 30 deliberately avoids Stage 31 migration-program depth and Stage 32 leadership depth.

Requirements and ownership checklist

  • Auth owner: identity-provider/backend contract, redirect registration, token/session lifecycle, account partitioning, and revocation incident path; mobile owns external-user-agent integration, local session state, secure-use boundary, and UX.
  • Analytics owner: product taxonomy/schema registry, consent purpose, retention/deletion, ingestion/data quality, and consumers; mobile owns validation, queue, upload, and context snapshot.
  • Flags owner: typed registry, owner/purpose/default/expiry, rollout/experiment policy, invariants, and removal; mobile owns the validated snapshot, safe fallback, and exposure integration.
  • Shared requirements: anonymous/signed-in journeys, multi-account/logout, cold start/process death/offline, accessibility, latency/battery/storage/network budgets, supported versions/providers, threat model, audit, incident rollback, and testability. Define SLOs and quotas as product variables, not invented constants.

Architecture, dependency graph, and data flow

build config ───────────────→ safe local defaults
                                  ↓
Keystore-backed key use → Auth/session owner → immutable Context(account/session/device*)
         ↕ IdP/browser          ↓                    ↘
backend auth/resource APIs ← token coordinator       Flag client ← control plane
         │                       │                    ↓ validated snapshot
         └──── authorization ────┴→ product features ─┬→ exposure decision
                                                     ↓
consent → event API → schema/PII validator → durable bounded queue → uploader
                                                     ↓
                      analytics ingestion validation/dedupe → warehouse
separate observability pipeline ← health/latency/errors (redacted)

device* means a privacy-appropriate pseudonymous app-instance identifier, not hardware identity. Dependency direction is minimal local config → auth restore → consent/context → validated flag snapshot → features; analytics must not block auth or essential UI. A control-plane outage in flag or analytics configuration must not stop auth/resource data-plane calls. The feedback loop “analytics is green, so grow rollout” needs independent guardrails because telemetry loss can look like health.

AUTH — vocabulary, OAuth 2/OIDC, and trust boundaries

Identity is a subject/account representation; authentication is evidence establishing a principal/session; authorization is the server decision for a resource/action; session is bounded authenticated continuity; account is a product/tenant data boundary; device/app instance is execution/routing context, not a person. OAuth 2 is a delegated authorization framework; OIDC adds identity claims, ID tokens, and discovery. An access token calls a resource server; a refresh token obtains new tokens; an ID token is not a generic API bearer token.

Native apps use Authorization Code + PKCE through an external user-agent such as the browser/Custom Tabs or a provider-supported system flow, not an embedded WebView for general OAuth login. Generate a high-entropy code_verifier, send its derived challenge, and retain the verifier only for that transaction. Validate the exact registered redirect URI/App Link, verified HTTPS association where supported, expected issuer/client, one-time state binding, and OIDC nonce. The authorization server validates code, redirect, and PKCE; the backend/resource server validates signature, issuer, audience, expiry, scopes, and authorization. PKCE does not replace redirect, state, nonce, issuer/audience/scope, or server validation. Ship no client secret in the APK: TLS and obfuscation do not make shipped secrets safe.

AUTH — tokens, refresh, errors, and session state machine

SIGNED_OUT → AUTHORIZING(state, nonce, verifier) → EXCHANGING → ACTIVE
    ↑              ↘ CANCELLED/REDIRECT_REJECTED       ↓ expiry/401
    └ REVOKED/LOGOUT ← AUTH_BLOCKED ← REFRESHING(single-flight)
                              ↘ TRANSIENT_OFFLINE (qualified cached UX)

Prefer short-lived access tokens. Refresh-token rotation and reuse detection are authorization-server/provider policies, not a client-created guarantee. A token coordinator snapshots the token generation; concurrent 401s join one single-flight refresh using a Mutex/shared Deferred, then eligible callers retry exactly once only when request semantics are safe and replayable. HTTP 401 retry is unsafe for arbitrary non-idempotent operations; use endpoint idempotency and status reconciliation. A 401 is authentication/session evidence; 403 is authorization denial and normally not refreshable; timeout/DNS/5xx is a transient network/service failure and must not silently sign out. Account-disabled, consent-required, and provider codes need explicit mappings.

Use token expiry with bounded server/provider guidance for clock skew and a monotonic elapsed timer only within the same boot where appropriate; local wall time is not authority. Refresh failure taxonomy distinguishes invalid/revoked credentials from transient reachability. A connectivity callback does not prove backend reachability. Offline UX may expose qualified cached data while marking the session unverified; sensitive mutations wait for backend authorization.

AUTH — storage, accounts, logout, and platform APIs

Partition token set, generation, caches, queues, and work by immutable account/tenant key. On account switch, fence the old generation, cancel requests/work, clear memory, detach observers, activate the target partition, and only then rebuild context; never execute account A work as B. Logout clears local tokens, keys, and data under policy, cancels work, resets flags/context, and requests provider/backend revocation where supported. Logout cannot guarantee immediate invalidation without server support; processed requests remain, access tokens may live until expiry, and other devices require server session controls.

Android Keystore can keep key material non-exportable and gate key use under its threat model; it does not protect plaintext after legitimate use, logs, screenshots, memory, accessibility abuse, or a compromised unlocked runtime. Biometric is a local user-presence/key-use gate, not proof of remote identity or backend authorization. Credential Manager and passkeys provide conceptual credential mediation and public-key authentication, but availability, API shape, provider behavior, restore/sync, and fallback are Android/Jetpack/Play-services/provider/version-sensitive: follow current official docs and validate the backend ceremony. Do not invent a universal passkey UX or store a client secret.

ANALYTICS — taxonomy, schema, and identity

Use a reviewed schema registry: stable semantic event name, version, purpose/owner, required and optional typed fields, allowed enums/ranges, PII classification, retention, and deprecation. Prefer business facts such as checkout_submitted over widget names. Source timestamp records client observation; ingestion timestamp records server receipt. Event timestamp is not trusted global order. An envelope may contain event ID, schema version, source time, session ID, and privacy-approved pseudonymous user/app-instance IDs; do not use raw email, phone, or advertising ID by default. Anonymous→signed-in transition links only through an explicit privacy/backend policy; never unsafe-merge profiles merely because one device logged in.

Consent is purpose-specific state, not one boolean. Data minimization precedes collection; a PII denylist catches known hazards, but an explicit field allowlist/schema is the positive boundary. Never include access/refresh tokens, authorization headers, credential payloads, payment/chat content, or arbitrary exception/request bodies. Local validation rejects or quarantines malformed/unknown fields; server ingestion revalidates schema, size, tenant, consent metadata, and abuse limits.

ANALYTICS — queue, delivery, and data quality

CREATED → VALIDATED → PERSISTED → BATCHED → IN_FLIGHT → ACKED → DELETED
             ↘ DROPPED(policy/schema/consent/quota)
PERSISTED/IN_FLIGHT → RETRY_WAIT(backoff+jitter) → BATCHED
corrupt/full → QUARANTINE or bounded DROP with health counter

Persist before scheduling when durability is required; use bounded queue bytes/count/age, batch limits, compression, authenticated upload, exponential backoff with jitter, server Retry-After, network/battery constraints, and quotas/backpressure. Sampling follows documented policy before upload or carries weights; never sample mandatory audit/security data into product analytics. At-least-once-oriented retry can duplicate: a stable event ID permits ingestion dedupe within documented retention, but delivery, order, and exactly-once are not guaranteed. Preserve local sequence only as a diagnostic/session hint; batches can be late, duplicate, or out of order after offline/retry. Server consumers use event IDs, ingestion partitions, and business versions rather than trusting source timestamps as global order.

Schema evolution is additive/versioned with tolerant readers, dual validation, and deprecation telemetry; a meaning change requires a new event/version, not silent reuse. A data-quality owner monitors reject/unknown/duplicate/late rates, required-field nulls, cardinality, volume, and producer version. Product analytics remains separate from operational observability: crash, latency, and queue health have different purpose, access, retention, and sampling.

FEATURE FLAGS / REMOTE CONFIG — registry and snapshot

A typed registry entry includes key/type, owner, purpose, safe local default, allowed range, expiry/removal issue, dependencies/invariants, audience, privacy classification, and whether it is an experiment or kill switch. Build-time config selects an immutable endpoint/environment/capability and must not contain secrets; runtime config tunes behavior inside a shipped safe envelope. Flags are neither authorization nor secret storage, and auth state must not be controlled solely by Remote Config.

LOCAL_DEFAULT → CACHE_LOADED(last-known-good) → FETCHING → FETCHED_UNVALIDATED
       ↑                  ↑                         ↓ validate schema/type/version/invariants
       └ FALLBACK/REJECTED ← MALFORMED          ACTIVATED(snapshotVersion)
ACTIVE → STALE_OFFLINE; next valid activation atomically replaces whole snapshot

Separate fetch from activate: fetch success does not imply activation or valid business invariants. Validate signature/transport/provider contract where applicable, schema, types, ranges, dependencies, and mutually exclusive states, then atomically publish an immutable snapshot; retain last-known-good plus local default. Cache expiry/min-fetch intervals and real-time update APIs are provider/version-sensitive. Real-time config is not hard real-time; stale flags may persist offline or until process/fetch/activation, so an offline kill switch cannot guarantee immediate effect.

FEATURE FLAGS — targeting, experiments, and safety

Provider/server-side targeting can return evaluated values while some systems expose client-visible rules/parameters; assume a motivated client can inspect or alter any shipped or evaluated client state. Deterministic bucketing hashes the experiment/flag ID (or salt) plus a stable, privacy-appropriate unit key into a fixed bucket range with a specified algorithm, and the allocation maps buckets to variants; changing the key or the salt reshuffles assignments (churn). Sticky assignment persisted locally or owned by the server can reduce churn but complicates deletion, cross-device consistency, and experiment contamination. Deterministic bucketing does not guarantee statistically valid experiments: allocation, eligibility, sample-ratio mismatch, interference, novelty, and analysis still matter.

Emit experiment exposure only when the user actually receives/renders the treatment or crosses the precisely defined exposure boundary, not at fetch, activate, assignment, or app startup. Include experiment, variant, and snapshot attribution consistently. A staged rollout uses cohorts, guardrails, and stop criteria; a kill switch has safe default/LKG semantics; a circuit breaker/fallback protects a failing data-plane dependency without trusting analytics alone. Validate dependencies such as A requires B, invariants, and unsupported combinations before activation. Expired flags fail CI/registry review, are disabled, have code paths and analytics removed, and have server keys deleted to control flag debt.

Integration: startup, logout, account switch, and consent

Cold start/process death/offline: (1) load immutable build config/local defaults; (2) open account-partitioned encrypted-as-designed stores and recover queue integrity; (3) restore auth metadata/token handle without assuming validity; (4) load consent; (5) load and validate the LKG flag snapshot for anonymous/account context; (6) publish one immutable context generation; (7) start features; (8) asynchronously refresh session/config and upload eligible analytics. Network failures degrade independently.

Logout: bump generation and fence calls → cancel/join refresh and account work → revoke server/provider if reachable → clear local credentials and sensitive account data → purge or reclassify queued events under consent/retention policy → reset flags to an anonymous safe snapshot → publish signed-out context. Account switch: perform old-account teardown, never merge profiles, then open the target partition and fetch the target session/flags. Consent withdrawal: stop new collection immediately for that purpose, delete/quarantine local queued data, propagate the backend deletion request/status, and reset identifiers as policy requires; local deletion alone does not satisfy backend deletion.

Every request, event, and exposure captures a consistent context generation including account pseudonym, session, consent version, and flag snapshot/experiment rather than reading mutable globals field by field. Analytics must not gate auth availability; flag failure must not erase auth; an auth transition rotates account-scoped analytics/flag context without an unsafe anonymous-profile merge.

Failure matrix

FailureClassification / safe responseRepair / evidence
Redirect replay/tamperAuthentication transaction rejected; consume state onceValidate URI/state/nonce/verifier/issuer; audit redacted reason
Concurrent 401 stormOne refresh; waiters retry once only if safeGeneration/single-flight metrics and MockWebServer race test
403Authorization failure, no refresh loopBackend policy/support path
Timeout/5xx/offlineTransient; keep qualified session/cache, no forced logoutBackoff/jitter and reachability probe
Token revokedAUTH_BLOCKED/signed out for the affected sessionClear/fence and explicit re-auth
Queue corrupt/full diskQuarantine/drop by bounded policy; product flow continuesIntegrity recovery, counters, storage pressure test
Consent withdrawnStop purpose collection; local purgeBackend deletion workflow with auditable status
Schema mismatchClient reject/quarantine; ingestion rejectRegistry compatibility and producer alert
Duplicate/reordered uploadDedupe window; no source-time ordering claimEvent IDs and version-aware consumer
Stale/malformed flagsReject candidate; LKG/local defaultSnapshot validation and age alarm
Kill switch while offlineStale value may persistSafety in local default/circuit breaker; refresh on reconnect
Flag dependency violationReject whole snapshot/fail closed for risky featureInvariant test and owner alert

Guarantees and non-guarantees

  • PKCE does not replace redirect/state/nonce/issuer/audience/scope/server validation.
  • Keystore protects key material under its threat model, not a compromised unlocked runtime; TLS/obfuscation do not make shipped secrets safe.
  • Logout cannot guarantee immediate invalidation without server support; retrying HTTP 401 is unsafe for arbitrary non-idempotent operations.
  • A connectivity callback does not prove backend reachability.
  • Analytics delivery, order, and exactly-once are not guaranteed; a source event timestamp is not trusted global order.
  • Local deletion does not itself satisfy backend deletion.
  • Remote Config fetch success does not imply activation or valid business invariants; stale flags may persist offline, and real-time config is not hard real-time.
  • Flags cannot enforce authorization or protect secrets; auth state cannot depend solely on a flag.
  • Deterministic bucketing does not guarantee statistically valid experiments.
  • CI green does not prove privacy/compliance.

API/provider/version-sensitive guidance

Pin and verify current Android/Jetpack/provider docs for Credential Manager/passkeys, biometric authenticator and key invalidation, Keystore capabilities, verified App Links, Custom Tabs, backup/restore, and process/background behavior. OAuth/OIDC discovery, token rotation/reuse, revocation, logout, passkey ceremony, and refresh semantics are IdP/backend contracts. Remote Config min-fetch/cache/real-time activation and Analytics upload limits/consent APIs vary by SDK/provider/version; wrap them behind your contracts and test pinned versions. The server validates authorization, token audience/scope, schemas, quotas, and deletion regardless of the client SDK.

Decisions, trade-offs, and evolution

Longer sessions improve continuity but enlarge the revocation window; stronger local presence gates add friction without replacing server identity. Durable analytics improves offline coverage but costs storage/privacy and increases late duplicates; aggressive sampling lowers cost but weakens cohort analysis. LKG flags improve availability but retain stale risk; local safe defaults reduce blast radius but may disable value. Sticky assignments reduce churn but complicate deletion and cross-device semantics. Evolve with versioned auth/session contracts, additive event schemas, a typed flag registry, capability negotiation, shadow validation, and measured rollout; do not silently reinterpret old events or token/account partitions.

Observability, testing, privacy, and security

Keep separate redacted operational metrics: auth state/refresh waiters/outcome/latency, redirect rejects, 401 vs 403 vs transient errors; analytics queue bytes/age/drop/reject/duplicate/late/upload latency; flag snapshot version/age/fetch-vs-activate/reject reason/exposure and dependency failures. Bound cardinality and include no tokens, raw IDs, payloads, or PII. Audit access, retention/deletion, and sampling; privacy/security review covers data flows and threat model, not only code.

Deterministic tests with fake clock/IdP/ingestion/config plus real storage fixtures cover concurrent refresh and one safe retry; redirect replay/tamper; process death during auth/queue/fetch; account switch and stale-generation fencing; token revocation; queue corruption/full storage; consent withdrawal plus backend deletion workflow; schema mismatch; duplicate/reordered/late upload; stale/malformed config; deterministic bucketing vectors and key change; offline kill switch; dependency/invariant rejection. Add contract tests for audience/scope, event registry/ingestion, and provider APIs; property/state-machine tests; upgrade/backup fixtures; and end-to-end privacy assertions. CI green is evidence, not compliance proof.

Realistic production incident

A refresh token expired during a campaign. Twenty parallel API calls each refreshed independently; provider rotation detected reuse, some requests retried non-idempotent writes, and a remote flag increased rollout because analytics uploads were failing and the dashboard treated missing errors as success. Users oscillated between signed out and signed in, and duplicate writes occurred. Containment froze rollout server-side, disabled unsafe retry, fenced affected sessions, and reconciled operation IDs. Root cause was no single-flight/generation, collapsing 401/403/network into one error, and a telemetry-dependent positive feedback loop. The fix added one refresh coordinator, retry-once eligibility, server idempotency/status lookup, an independent rollout guardrail, missing-telemetry alarms, and control/data-plane isolation.

Code-review/design trap

Trap: a singleton PlatformManager reads mutable currentUser, logs arbitrary event maps with bearer headers, calls fetch() and assumes activation, stores a provider secret in BuildConfig, refreshes every 401, and uses new_ui_enabled to bypass backend role checks. Tests are green. Block it: immutable generation-scoped context, typed separated interfaces/stores, token redaction and schemas, single-flight safe retry, validate-and-activate snapshot, no shipped secret, server authorization, and privacy/contract/failure tests.

Likely practice Q&A

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: How do you separate the three subsystems? A: Auth owns session/identity context, analytics owns the consented event pipeline, and flags own the typed policy snapshot; integrate through versioned context/contracts.
  2. Q: What does PKCE provide? A: It binds code exchange to a verifier and mitigates interception, but does not replace redirect/state/nonce/server validation.
  3. Q: How do you handle twenty concurrent 401s? A: One single-flight refresh for the token generation; safe callers retry once, others reconcile or do not retry.
  4. Q: How do 401, 403, and timeout differ? A: Authentication/session, authorization, and transient network/service failures require different states and UX.
  5. Q: Does biometric authenticate the backend? A: No; it is a local user-presence/key-use gate, separate from backend session and authorization.
  6. Q: What is analytics delivery semantics? A: A bounded durable queue and at-least-once-oriented retry allow loss, duplicates, and reorder; never promise exactly-once.
  7. Q: When do you emit an exposure event? A: Only when treatment is actually exposed at the defined boundary, not during fetch or assignment.
  8. Q: Fetch versus activate? A: Fetch obtains a candidate; validation plus activation atomically publishes it, otherwise use LKG/default.
  9. Q: Can a flag protect an admin action? A: No; a UI flag is not authorization, so the backend checks principal, audience, scope, and role.
  10. Q: How do you switch accounts? A: Fence the generation, cancel and clear the old partition, never merge profiles, then open target session/flags/context.

Senior follow-ups

  1. How would you formally define a retry-safe endpoint if refresh succeeded but the original non-idempotent response was lost?
  2. How does consent withdrawal propagate through local queue, ingestion, warehouse, derived tables, and backups with auditable status?
  3. How can a stable bucketing key survive anonymous→signed-in transition without a privacy-unsafe merge or sample contamination?
  4. How does a kill switch behave with a stale offline snapshot while its analytics control signal is partially unavailable?

Unanswered self-checks

  1. Which component can atomically change the account/context generation, and who fences stale callbacks?
  2. Which events and fields are necessary, for which purpose, retention, and deletion SLA?
  3. Which flag combinations are invalid, and what is safe behavior without the control plane?
  4. How do you prove an analytics outage cannot automatically accelerate a dangerous rollout?

English answer skeletons

30-second answer

“I separate auth, analytics, and flags into owned failure domains. Auth uses Authorization Code with PKCE in an external user-agent, verified redirects, short-lived access tokens, generation-aware single-flight refresh, account partitioning, and backend authorization. Analytics uses consented typed schemas, a bounded durable at-least-once-oriented queue, server validation, and no sensitive payloads. Flags use a typed registry, safe defaults, validated last-known-good snapshots, deterministic privacy-aware bucketing, and real exposure events. Startup publishes one consistent context; logout, account switch, consent change, offline state, and process death have explicit teardown and recovery.”

2-minute answer

“I start with ownership, journeys, privacy and failure boundaries. Identity, authentication, authorization, session, account and device are distinct. A native app uses OAuth Authorization Code plus PKCE through an external user-agent; state, nonce, verifier and exact verified redirect each have separate replay/tamper duties. The backend validates issuer, audience, scope and authorization. Access tokens are short-lived; concurrent 401s join one generation-aware refresh and eligible requests retry once, while 403 and transient network failures follow different paths. Tokens and all work are partitioned by account; biometric only gates local presence, Keystore has a bounded threat model, and no APK secret is trusted. Analytics events come from a versioned schema registry with required fields, pseudonymous context, purpose consent, minimization and PII controls. A bounded persistent queue batches under constraints with backoff and jitter; duplicate, late, reordered and lost events are expected, so ingestion validates and deduplicates without promising exactly-once or trusting source timestamps. Product analytics is separate from observability. Flags are typed with owner, default, expiry and dependencies. Fetch is not activation: validate a complete candidate and atomically publish it, otherwise use last-known-good or local defaults. Targeting rules may be client-visible; flags never authorize or hide secrets. Bucketing is deterministic but not proof of experiment validity, and exposure fires only when treatment is actually exposed. Startup loads defaults, account storage, session, consent and a validated snapshot before asynchronous refresh. Logout and account switch fence generations, cancel work and reset context; consent withdrawal stops collection and starts backend deletion. I test races, replay, process death, corruption, stale config and failure isolation, with independent rollout guardrails so missing analytics cannot look healthy.”

Official references

  • IETF RFC 8252 — OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps; RFC 7636 — PKCE; OpenID Connect Core; RFC 7009 — Token Revocation
  • Android Developers — Verify App Links; Android Keystore; Credential Manager; Passkeys; Biometric authentication
  • Firebase Analytics documentation; Analytics data collection and consent controls; Events
  • Firebase Remote Config for Android; Loading strategies; Real-time Remote Config; Firebase A/B Testing
  • Android security best practices; Privacy and security
Migration design: XML Views→Compose, RxJava→Flow/coroutines, modularization and safe deliveryexpand / collapse

Objective, discovery, and senior mental model

A migration is not a rewrite goal. It is a controlled change to a production system for a verifiable business outcome under bounded risk. Start with business goals such as faster delivery of named journeys, reliability, accessibility, support cost, build/CI feedback, or retiring an unsupported dependency. Do not prescribe Compose, Flow, Clean Architecture, or more modules as automatic goals.

Build a pain/cost baseline: lead time, defects/incidents, crash/ANR/jank, flaky tests, and clean/incremental/CI build time. Map the dependency/build graph and critical path, runtime behavior and traces, state/data authorities, ownership/on-call, release cadence and installed-version tail, critical flows, and compatibility constraints: min/target SDK, devices/input/accessibility, backend/schema, partner SDKs, and old clients. Record unsupported assumptions, unknown side effects, and evidence gaps. Agree success, guardrail, budget, stop/pivot, and deadline criteria with product and reliability owners; do not invent metrics.

Migration strategies and exceptions

StrategyFitRisk
Big bang/rewriteSmall isolated system, short lifecycle, hard legal/vendor deadline, or unsafe-to-change legacy with a full parity lab and rehearsed cutoverLong divergence, late integration, difficult rollback
Branch by abstractionA stable contract/adapter can switch implementationsTemporary indirection can become permanent
Strangler/incremental vertical slicesLive product with independently measurable user flowsMixed-stack bridge tax, but small blast radius
OpportunisticTouch-to-migrate near low-risk product workUneven topology and no natural finish

Default to reversible incremental vertical slices, not a horizontal rewrite of every screen/operator/module: one capability crosses UI→state→domain/data→telemetry and can route back without losing data. A big bang is an exception only when the boundary is genuinely small, coexistence is riskier, the deadline is hard, and rehearsals prove cutover. Opportunistic work needs a sunset backlog or legacy never disappears.

Migration control plane

  • RFC/ADR: problem and evidence, alternatives, target and interim architecture, non-goals, compatibility, decision owner, date, and revisit trigger.
  • Rules/map: allowed dependency directions, forbidden new legacy edges, current→interim→target topology, and a slice backlog with owner, risk tier, dependencies, evidence, and deletion gate.
  • Delivery: capacity budget, risk-tier quality gates, telemetry dashboard, release cohorts, deprecation policy/deadline, and an exception path.
  • Checkpoints: named go/hold/rollback/roll-forward decisions before merge, activation, cohort growth, and deletion; incident and rollback owners are explicit.
  • Exit: bridge use is zero, legacy dependency/build wiring/flags are removed, docs/on-call are updated, and outcomes are measured. Migration complete means legacy dependencies/bridges/flags are removed and outcomes verified, not merely new code added.

Dependency/topology diagram

                  RFC/ADR + migration map + risk gates + telemetry
                                      │
App composition root / Nav host ──────┼──────── release flag (routing only)
        │                             │
 legacy Fragment/XML ─ ComposeView ─ new plain Compose UI
        │                    \         ↑ state + callbacks
 AndroidView/Binding ←──────── Compose route/state holder
        └──────────── one state owner / one navigation / one analytics authority
                                      │
 UI state holder → authoritative use case/repository contract
              Rx façade ⇄ tested adapter boundary ⇄ Flow/suspend pipeline
                                      │
      data/API/DB authority (expand → migrate/backfill → contract)

Gradle dependency direction: :app(composition root) → feature API
 feature implementation → narrow platform/data APIs; no reverse edge/cycle
Telemetry compares old/new outcomes; routing back is safe only while data/contracts remain compatible.

Migration-slice template

  • Outcome/scope: user journey and business goal; explicit non-goals.
  • Baseline: current runtime trace, owner, dependencies, cost/quality metrics, critical states, and characterization tests.
  • Semantics: source of truth; lifecycle/scope; threading, cancellation, error and backpressure; restoration, navigation, analytics, accessibility, and compatibility.
  • Change: old/interim/target topology, adapters, public API/resources/schema, ownership, and deletion issue.
  • Risk/delivery: tier, flag limits, dark/shadow policy, cohorts, guardrails, halt threshold, rollback, and roll-forward for irreversible state.
  • Evidence/exit: tests, dashboards, parity sample, support/runbook; remove old route, bridge, flag, and dependency after the observation window.

XML Views→Compose: interop and lifecycle

Migrate a leaf or complete screen boundary; do not nest View↔Compose↔View merely for migration convenience. In a View/Fragment host, use ComposeView, assign a stable ID when saved state needs it, establish the correct LifecycleOwner/SavedStateRegistryOwner/ViewModelStoreOwner, and choose ViewCompositionStrategy for the host lifecycle. For a Fragment, disposal normally follows the Fragment view lifecycle. A wrong owner/strategy can retain a composition, duplicate collectors, or dispose visible UI; test recreation, back stack, and leaks.

In Compose, use AndroidView for a View and AndroidViewBinding for XML/ViewBinding. factory creates the instance; update idempotently applies current properties; listener/resource cleanup must be symmetric. Do not cache a View outside factory without proven ownership, perform analytics/network work in update, or create Fragments arbitrarily inside AndroidView. Fragment-in-Compose must follow the official interop container and FragmentManager ownership with unique IDs. Verify version-sensitive APIs against pinned Compose/Fragment/Navigation documentation.

Compose: state, restoration, navigation, and UX parity

Split a route/state-holder composable that owns ViewModel/DI, lifecycle-aware collection, effects, and navigation from a plain UI composable that takes immutable state and callbacks. A slice has one state owner; Views and Compose must not maintain two mutable copies. There is also one authority for navigation, analytics impressions, and actions. remember survives recomposition; rememberSaveable covers only a saveable boundary and is not durable storage. Restore business state from a repository/SavedStateHandle contract. Define IDs, keys, and restoration behavior before cutover.

During Fragment/Navigation coexistence, keep one back stack: Compose emits callbacks and the host navigates until a destination is fully migrated. Align Material/View theme tokens, typography, density, dark/high contrast, semantics/content descriptions, traversal/focus, keyboard/D-pad, IME, insets, system bars, dialogs, and back. RecyclerView→lazy list migration preserves stable item identity/content type, anchor ID+offset, selection/focus, and pagination; an index alone fails on reorder. Never duplicate state, analytics, or navigation across both trees.

Compose: performance, tests, and limitations

Characterize the old UI first. Use state/unit tests, semantics/accessibility tests, screenshot/golden coverage across representative fonts/themes/sizes, navigation/restoration/process recreation, View↔Compose integration, and baseline/macrobenchmarks for startup/scroll/jank in release/profileable builds. Compose does not inherently make UI faster; compare frame timing, allocations, and critical interactions. Baseline Profiles help compiled paths but do not repair expensive composition/layout or wrong state reads. Previews help enumerate plain UI states but do not prove lifecycle, DI/Navigation, resources/configuration, IME/insets, accessibility services, animation timing, or device rendering.

Compiling interop does not prove lifecycle/state/accessibility parity. Screenshot parity does not prove semantics/focus; semantics tests do not prove pixels/performance. Test disposal during detach/re-attach, Fragment view recreation, and pooling/reuse; inspect listener, owner, and composition leaks. Every interop layer needs an owner, telemetry, and deletion date.

RxJava→Flow/coroutines: inventory before conversion

Inventory every pipeline before code changes: Single/Maybe/Completable/Observable/Flowable; cold/hot/connectable; subscriber count and replay; empty/null/error/completion; ordering/concurrency; retry/timeout; scheduler boundaries; backpressure strategy; disposal side effects; and scope ownership. There is no safe universal 1:1 operator mapping; mechanical renaming hides semantic regressions. A suspend function often fits a one-shot result and Flow a stream, but Maybe emptiness, Completable completion, nullability, and terminal errors need explicit types/contracts.

Bridge temporarily through pinned and tested kotlinx-coroutines-rx2/rx3 adapters or one narrow adapter. Exactly one authoritative pipeline performs I/O, cache writes, and analytics; never let Rx subscribe to Flow while a reciprocal adapter feeds the same Rx chain. Every mixed Rx/coroutine boundary requires cancellation tests in both directions plus error/completion/empty, disposal cleanup, threading, and double-subscription tests.

Flow/coroutines semantic map

  • Cancellation: Rx Disposable requests disposal under an operator contract; coroutine cancellation is cooperative, so blocking/non-cancellable code must cooperate or be bounded. Structured concurrency gives the scope to the caller/UI state holder; repositories generally expose suspend/Flow, not hidden fire-and-forget scopes.
  • CoroutineContext: subscribeOn/observeOn do not map to one global dispatcher. withContext moves a suspend block; flowOn affects only upstream and preserves downstream context. Document main-safety.
  • Errors: Flow has exception transparency; catch handles upstream, not downstream collector failures. Do not swallow CancellationException. retry/retryWhen restart upstream and can repeat effects, so define eligibility, idempotency, and backoff.
  • Rate mismatch: Flow normally suspends the producer/collector chain; it is not a universal equivalent of Rx Flowable strategies. buffer, conflate, collectLatest, and drop policies alter guarantees and must be explicit.
  • Composition: combine emits latest values after every input has emitted; merge interleaves; zip pairs; flatMapLatest cooperatively cancels prior work. They are not interchangeable.
  • Hotness/events: StateFlow is conflated current state with an initial value, not an event log. SharedFlow specifies replay/buffer/broadcast. Channel.receiveAsFlow() fans out each element to one consumer, not every consumer. No collector/process death requires durable state/queue when delivery matters.
  • Lifecycle/callbacks: use repeatOnLifecycle/collectAsStateWithLifecycle as appropriate. repeatOnLifecycle stops/restarts collection but does not fix wrong upstream scope/sharing. callbackFlow registers callbacks and awaitClose unregisters; handle trySend failure.

Virtual-time tests use runTest, a shared TestCoroutineScheduler, test dispatchers, and explicit runCurrent/advanceTimeBy/advanceUntilIdle. Assert cancellation, retry timing, latest cancellation, hot replay, and no leftover jobs. Virtual time does not model real blocking or thread races.

Legacy modularization: boundary before module

Distinguish package cleanup (namespace only), source sets/source modules, Gradle modules (compilation/dependency boundary), and Play dynamic features (delivery/install boundary). Choose boundaries by ownership, cohesion, change coupling, public capability, dependency/build graph, and deployment/test needs—not a layer diagram or target module count. Create a package/API seam first and invert dependencies only where it separates policy from mechanism; extract a module only when evidence justifies its cost.

Define a narrow public API, api versus implementation, dependency direction, and composition root. DI wiring, navigation contracts, resources/themes, manifests, database entities/migrations, and network DTOs need explicit owners; the app/composition root assembles implementations. Prevent cycles, reverse implementation edges, and a :common/:shared dumping ground. Binary, source, and resource compatibility differ: public signatures/defaults/inline/types, Java/Kotlin interop, resource names/themes, and manifests can break consumers even in a monorepo.

Build, compatibility, and version guidance

Module extraction does not automatically improve build time and may worsen configuration/critical path. Baseline clean builds, ABI-compatible incremental changes, implementation changes, resource changes, IDE sync, and representative CI cache/parallel critical paths. Profile Gradle/Build Analyzer/scans before and after. Version catalogs and convention plugins centralize versions/build policy; they are enablers, not architecture, and a monolithic convention plugin can broaden invalidation.

Version-sensitive: pin Android Gradle Plugin, Gradle, Kotlin, Compose BOM/compiler plugin, Lifecycle, Navigation, Fragment, RecyclerView, coroutines, RxJava, and Rx interop adapters; read their release and migration notes. Do not project current ViewCompositionStrategy, typed navigation, strong skipping, Baseline Profile, K2, or dynamic-feature assumptions onto a different pinned version. Prefer one compatibility-axis update per rehearsed slice, run consumer/build/plugin tests, and record verified combinations. Android API/device/OEM behavior and old installed clients remain runtime constraints.

Safe delivery and data evolution

Characterize critical behavior before refactoring; add golden, contract, screenshot, accessibility, migration, and performance tests where useful. A dark launch or shadow read should compare side-effect-free or sandboxed outputs. Shadow traffic can create side effects/privacy/cost, so enforce consent, redaction, rate limits, isolation, and deletion policy. A feature flag may route an implementation but cannot fix duplicate pipelines, and feature flags do not roll back incompatible persisted data.

Roll out internal→canary cohorts→small production→growth with crash/ANR/jank, latency/error, data parity, and business guardrails plus predefined halt criteria and owner. Staged rollout limits blast radius but doesn't prove safety or instantly remove installed versions. Evolve database/network/schema with expand→migrate/backfill→contract: additive tolerant readers/writers and server support first; measured migration second; remove old fields only after old-client-tail evidence. Dual-read/write needs one authority, deterministic comparison/reconciliation, divergence telemetry, and a deadline; dual-write has no atomic cross-system guarantee.

Rollback must be designed before rollout. Database migrations, server contracts, destructive writes, and privacy deletion may be irreversible; those need roll-forward/repair rather than an APK rollback. A flag cannot restore persisted bytes or schema. After an observation window, the cleanup gate removes old code/dependencies/module edges, adapters, flags, temporary telemetry, compatibility writes, and runbook debt.

Sequence for one vertical slice

  1. Choose a low/medium-risk saved-items journey outside payment/auth authority; baseline behavior, scroll/focus, Rx semantics, build graph, and metrics.
  2. Characterize repository contract, UI state, empty/error/retry, navigation, analytics, and DB schema; write the ADR, risk tier, and rollback.
  3. Create one authoritative suspend/Flow pipeline behind the existing interface; an Rx adapter keeps the old screen alive. Boundary tests prove cancellation, error, empty, and threading semantics.
  4. Build plain state-driven Compose content and host it in the Fragment via ComposeView with the right view-lifecycle strategy. Fragment owns navigation; ViewModel owns state; one analytics path exists.
  5. Preserve stable item IDs and list anchor; test recreation, process restoration, accessibility/focus/IME/insets, screenshots, and macrobenchmark parity.
  6. Route a canary, compare old/new operational and business outcomes, and halt on breach. Route back only while data stays compatible; otherwise execute roll-forward repair.
  7. Grow, observe the installed-version tail, then remove XML, Rx adapter, flag, and unused dependency. Re-measure goals and close only after outcomes are verified.

Risk register / failure matrix

FailureDetectionContainment/repair
Composition outlives Fragment viewLeak trace, duplicate collection after back stackCorrect owner/strategy; recreation regression test
View and Compose both own state/nav/analyticsDuplicate event/navigation, divergent UIOne authority; projection-only adapter
Lazy list loses anchor/focusParity replay and accessibility testStable ID+offset and deterministic fallback
Rx→Flow changes empty/error/retryContract and virtual-time boundary testsExplicit result type; revert adapter route
Cancellation swallowedActive jobs and duplicate writesRethrow cancellation, caller-owned scope, reconcile effects
Wrong hot-stream replay/fan-outRotation/multi-collector loss or duplicatesSelect StateFlow/SharedFlow/Channel/durable queue by contract
Module adds cycle/build regressionDependency rule and clean/incremental/CI profileMove composition root/API; merge/revert low-value boundary
Shadow path writes/exports dataAudit, cost, and side-effect alarmsKill shadow, isolate sandbox, purge by policy
Dual writes divergeMismatch count/ageFreeze cutover, authoritative repair/backfill
Rollback cannot read new stateDowngrade/old-client contract testsHalt and roll forward compatible reader/repair
Canary green, broad cohort failsSegmented crash/ANR/jank/business metricsStop growth, cohort-aware disable, incident runbook

Guarantees and explicit non-guarantees

  • Compiling interop does not prove lifecycle/state/accessibility parity.
  • Compose does not inherently make UI faster.
  • Flow is not drop-in Rx and StateFlow is not an event log.
  • Cancellation is cooperative.
  • repeatOnLifecycle stops/restarts collection but does not fix wrong upstream scope/sharing.
  • Feature flags do not roll back incompatible persisted data.
  • Staged rollout limits blast radius but doesn't prove safety or instantly remove installed versions.
  • Tests and CI green do not prove production parity.
  • Modularization does not automatically speed builds or enforce ownership.
  • Shadow traffic can create side effects/privacy/cost.
  • Dual-write has no atomic cross-system guarantee.
  • Rollback must be designed before rollout.
  • Migration complete means legacy dependencies/bridges/flags are removed and outcomes verified, not merely new code added.

Decision framework

  1. Name the outcome, baseline, constraints, unsupported assumptions, and stop criteria.
  2. Map runtime/build/dependency/data topology, authorities, owners, critical flows, and installed-version tail.
  3. Choose the smallest vertical seam; compare no migration, opportunistic, abstraction/strangler, and big bang.
  4. For UI, async, and modules, document semantics, lifecycle, compatibility, interop tax, and deletion gate.
  5. Design evidence, telemetry, data compatibility, rollout, rollback, and roll-forward before implementation.
  6. At checkpoints grow, hold, or pivot; finish only after legacy deletion and measured outcomes.

Trade-offs and evolution

Small slices reduce blast radius but pay mixed-stack adapter cost longer; large slices shorten coexistence but concentrate unknowns. A stable abstraction enables routing but can fossilize a poor legacy contract. UI parity separates migration risk from redesign but delays visual change. Dual-read provides evidence at latency/privacy cost; dual-write increases divergence risk. More modules can improve ownership or parallel compilation only with a suitable graph, otherwise they add configuration, ABI, and resource edges. Evolve one dimension at a time, revisit ADRs at evidence checkpoints, and budget adapters as temporary debt.

Observability and testing plan

Segment dashboards by implementation, cohort, app version, and device: route exposure; crash/ANR; jank/frame time; startup; memory/leaks; measurable accessibility failures; navigation/restoration errors; cancellation/retry/duplicate effects; Rx/Flow adapter use; data divergence/backfill age; clean/incremental/CI critical path; business completion/conversion; and support contacts. Privacy-safe correlation links route version to outcome. Missing telemetry is unknown, not success.

Test by risk: characterization/unit/property; Rx↔coroutine contract and runTest virtual time; DB/network/schema/old-client and downgrade compatibility; Fragment/View/Compose integration and process recreation; semantics/focus/IME/insets/screenshot; macrobenchmark/Baseline Profile; staged synthetic and canary evidence. Tests and CI green do not prove production parity, so checkpoints use lab and runtime evidence.

Realistic production incident

A team migrated a search Fragment. Its ComposeView composition outlived the Fragment view, while the old Rx source and a new stateIn(applicationScope) pipeline both executed searches. After rotation, two collectors wrote history and analytics. flatMapLatest could not cancel a blocking legacy call, so stale results sometimes won. The canary looked green because rotations were rare, but broad rollout increased duplicate events and jank. The team stopped rollout and routed UI back while keeping the additive schema, disabled the new writer, and reconciled history. Root cause: mechanical operator mapping, wrong scope/sharing, duplicate authority, and wrong composition disposal. The fix used Fragment-view lifecycle disposal, one pipeline behind an adapter, a cancellable/bounded bridge, request-generation fencing, rotation/cancellation tests, and cohort telemetry.

Code-review/design trap

Trap: a PR puts a ComposeView in each RecyclerView item, inflates the old layout inside AndroidView, collects both Rx and StateFlow, uses a GlobalScope bridge that swallows errors, invokes navigation and analytics twice, and exports everything from a new :common module. “It compiles and screenshots look close” is not acceptance. Require one meaningful UI boundary, one state/navigation/analytics owner, explicit lifecycle disposal, tested cancellation/error bridging, narrow APIs and direction, parity/performance/accessibility evidence, and a deletion issue.

Likely practice Q&A

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Q: Where do you start a migration? A: Business outcome, measured pain, topology/owners/constraints, unsupported assumptions, success and stop criteria.
  2. Q: Big bang or incremental? A: Default to reversible vertical slices; big bang only for a small isolated boundary with rehearsal and lower coexistence risk.
  3. Q: How do you put Compose in a Fragment? A: ComposeView with deliberate lifecycle/save-state ownership and ViewCompositionStrategy, then recreation/disposal/leak tests.
  4. Q: How do you put a View in Compose? A: AndroidView/AndroidViewBinding with factory/update/cleanup contracts and no effects in update.
  5. Q: How do you prevent duplicate behavior? A: One state, navigation, and analytics authority; plain UI takes state/callbacks and the bridge only projects.
  6. Q: Is there an Rx→Flow operator table? A: No safe universal 1:1 mapping; inventory hot/cold, error/empty, backpressure, and cancellation first.
  7. Q: Is StateFlow an event stream? A: It is conflated current state, not an event log; model replay, fan-out, and durability explicitly.
  8. Q: When should a Gradle module be extracted? A: When ownership/cohesion/dependency/build evidence justifies compile/config/API cost, not for package cleanup.
  9. Q: Does a flag guarantee rollback? A: It can route compatible code; it cannot undo DB/schema/server effects.
  10. Q: When is migration done? A: Outcomes are verified and old route, adapters, dependencies, flags, and temporary telemetry are removed.

Senior follow-ups

  1. How would you migrate checkout if data written by the new client is unreadable by a previous installed version?
  2. Design an Rx↔Flow bridge for a hot replaying source with two collectors and cancellation in both directions.
  3. How would you prove RecyclerView→LazyColumn scroll, focus, and accessibility parity through reorder and process recreation?
  4. Which build experiments show whether extracting a feature module improved the representative CI critical path?

Unanswered self-checks

  1. Which single authority performs each side effect during coexistence, and how is the duplicate path technically prevented?
  2. Which persisted/server state makes rollback impossible, and what roll-forward repair exists?
  3. Which exact cohort guardrails halt rollout, who decides, and what does missing telemetry mean?
  4. Which deletion gate proves the bridge, flag, or module edge is no longer needed?

English answer skeletons

30-second answer

“I treat migration as an outcomes-and-risk program, not a rewrite goal. I baseline business pain, runtime and build topology, ownership, critical flows, compatibility, and stop criteria. I default to reversible vertical slices with one state and side-effect authority. Compose/View and Rx/coroutine bridges are temporary, lifecycle- and semantics-tested boundaries. Data evolves expand-migrate-contract, rollout uses cohort guardrails, and rollback is designed before activation. The work is complete only when legacy bridges, flags, and dependencies are removed and outcomes are verified.”

2-minute answer

“I begin with discovery: the business outcome, measured cost, dependency and build graph, runtime behavior, owners, release cadence, installed-version tail, critical journeys, compatibility constraints, unsupported assumptions, success and stop criteria. I compare doing nothing, opportunistic change, branch by abstraction, strangler slices, and a big bang; for a live product I normally choose a reversible vertical slice because it limits blast radius and produces evidence early. An RFC/ADR defines target and interim architecture, dependency rules, risk tier, owner, budget, quality gates, telemetry, deprecation, and rollback or roll-forward checkpoints. For XML to Compose I place one meaningful interop boundary, choose ComposeView lifecycle/disposal deliberately or AndroidView factory/update/cleanup deliberately, retain one state/navigation/analytics owner, and prove restoration, accessibility, focus, IME, insets, list identity, screenshot, and measured performance parity. For Rx to Flow I inventory hot/cold, empty/null/error/completion, scheduler, retry, backpressure, replay/fan-out, and disposal before converting; there is no universal operator mapping, cancellation is cooperative, and every mixed boundary gets cancellation and error tests. For modules I choose boundaries by ownership, cohesion, and the measured graph, define narrow APIs and a composition root, and profile clean, incremental, and CI builds. Data uses expand-migrate-contract; shadow traffic is isolated; canaries have crash, ANR, jank, data, and business guardrails. Flags cannot undo incompatible data, so rollback is designed first and irreversible cases have a roll-forward repair. Finally I remove old routes, adapters, flags, and dependencies and remeasure the outcome.”

Official references

  • Android Developers — Compose migration strategy; Compose in Views; Views in Compose; Testing migration
  • Save UI state in Compose; Compose accessibility; Compose Baseline Profiles
  • Android coroutines best practices; Kotlin Flow; Coroutine cancellation; kotlinx-coroutines-test
  • RxJava 3 Javadoc; kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 adapters
  • Android app modularization guide; Optimize build speed; Profile your build
